talks.title: Droning About The Supply Chain
talks.teaser: Traces who owns a cheap consumer drone and what its chips and EULA reveal about hardware supply chain risk.
talks.summary:
The speaker compares consumer drones to operational technology, mapping the radio link, flight controller and motor drivers onto familiar industrial parts such as an HMI, a PLC and process loops. Using a budget Potensic drone and a DJI Mavic 3 Enterprise, he works through who owns and builds each product. Filings and app user agreements lead through several layered companies, and the teardown shows many unlabeled or sanded parts whose vendors are hard to confirm.

The middle section follows DJI's chip history, from Artosyn and Leadcore parts in 2016 to an in-house P1 system-on-chip in 2018 that resembles a modified Leadcore design. He highlights an end-user agreement that gives the vendor rights to users' footage and frames, and notes that drone release notes and safety documentation are vague. He also gathered about 100 GB of DJI software, and said the older releases were not encrypted.

He argues that large drone fleets behave like traditional automation, that operator training has not kept pace, and that hardware transparency will likely need legislation and third-party checks. In the Q&A he said that transparency is hard to enforce when buyers choose the lowest bid, and he left the geopolitical questions open.

talks.title: Harmonics and Oscillations and Boom
talks.teaser: Explains how compromised solar inverters and batteries could be used to disrupt grid transformers and cause long-term outages.
talks.summary:
The talk lays out speculative attacks on the electric grid that abuse distributed energy resources such as smart inverters and large batteries. The speaker argues these devices could become a real risk as more of them are deployed, even though the attacks are not considered feasible today.

The first scenario, called a swarm of harmonics, has an attacker take over many smart converters and use them to map the network by sending and listening for injected pulses. The converters would then be time-aligned so that their harmonic outputs arrive together at a chosen transformer, which could fail inside from insulation breakdown faster than protection can respond. Filters in inverters could also be altered in firmware. The second scenario uses large batteries and inverters switched on and off at 0.2 to 0.8 Hz to drive oscillations that split the network into islands and collapse it. The speaker describes restoration after a total blackout as slow, with estimates of around 14 days at best and months in the worst case.

The talk stresses that utilities cannot currently see harmonics because of anti-aliasing filters and low sampling rates. Proposed responses include higher sampling rates, anomaly detection and automatic disconnection inside devices, hard firmware limits, and protection that isolates feeders. Q&A raised timing and communication delays, firmware update control, and whether DC distribution would help.

talks.title: OT Warriors Lock It Down
talks.teaser: Defense officials outline how to fund, staff and zero-trust OT systems so critical missions stay protected.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the speaker's long frustration at trying to convince senior IT and OT leaders that operational technology underpins every mission and needs funding, skilled people and defined processes. Using a naval firefighting incident, the speaker argues that the right people must be assigned to the right jobs. Household security comparisons, from locks and monitoring to police and national response, frame how OT sensors, local defenders and national cyber teams should fit together.

The middle of the talk covers workforce and policy. The speaker has pushed since 2017 to add an OT work role to the NIST cyber workforce model, which the Department of Defense adopted, and reported a 500% increase in interest over the 18 months after the role was published. Congressional direction is cited as well: a FY22 provision that first named OT and required mapping mission-relevant terrain, and a newer requirement to study how to make attacks on critical infrastructure harder. A earlier pilot, in which a vendor installed products on a base without the risk management framework, led to a shift toward testing in labs first. The speaker also questioned charging OT and IT the same pricing for AI-based monitoring.

The close describes a new coordinating office meant to bring policy, processes, training, funding and advocacy together for OT cyber, modeled on an older office for weapon systems. The speaker urged asking cyber staff rather than OT staff for money and building training pipelines. In audience questions, the speaker noted a control framework with almost 50 fewer security controls than the IT version and acknowledged contracting hurdles at sites with long incumbent contracts. The practical takeaways are to prioritize the most critical assets, tie OT to zero trust in an adapted form, and build skilled people before buying tools.

talks.title: AI Analysis of OT Packets For SOC Analysts
talks.teaser: Explains how a local language model with protocol-aware retrieval helps SOC analysts interpret DNP3 and BACnet alert packets.
talks.summary:
Packets that trigger alerts on industrial control networks are hard for SOC analysts to read. Wireshark output is structured but says little about what a message means, so analysts often search protocol specifications or wait for on-site staff to fill in context. In a small survey of seven analysts, five said they consult protocol documents frequently, and most felt current tools only cover the basics.

The proposed system uses a local language model rather than a cloud service, because packet contents and specifications can be confidential. Instead of treating the packet as a question for retrieval, it looks up a description of the service from a dictionary keyed on the service code. It then retrieves 10 to 15 candidate passages from the specifications and reranks them by object and device keywords found in the packet. The model receives the decoded fields plus one or two passages. In a DNP3 example, the output described internal indication flags and cited the matching specification section. For a BACnet packet from a building network, it explained a request to set an air conditioner's temperature to 100 at the highest priority, and noted the device might not accept that value.

The method was compared with the bare model and with standard vector and keyword retrieval, using 110 DNP3 packets and 70 BACnet packets, 50 from open sources and 20 from a building network. Analysts rated the outputs on reliability, usefulness and time savings, and the method scored higher than the plain model. They found the service explanations helpful for deeper analysis and as a learning aid for Wireshark. They still said that telling normal from abnormal behaviour needs site context and coordination with local staff. The speaker suggested the design can extend to other protocols and additional networks.

talks.title: Extending Zero Trust To Your Vendors OR When Managed Security Services Fail
talks.teaser: Shows weak logins and a DMZ-crossing design in a vendor's OT remote access product, and how to vet such vendors.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at a planned vendor-managed remote access service for an OT environment, built on a long-standing trusted vendor relationship. During testing, switching off an OT hub produced a connection timeout instead of the expected login page. Investigation showed the DMZ gateways were routers forwarding encrypted tunnels straight to a host in OT, so no authentication happened at the edge and the firewall could not inspect the traffic.

Lab testing of the product exposed several common weaknesses. Invalid and valid usernames returned different responses, and about 40,000 names were tried in 20 minutes with no throttling and no logging before a password was entered. The default six-digit codes allowed effectively unlimited retries, and roughly 6,000 codes could be tested every two minutes, so the speaker brute-forced their own MFA in about three to four hours. A built-in admin account also existed, with credentials held by the vendor. The vendor had known of these issues since 2024, and its suggested mitigations did not remove them in the upgraded version.

The speaker argues for applying zero trust to vendors: scrutinise critical vendor products as if they were built in-house, check whether certifications such as SOC 2 and ISO 27001 cover the specific risks, know common weakness lists, and commission your own penetration tests. Framing findings as consequence and likelihood helps secure funding. A later firewall comparison showed paper criteria hid protocol differences, and lab testing changed the chosen vendor.

talks.title: Identifying And Overcoming Cognitive Bias In Detection Systems
talks.teaser: Shows how analyst and model biases blind OT security teams, and how risk context and anomaly detection can counter them.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that security operations analysts in operational technology environments carry cognitive biases that can hide new threats from them. The speaker describes availability bias, which favours noisy, memorable threats such as ransomware over slow, low-intensity activity. Confirmation bias pushes analysts toward evidence they already recognise, and anchoring keeps them fixed on signals that worked in the past. Survivorship bias narrows attention to one tool or signal. Attitudes toward automation split staff into those who trust AI blindly, those who keep things as planned, and those who reject algorithms outright.

To show why signature and indicator-based detection misses current attacks, the speaker walks through cases where attackers abused trusted tools and built-in features. In a healthcare example, lateral movement reached a remote medical imaging device through a built-in remote file copy function, with no signature to flag it. In another case, a mailbox takeover led to movement from IT into OT and the theft of turbine and vibration files. Several state-linked campaigns misused trusted routers, software and services. Individually these events look like noise. An IoT camera contacting a rare website alongside unusual SSH activity, or a compromised vendor-installed device, becomes significant once asset value and surrounding events are considered.

The practical advice moves the focus from false positives toward false negatives. Teams should rank anomalies by the importance of the asset and the potential damage, treat baselines as an ongoing process instead of fixed history, and combine several machine learning methods so their outputs can be compared. Governance should avoid depending on a single person and keep humans responsible for auditing AI tools. Analysts can challenge their own biases by asking which signals they ignore, which tools they over-rely on, and how an attacker would approach their environment.

talks.title: S4 Legend Interview: Mark Weatherford
talks.teaser: A veteran security leader reflects on career zigzags, asset management basics, AI-driven speed, and fragmented regulation.
talks.summary:
This interview with Mark Weatherford, held as part of the S4 Legend series, traces his career from a childhood fascination with electronics and Navy repair work on Teletype machines to information security leadership, startup advising and government roles. He describes his path as unplanned and says his ability to separate useful technology from overhyped pitches came from years of vendor presentations and from trusting people more than products.

He recounts a visit to Capitol Hill, where he told staff drafting electricity grid security legislation that the rules had no workable technical implementation, and he argued that lawmakers need practitioners in the room. At the Department of Homeland Security he sat with operators at the national cyber integration center to learn how they reacted to incidents. He stressed that basics such as asset management are still poorly done, and that AI speeds up both attackers and defenders. He also argued that conflicting state, federal and EU rules raise costs and pull staff toward paperwork.

Looking ahead, he said the most important professional skill is the ability to unlearn and relearn, because expertise ages quickly, and he named a continuing gap in operational technology visibility. He closed by describing his current Nvidia work, including a program that gives field CISOs a direct contact for problems with suppliers, and advised listeners to get to know their local legislators and offer their help.

talks.title: 3 Step Success Story In Semiconductors
talks.teaser: Traces how semiconductor makers shifted from shop-floor OT protection to supplier controls after a 2018 WannaCry outage.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a 2018 malware incident that halted production at a Taiwanese chip maker. Machines kept rebooting until the WannaCry strain was identified. Although the plant had segmentation and firewalls, a device that arrived infected with newly purchased equipment reached a controlling server, which spread the infection across tens of thousands of machines. The reported loss was $86 million.

The speaker then walks through a three-stage approach built over seven years. The first stage protects the shop floor: since these sites rarely patch, protection matters more than visibility. Allowlisting adds management cost on servers that change often, and many endpoint products lack support for legacy Windows versions. Intrusion prevention systems at the switch level provide segmentation and virtual patching, with a fail-safe bypass. The second stage controls what enters the factory, including equipment that must meet the SEMI E187 standard and portable media checked at a kiosk before use. The third stage covers suppliers, tiered by criticality and assessed through questionnaires based on ten critical controls, followed by evidence requests and on-site audits.

The closing message is that questionnaires alone are not enough. Periodic audits and AI-assisted review help find risky suppliers, while industry alliances work to unify questionnaires. The speaker urges organizations with highly automated OT and suppliers to adopt the staged approach before a crisis forces it.

talks.title: OT SecOps Or Bust
talks.teaser: Explores an OT SOC maturity framework and edge detection tactics that stop IT-originating threats before they reach operations.
talks.summary:
Industrial incidents often reach operational technology from IT paths, while many programs still concentrate detection inside the OT segment and lose months of lead time at the boundary. The presentation argues that defense in OT is fundamentally about time, citing partner research that most observed adversary activity happens before OT impact and that a large majority of attacks cross from IT.

It introduces a maturity stack—architecture hardening, passive tools, then active defense leaning on threat intelligence—and frames OT security operations through people, process, and technology. A collaborative framework from Palo Alto Networks, Siemens, and Idaho National Lab lays out principles such as safety-first detections, defense in depth, and IT–OT convergence without collapsing accountability. The walkthrough covers Purdue-level log sources, contextual monitoring, per-level KPIs, and why split SIEMs and weak escalation leave OT alerts uninvestigated.

A three-step edge strategy closes the loop: map edge telemetry to MITRE ICS techniques, use predictive chaining with the Attack Chain Estimator on top TTPs from large-scale firewall data, and prioritize shared log sources across attack chains before stitching IT and OT evidence in the SOC. Practitioners should treat the model as an ongoing journey rather than a one-time project.

talks.title: What Risk Have You Accepted In A Company Acquisition?
talks.teaser: Shows how to translate OT security gaps in acquired facilities into financial risk that deal teams will fund.
talks.summary:
This talk looks at how security teams can handle risk when their company acquires or divests industrial facilities. The speaker, who came up in oil and gas, argues that deal teams treat risk as a business bet, so security findings only get funded when they are framed in terms that matter to them. Three points frame the discussion: security is one input among many for a deal team, findings rarely kill a deal, and leadership needs impact described in plain language.

The method starts with the organization's corporate risk matrix, which ranks likelihood against consequences such as financial, operational, safety, environmental and reputational impact. The speaker recommends assessing at facility level, using a bow-tie analysis aligned to the 62443-3-2 standard, with loss of control as the worst case. Preventive barriers are listed and ranked, and recovery barriers such as tested backups, response plans and mechanical safety systems are credited. In one example, a flat network with internet access reaching operator workstations meant a compromise could shut in a facility with a 10 to 25 million dollar consequence, which made it unacceptable. Abandoned legacy systems in a perimeter guard shack were judged acceptable because they did not affect operations.

Remediation budget is tied to a schedule in phases: days 0 to 30 for triage to stop the worst risks, then days 30 to 60 for remediation before integration. In the Q&A, the speaker described an upstream company where exposed field internet connections were found and then funded for remediation. For very large acquisitions, the advice was to start at regional level, weighing profitability and operational risk, then move down to critical assets. The main takeaway is to use the acquirer's own risk matrix and translate findings into its terms.

talks.title: Great Debate: Human In The Loop
talks.teaser: Two debaters argue whether organizations will let AI agents act on industrial systems without real-time human approval.
talks.summary:
An industrial security debate takes up the motion that within one to three years AI will perform operational and management actions without human approval, with medium consequence incidents possible if it is wrong. Marissa argues for the proposal. She contends that organizations choose efficiency, scalability and economic pressure over perfection, that operational technology already runs thousands of automated actions a day with humans supervising rather than approving each one, and that autonomy will first appear in management and coordination layers before reaching operations.

Jalal argues against. He says the timeline is unrealistic for cyber-physical environments, where safety certification, management of change, accountability and traceability are unresolved, and where failures can cascade across dependent systems. He asks which frameworks would certify an AI agent, how such an agent would handle permit-to-work and change processes, and how an agent could reach SIL 2 or SIL 3 compliance. He compares the slow progress of autonomous cars and argues that the core issue is assurance and governance, not speed.

In the rebuttals and lightning round, the debaters clash over whether human oversight can keep pace with machine-speed data. Marissa says supervision scales while per-action approval does not, and Jalal answers that safety barriers exist for a reason and the human should stay in the loop. The session closed with a note that the motion's wording used "could" rather than "will". The takeaway is that the disagreement centers on governance, certification and accountability more than on technical capability.

talks.title: Current and Predicted Market Impact of the US Cyber Trust Mark
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Current and Predicted Market Impact of the US Cyber Trust Mark.
talks.summary:
### Overview
This presentation examines the behavioral economics and consumer security decisions surrounding Internet of Things (IoT) devices, focusing on the current and anticipated market impact of the US Cyber Trust Mark (CTM). Grounded in empirical user studies and focus groups, the speaker explores whether consumers understand security labels, whether labels alter purchasing behavior, and how labeling designs intersect with trade policy and country-of-origin biases.

### Key Topics
- **Consumer Decision-Making & Usability:** Users balance perceived costs and benefits; many default to insecure options or fail to patch because of downtime, complex privacy policies, or unusable security tools (such as PGP or hardware tokens).
- **Evolution of IoT Labeling:** Originating from initiatives dating back to 2015 and legislative efforts such as the Cyber Shield Act, security labeling programs evaluate products across defined technical baselines (e.g., Underwriters Laboratories (UL) IoT Security Top 20 principles, IEEE IoT standards, FTC, and DOT guidelines).
- **Comparative Label Testing:** Testing evaluated several formats, including binary US Cyber Trust Mark variants, UL graded shield models, Carnegie Mellon University (CMU) nutrition-style privacy labels, and a five-star/five-lock design.
- **Willingness to Pay (WTP):** Using real monetary incentives on the Prolific platform, researchers tested consumer spending choices on a simulated Amazon marketplace.
- **Country-of-Origin & Trade Policy:** An unexpected finding showed that security labels—especially binary formats—heavily interact with perceptions of foreign risk, functioning de facto as trade policy favoring US-manufactured products.

### Technical Details & Study Findings
- **Label Comprehension & Usability:** The CMU nutrition-style label produced higher factual accuracy regarding specific device features, while simple binary labels and the five-lock design yielded the best balance of helping consumers accurately identify secure devices without inducing design fatigue. The UL graded label caused confusion because consumers associated 'gold' rather than 'diamond' or 'gray' with the highest security tier.
- **Marketplace Behavior:** When given $15 to purchase a smart light bulb and retain leftover funds, consumers showed that the presence of security labels consistently reduced purchases of expensive, insecure devices (by 10% to 20%).
- **Security vs. Privacy Awareness:** Consumers who prioritized security were 28% more likely to purchase a secure product and paid approximately 20% more for secure items. In contrast, self-identified privacy-conscious consumers (roughly one in five participants) were unwilling to pay a premium for more private devices and mirrored general consumer spending.
- **Country-of-Origin Effects:** In tests comparing products labeled 'Made in China' and 'Made in Australia' (with and without FCC/DOD high-risk warning prompts), 75% of participants using binary labels chose the less secure American product over a secure Chinese alternative, even without warning prompts.
- **Focus Group Insights:** Consumers struggled to define what qualifies as an IoT device (often failing to recognize smart locks or connected cameras as IoT unless connected to specific assistants like Alexa), demonstrating that a key initial function of the Cyber Trust Mark will simply be defining the scope of consumer IoT.

### Takeaways
While immediate broad market shifts may be modest among general consumers, the Cyber Trust Mark creates immediate impact among security-conscious buyers and small-business supply chains that rely on consumer-grade hardware. Security labels penalize expensive, insecure products by aligning price signals with actual device security. Long-term adoption is expected to mirror the Energy Star model, where initial indifference gives way to high consumer reliance as familiarity grows.

talks.title: A Converged Actor Framework
talks.teaser: Maps the blurring lines between state actors, hacktivists and ransomware groups targeting OT and ICS environments.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that many owners and operators of control system environments look no further than their own plants and assume only state actors would target them. The speaker calls this a dangerous blind spot. Recent incidents point to a wider threat: the Colonial Pipeline attack, where a ransomware group halted the longest US gasoline pipeline for ten days, and a hacktivist group tied to Iranian interests that wiped logic on internet-exposed Unitronics controllers still using default passwords.

Walking through the threat landscape, the speaker describes state actors such as Sandworm, whose 2017 intrusion into a Middle Eastern petrochemical plant reached the safety system. Hacktivist attacks are frequent but rarely disrupt operations, while Jaguar Land Rover's five-week outage, which the speaker says cost over $2 billion, came from attackers working in IT. Groups such as Cyber Army of Russia Reborn appear to take direction from states, blurring the lines further. To organize these cases, the talk applies the diamond model and separates the operator at the keyboard from the owner pulling the strings.

The talk also weighs attribution: useful for understanding a campaign, but secondary while a plant is trying to restart. The closing message is that attacks are rising in frequency and could rise in impact. Owners are urged to spend about 15 minutes a week reviewing real-world incidents and asking whether the same could happen to them.

talks.title: Generating Malicious OT Data To Test Systems
talks.teaser: Shows how practitioners build representative OT traffic and logs to prove detections catch real control-system misuse and protocol abuse.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens on an uncomfortable gap in operational technology defense: many teams deploy signatures and analytics without proving those controls ever fire on genuine OT attack behavior, especially when alerts lean on threat intelligence rather than observed plant traffic. OT raises the stakes through proprietary field protocols, cyber-physical coupling, and sparse ground truth, so shallow Modbus-centric views can miss vendor-specific semantics such as Schneider UMAS under function code 90 and the blind spots that creates next to documented authentication weaknesses.

The core method starts from explicit detection intent—target behaviors like abnormal sequencing or documented breaker manipulation—then chooses the lowest-fidelity lab that still produces valid observables. Examples span a free IEC 60870-5-104 master simulator that outperformed strict OEM stacks for malware PCAP generation, paid DNP3 tooling that ingests substation configuration, Schneider M221 plus free engineering software for UMAS, and Python extensions atop open Modbus libraries for proprietary layers. The talk also covers mixed real-and-emulated ranges, factory acceptance testing captures, and costly multi-device procurements driven by supply-chain and licensing friction.

Practitioners should treat representative data generation as deliberate engineering, not guesswork: generate PCAPs and host artifacts, confirm humans can explain the hits, map exercises to MITRE ATT&CK for ICS, and balance budget versus fidelity without overspending when emulation suffices. Live operational noise remains preferable for tuning when available, while lab fidelity and capture length depend on whether the technique needs single packets or extended command sequences.

talks.title: Interview with Acting CISA Director Nick Andersen
talks.teaser: Covers the agency's OT security strategy, rebuilding its team, and measuring resilience across critical infrastructure sectors.
talks.summary:
This interview, recorded for the Unsolicited Response show, has Acting CISA Director Nick Andersen discuss the agency's operational technology security work while it operates without a Senate-confirmed director. He says the agency keeps moving on OT initiatives, is hiring additional staff, and is reshaping its sector coordination with a dedicated OT-focused council. The host raises the loss of many technical OT staff under the prior administration, and Andersen describes rebuilding the team with federal hires and special government employees drawn from industry.

The middle of the conversation covers what the agency is cutting back. Andersen describes "ruthless prioritization," narrowing effort to fewer entities tied to national security, defense, critical infrastructure, public health and safety, and the economy. He explains that the list is built by combining a view of what the nation considers important with several years of intelligence reporting on where adversaries have prepositioned access. Joint work plans with owners and operators are meant to reduce measurable risk, and federal partners may lead engagements when another agency has the better relationship.

The discussion ends with measurement and expectations. Andersen says success would be shown by a demonstrable level of persistence for essential services within 24 months, supported by vendors building products that are more secure by default and by operational requirements such as running without telecommunications for a period. He acknowledges that asset-level downtime metrics are hard to define, that regulation limits what can be forced on owners, and that a public metric is still unclear. The practical takeaway is to tie resilience planning to essential functions, define tolerable downtime, and test recovery, even at smaller utilities.

talks.title: Gaming With Metrics To Achieve An OT Security Program
talks.teaser: Shows how a medieval-themed game helped turn OT engineers into cybersecurity champions and track segmentation progress.
talks.summary:
The talk describes how a team used gamification to build an OT cybersecurity program in manufacturing. Threats to these environments keep rising and budgets grow, yet results come slowly, because engineers, operators and technicians who are not security specialists need to become security champions. The speaker argues that people remember stories, metaphors and challenges better than facts and figures, so the program was wrapped in a medieval kingdom story.

Champions first hear the story, where castles stand for central IT systems, farms and mines represent OT devices at plant level, and rivers and roads stand for the links between them. A discovery chapter follows, in which they find OT assets, then a segmentation workshop where asset pieces are placed on a pasteboard and fenced into zones that resemble a firewall zoning diagram. A story-based dashboard tracks the assets found, the context gathered about them, and a treasury of resources, and champions can see each other's progress, which adds competition.

The reported benefits include a playful tone that made people less afraid to ask basic questions, a human-level community spirit, and measurable progress from splitting large goals into smaller targets. To handle a changing environment, the team adjusts target scoring, adds new areas as challenges, and turns each new project into a chapter with its own indicators. The speaker advises starting with what motivates people, borrowing from games and storytelling, and writing your own story.

talks.title: OT Threat Predictions For The Next 1
talks.teaser: 3 Years examines OT Threat Predictions For The Next 1.
talks.summary: A morning keynote frames how geopolitics and technology shifts alter operational technology risk over the next few years. The speaker contrasts short-term flashpoints, such as Middle East force movements and reckless agent tooling on corporate networks, with longer arcs like China's Volt Typhoon pivot toward sustained critical-infrastructure access and Russia's Berserk Bear finally crossing from espionage into disruptive action in Poland. Red-flag discussions cover OT traversal policy changes, near-abroad destructive tests, and the first appearance of purpose-built OT malware. The talk then examines Russian hybrid pressure in Europe, third-party hacktivist fronts, and criminal partnerships before turning to AI-driven scale, patch-gap speed, and autonomous vulnerability discovery. Defenders are urged to treat hypothetical nation-state contingencies as present-day prevention work while embracing AI for detection and response parity.

talks.title: Honeypots For Threat Intelligence
talks.teaser: Shows how honeypots still catch real attackers, from ransomware affiliates to OT intruders, and what to plan first.
talks.summary:
Honeypots date back decades, to a 1986 case at a US national lab later documented in The Cuckoo's Egg. The talk argues the approach still yields value today. The first 2024 example was a simulated healthcare organization with an exposed email server, an RDP server, and an internal domain controller and workstation. A ransomware affiliate hit the RDP entry point, and the team made contact and negotiated, bringing the group's opening demand of about $20,000 down to $10,000.

The second case used a simulated water treatment facility with an open-source HMI and a mix of real and simulated PLCs. An intruder got in through a cross-site scripting flaw, and a group later posted screenshots and video of the attack on Telegram. The team rebuilt the timeline: default credentials, database enumeration, new user creation, defacement, removal of PLCs as data sources, changed setpoints, and disabled alarms. The speaker also cites large organizations using similar traps, such as Amazon's MadPot for capturing zero-days, and a firm whose AI-generated fake data site drew in the group ShinyHunters.

For a deployment, the speaker recommends defining goals and KPIs first, getting management and legal approval, using fake data, and filtering outbound traffic so devices cannot join botnets. Projects can move in phases, from off-the-shelf low-interaction honeypots to real devices and networks, then fake identities, documents and tokens, and finally engagement. Honeypots suit mature organizations and should come after asset inventory, threat detection and network segmentation.

talks.title: Distress Tolerance In Your Job, Life, & OT System
talks.teaser: Explores distress tolerance and DBT coping skills, such as paced breathing, for people under pressure during incidents.
talks.summary:
In this interview, psychologist Shireen Rizvi discusses her book Real Skills for Real Life, which draws on dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) and is written for a general audience rather than clinicians. She explains that DBT was first developed for people with chronic, complex mental health problems, but its concrete coping skills have spread well beyond that group. Emotions are not the enemy in her view; they become a problem when they are too intense for the situation or feel impossible to control.

The conversation then turns to distress tolerance, which aims to get through a hard moment without making it worse rather than solving the underlying problem. Rizvi separates stress, a normal adaptive response, from distress, the subjective and lasting sense of being overwhelmed. She demonstrates paced breathing, which uses diaphragm breathing, a slower cycle, and an exhale longer than the inhale, such as breathing in to a count of four and out to a count of six. She also describes wise mind as a balance between emotion mind and reasonable mind, and explains that validation and radical acceptance help people stay effective. Catastrophizing thoughts and a racing heart are cues to step away briefly.

Applied to a scenario where a water treatment system is hacked and leaders demand answers, the discussion suggests that people in charge should regulate themselves first and address emotional aftereffects once the crisis is over. Rizvi argues that practicing these skills in small everyday moments makes them available under pressure, and she suggests that the emotional side of incident response could be considered alongside the procedural plans. The main takeaway is that managing one's own emotional state is a practical part of staying effective during an incident.

talks.title: Frenos' Session In The S4x26 POC Pavilion
talks.teaser: Shows an on-prem tool that models OT networks as a digital twin and simulates attack paths to rank mitigations.
talks.summary:
The session is a vendor demonstration of a platform that helps operators assess security posture in operational technology networks and decide which mitigations to prioritize. The presenters frame the problem as a shortage of experienced OT security staff and the difficulty of running penetration tests on critical systems. Their method ingests asset and vulnerability data from existing OT visibility tools, plus firewall configuration files, builds a graph-based digital twin of the network, and has an AI reasoning agent attack that replica rather than the live environment.

The live demo ran on a laptop with no changes made to the environment. The assessed network received an F score, and removing overly permissive any-any firewall rules was estimated to cut risk by 25 to 28 percent. The presenters showed path validation between an enterprise network and an OT zone, a modeled attack path that follows a threat actor profile step by step, and a mitigation view with scored recommendations. Installation took 11 minutes and 42 seconds, and 154,000 simulations ran in about 17 minutes.

In the Q&A, the presenters said the model draws on around 4,000 sources, that accepted risk or compensating controls are fed back into the twin, and that continuous operation suits a GPU server better than a laptop. They also noted the tool does not yet recommend replacement firewall services. The takeaway is that results depend on the completeness of imported data, since visibility gaps can distort priorities.

talks.title: Dragos' Session In The S4x26 POC Pavilion
talks.teaser: Walks through an OT visibility platform that finds industrial assets, rescores vulnerabilities and flags unusual traffic.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a problem familiar to operational technology teams: many industrial devices cannot be patched, and legacy networks often have no record of which devices talk to each other. The speaker, from Dragos, set the goal as finding critical assets, the vulnerabilities that affect them, and ways to reduce risk when patching is not possible. The platform was described as a passive sensor fed by a span port, supplemented by an active query tool that polls specific targets, with a site store handling analytics and the web interface.

The demo covered a newer release with a reworked data model, role-based views and an asset inventory that records communications even when a device's identity is unknown. Vulnerabilities are scored with an OT-adjusted view that considers effects such as loss of view or loss of control, because a raw CVSS score alone does not show process impact. Detections were shown in several forms: deviations from a learned baseline with packet captures attached, indicators of compromise, and threat behavior mapped to the ICS kill chain and MITRE ATT&CK for ICS. In the question round, the speaker covered the limits of passive visibility on TLS-wrapped and wireless traffic, how credentials are handled for active collection, integrations with ServiceNow and Splunk, and how overlapping IP addresses across sites are kept apart using network IDs.

The main takeaway is that visibility is bounded by what crosses the wire, so teams should expect span-port setup to be difficult and plan for active or manual collection to fill gaps. The speaker also noted that proof-of-concept deployments are usually messy and take time to stabilise, and that adding more sensors is not always the answer.

talks.title: Calculating Return On Mitigation
talks.teaser: Shows how to compare security spending against business returns by quantifying risk, using a worked OT ransomware example.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that security investments are usually judged only by return on investment, which leaves out risk. An analogy compares two cars that reach the same speed, where the pricier one adds only a seatbelt upgrade, to show why protection deserves its own measure. The speaker then turns to industrial facilities, where modernization, analytics and agentic AI add connectivity and widen the attack surface.

The proposed measure is return on mitigation, built on a risk equation of threats times vulnerabilities times consequences. Threats cannot be removed, so the focus goes to vulnerabilities, addressed through asset inventory, patching, access controls and detection, and to consequences, addressed through tested backups and recovery. Multiplying probability by financial impact gives a quantified risk. In a ransomware example, a 0.3% probability and a $150 million estimated loss put $450,000 at risk each year. Segmentation and secure remote access costing $110,000 cut the probability to 0.1%, reducing risk by $300,000, or about $2.7 mitigated per $1 spent.

The talk compares sample projects and concludes that the right choice depends on budget, risk tolerance and regulation. Limited capital favors a project with good ROI that does not add exposure, while regulated or risk-averse organizations lean toward mitigation projects. In the Q&A, configuration-management tools for control systems were cited as delivering both risk reduction and operational gains, and data centers were flagged for depending on power and water infrastructure that often gets little cyber attention. The takeaway is to weigh ROI and return on mitigation together.

talks.title: Operation Grim Beeper: A Cyber-Physical Attack
talks.teaser: Traces the 2024 Lebanon pager attack as a hardware Trojan, linking supply chain, firmware and battery design to ICS risk.
talks.summary:
The talk examines Operation Grim Beeper, the explosive attacks on pagers and walkie-talkies in Lebanon in September 2024, treated as a cyber-physical supply chain compromise. The speaker traces the supplier network from a Taiwanese manufacturer's licensing deal to a small registered firm and a set of intermediaries, then looks at firmware that reacted to a specific signal and a battery with an unexpected extra contact.

Two proof-of-concept builds illustrate the mechanism: a 3D-printed battery mock-up that lights a hidden LED through a spare contact, and a radio-triggered heating coil that melts paraffin wax at a set temperature. The speaker compares two ways signals could have reached the pagers, an external radio network that would struggle with coverage, and an internal paging path that needs a compromised asset. He classifies the attack as a hardware Trojan with co-developed firmware inserted at design time, and maps possible outcomes in ICS environments into physical harm, asset damage, and control loss.

On standards, he finds that MITRE's EMBED threat catalog lacks a threat for malicious embedded functionality and recommends adding one. Mitigations fall into pre-deployment product validation, behavioral firmware validation, and runtime monitoring, and he notes that digital signing would not have stopped this attack. He closes with open questions about how many hardware Trojans are dormant in the field and how to assess their risk.

talks.title: Emerging Markets OT Security Regulation
talks.teaser: Compares OT security regulation across Brazil, Saudi Arabia, India and Indonesia, and how emerging-market trends shape it.
talks.summary:
The talk compares how emerging markets regulate operational technology security against EU and US models. It opens with macro trends shaping risk and investment, including supply chain diversification toward Mexico, India and Vietnam, fast urbanization with smart meter rollouts, power demand from AI compute, and limits on skills, budgets and geopolitical room. A scoring lens then weighs ease of compliance, acceptance of standards such as IEC 62443, regulator accessibility and engagement style.

Four markets are covered. Brazil has no OT-specific rule yet, as a cybersecurity framework remains in the Senate, so the speaker presents it as a window to shape policy. Saudi Arabia runs a layered regime under its National Cyber Agency, where 62443 covers much of the OT controls but must be mapped to local controls, and strict localization rules govern managed security provider licensing. India's power sector rules are still in draft, and the talk examines CERT-In's SBOM guidance, which requires machine-readable formats and extends beyond software, though it mixes static and dynamic fields and lacks compensating controls. Indonesia's compliance path remains unclear, since sector regulators named in a 2022 rule have largely not been defined and a 2023 rule sets 24-hour incident reporting.

The closing advice is that 62443 still helps in several markets, that development banks and national champions also shape rules, and that practitioners should engage regulators directly. In questions, the speaker said data protection and sovereignty sit outside this scope and a reusable rubric for new markets is planned.

talks.title: The Future With ISO 22373 for Trustworthy OT Supply Chains
talks.teaser: Shows how ISO 22373 builds verifiable trustworthiness claims across OT supply chains, using a humanoid robot procurement example.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the 2024 pager attack in Lebanon and Syria as an example of how a tampered supply chain can turn an everyday device into a weapon. Asking whether people trust their phones, the speaker defines trust as confidence that something behaves as expected, and trustworthiness as the ability to meet stakeholder expectations in a verifiable, measurable way. The same questions apply to critical infrastructure, smart factories and smart cities, where supply chains span many countries and firms of very different sizes.

An ISO working group found that existing standards covered only single use cases or single stages of a supply chain. ISO 22373 is presented as a technology-agnostic approach that divides the chain into trust domains, each setting trustworthiness targets through risk-based assessment and exchanging verifiable claims at trust interaction points. It rests on four building blocks: secure identities, proof of capabilities, a persistent link between digital claims and physical products, and standardized communication. A trustworthiness profile lets buyers and suppliers share expectations and proof, including expiry dates, without exposing intellectual property. A humanoid robot on a shop floor is the worked example, with targets for authenticity, security, safety and productivity, and expectations such as provenance certificates and conformance to ISO 10218.

The speaker closes by stressing that the standard creates transparency rather than guaranteeing trustworthiness, that no single solution fits every case, and that achieving trustworthiness is an ongoing process. In questions, certification bodies were named as one possible source of help, and existing risk assessments such as IEC 62443 were said to be reusable, with the context shaping the criteria.

talks.title: Systemic Security Issues In "SoftPLCs"
talks.teaser: Shows that soft PLCs tested across vendors allowed privilege escalation, exposing gaps in the MITRE ICS framework.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at security risks from soft PLCs, which are industrial controllers running a full operating system, often as software on a standard PC. Compared with traditional PLCs, they add shells, third-party application installs, cloud connectivity, and richer file systems such as NTFS and Unix symlinks, which widens the attack surface. The research asked whether threat models built for traditional ICS systems still hold for them.

The researchers reviewed security models from five major vendors and found that each one could be broken. They reported more than 25 vulnerabilities across more than 20 products and achieved privilege escalation on every system tested, with no single bug class affecting all of them. One example, on a Twinkat-based product, showed a low-privileged user reaching a shell and abusing a poorly protected named pipe to ask a privileged service to create a new administrator account. Other findings included tampered third-party apps, symlink abuse to alter configuration files, hijacked privileged services, and readable user private keys.

Mapping these results to the MITRE ICS framework exposed gaps in its privilege escalation and execution phases. The speaker drew four additional techniques for each phase from the enterprise framework and proposed a hybrid extension. Future work covers malware use cases such as persistence and lateral movement. The takeaway is that modern ICS needs modern threat models, and defenders may borrow IT controls such as endpoint protection and OS hardening for soft PLCs.

talks.title: Case Study: Operationalizing Multi-Source Threat Intelligence
talks.teaser: Explains how a utility team turns multi-source threat intelligence into tactic-based emulation tests on OT networks.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a utility workshop where organizations tried to agree on what is systemically important to them and how to share sensitive intelligence. The speaker argues that threat intelligence delivered as indicators such as IP addresses and hashes falls short for operational technology. The case study instead asks what an adversary is after and how it operates, then maps those tactics against the organization's own consequences and crown jewels.

The method combined several intelligence sources, prioritized tactics by overlap between actors and campaigns, and built a digital model of the environment from configuration, visibility, network and asset data. Rather than rely on a lab, the team proposed testing production OT environments with controlled emulation: agents built to resemble substation devices were placed on the same network as control RTUs, and the mapped techniques were run against them. The aim was to see whether syslog, firewalls and OT monitoring would catch the activity, and to quantify what closing each gap would cost.

The takeaways were that intelligence must be relevant and actionable for defenders, that continuous testing beats a once-a-year exercise, and that protect and detect must work together so architecture can absorb adversary activity. The framework is to be shared with other utilities and EPRI.

talks.title: Securing The Diversity In Universal Theme Park's Ride & Show Network
talks.teaser: Explains how a theme park operator secures ride and show networks, where safety timing and guest safety come first.
talks.summary:
The talk covers how Universal Creative secures attraction operational technology (AOT), the networks behind its rides and shows. These link industrial control systems, life safety PLCs, ride vehicles, animatronics and effects, all relying on millisecond timing. Because guests ride within the machinery, safety functions must fail into a safe state. One augmented reality attraction, for example, uses 52 vehicles with five gaming units each, 260 machines in total, and a 30 millisecond latency budget for safety messages.

Many rides are about 20 years old and run proprietary systems and legacy protocols, so hardening is limited. Where systems cannot be hardened, the team adds compensating controls: less external exposure, defense-in-depth, strict physical access control, and out-of-band OT-aware intrusion detection kept off the control path. Vendors in several regions bring different PLCs and remote support needs complicate segmentation. IT policies have been extended with OT addenda, and a voluntary standard is being built with other major theme parks, aligned to IEC 62443 where possible.

The main takeaway is a risk-based approach: know where the physical access points to control networks sit, and monitor for configuration changes that move them. Other priorities include logs that can be queried in real time, incident response plans that are tested, regular user access reviews, hardened operating system images for vendor code, and OT-specific training for operators. In the Q&A, the speaker said health monitoring and security monitoring are kept separate, and quantitative risk assessments are still underway.

talks.title: S4 Great Debate: Cyber Resilience Act Impact
talks.teaser: Pits two debaters against each other on whether the EU Cyber Resilience Act will meaningfully cut OT cyber risk within three years.
talks.summary:
This structured debate examines whether the EU Cyber Resilience Act will significantly improve OT security and reduce OT cyber risk across EU countries within three years. Sarah Fluchs argues for the motion, pointing to an attack on Polish energy infrastructure where investigators found default credentials and no multi-factor authentication. She contends that responsibility should shift toward manufacturers, who would be legally accountable for their products, including third-party and open source components, and who would need software bill of materials and proactive vulnerability disclosure.

Sam Miorelli argues against. He notes the rules only apply to products placed on the market after late 2027, leaving little of the three-year window. He argues that recent major incidents involved compromised VPN credentials, exposed remote access and shared or default passwords rather than zero-days, so the act targets the wrong failure mode. He also warns that mandatory support periods could raise device prices, keeping older control systems in place longer, and questions whether SBOMs help operators who wait for OEM-approved patches.

In rebuttal, Fluchs said the act's effect would show up in product decisions and transparent security pricing, while Miorelli said it would lock operators into their existing vendors. In the cross-questions, Fluchs clarified that the act concerns known exploitable vulnerabilities and risk assessment rather than every CVE, and she could not name a public OT incident that depended on an unpatched OEM flaw. Miorelli argued that standards like NIS 2 and NERC CIP would do more. The moderator closed by asking whether audience positions had shifted.

talks.title: OT Incident Impact Score
talks.teaser: Proposes a crowdsourced 0-to-10 score to show the societal impact of OT incidents, cutting through media hype.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the observation that public alarm over operational technology incidents often runs ahead of their real effects, with some headlines about small water events drawing wide attention. The speaker argues that the OT security community contributes to that hype and proposes a quick way to rate societal impact. The proposed OT Incident Impact Score rates severity, reach and duration from 0 to 10, multiplies the three values and divides by 100 to produce a single figure. The aim is a result within about twelve hours, gathered from many people so that individual judgments average out.

The speaker then demonstrated a trial site where attendees log in with an email address and score past incidents, including Oldsmar, Jaguar Land Rover and the 2015 Ukraine attack, seeing the consensus after submitting. A panel followed. A media panelist said a score could help editors decide how much coverage an incident deserves, but wanted to know who was scoring and whether a recognized body would endorse it. An incident response panelist highlighted timeliness, the need to revise scores as facts change, and the value of benchmarking against past events. Another panelist warned that a score aimed at the general public lacks the rigor that decision-makers need.

The panel also covered near misses, which the score does not capture well, and drew on hurricane, wildfire and weather forecasting scales, which were refined over time through several iterations. The closing message was that scores will be imperfect and should be revisited as duration becomes clear. Practitioners were invited to score each new incident as it appears so the public and media get a more reliable picture.

talks.title: Connect For Industrial DataOps
talks.teaser: Shows how factories link legacy systems into a unified namespace so AI assistants can use plant data.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a night-shift scenario on a bottled water filling line, where rejected bottles pile up in a reject bin without ever tripping an alarm, and nobody has a quick way to tell whether a problem is developing. The speaker argues that industrial plants already hold plenty of data, but it sits in siloed systems, old databases, spreadsheets and unlabelled PLC tags, so AI tools have nothing useful to work with.

The proposed fix is a unified namespace (UNS): a contextual, hierarchical layer that connects to existing systems without replacing them and makes values such as bottle counts, fill rates and machine states available to any consumer. The speaker walks through the same plant's gaps. Maintenance records stay locked in a separate system, so a crew cannot see that a line is down for service. Time-based maintenance could shift toward use-case-based maintenance using running hours and counts. The ERP schedule could show spare line capacity during an outage. Cyber assets such as PLC firmware versions and ladder logic could also be added, so an unexpected program change could be spotted as a cause of a fault.

The talk closes by tying this to AI. Model context protocol is presented as a way for assistants to request plant data and, eventually, take actions, with the aging workforce as the reason to capture tribal knowledge. For security practitioners, the takeaway is to find out whether their organisation has a UNS initiative, engage with it early, and help secure the data layer before it is widely adopted.

talks.title: S4x26 Welcome Keynote: Connect
talks.teaser: Maps how AI-driven links into OT systems, cross-field learning and in-person networking will reshape OT security.
talks.summary:
Dale Peterson opens S4 by explaining the year's theme, connect. He expects a surge of links into OT systems and OT security tools, driven largely by agentic and generative AI. At an Ignition community conference, he saw vendors wire up live plant systems, with projects that once took years finished in a month or a week. He also found that the people he asked lacked an OT cyber asset inventory. He argues that OT security vendors have been slow to connect with one another, though that is starting to change.

His second point is that OT security staff need to borrow from fields beyond their own, such as engineering, operations, safety and business risk management, and even distant areas like psychology. He points to dialectical behavior therapy and its distress tolerance skills as a possible source of resilience ideas for incident responders, with a psychologist speaking later in the week.

His third point is about people. He warns that a flood of AI-generated OT security content is basic, unprioritized and drifting toward premature consensus. He urges attendees to find trusted subject matter experts, including voices that disagree, and to build relationships face to face, since connections form at close range. The week, he says, is a chance to find mentors and curate reliable sources.

talks.title: S4x26 POC Pavilion
talks.teaser: Explains how OT security vendors win a spot in S4's pavilion by demoing live on a real manufacturing system.
talks.summary:
Dale Peterson, founder and program chair of S4 Events, introduces the Proof of Concept Pavilion, a new area for the upcoming S4 conference in Miami Beach. Its aim is to let attendees see operational technology security products solve a real problem on an asset owner system, instead of watching scripted demos on an exhibit floor. Eight vendors will be chosen from applications that explain the problem being solved and how success would be measured.

Selected vendors must install their product on a real manufacturing environment supplied by a pavilion sponsor, with four production lines run by two different control system platforms plus an Ignition supervisory layer. Each vendor presents on the pavilion stage for an hour across three days: a short introduction, an architecture walkthrough, a 15-minute live demo, then questions from the organizers and from the audience. Vendors must also report how long the deployment took and what it would cost an asset owner to install and run each year. Anyone who does not demonstrate on that system will not be admitted to the pavilion.

Peterson acknowledges that vendors committed to earlier pavilions in the event series often failed to deliver, and says the organizers will enforce the rules and publicly call out weak demonstrations. Participants receive a documentation package and a network architecture drawing, and can ask questions over several weeks before installing. The application package is available now, and the call for presentations opens June 15.

talks.title: What To Do 1st, 2nd, 3rd
talks.teaser: Shows how OT assessors can turn long findings reports into short, achievable priority lists, and which practices to drop.
talks.summary:
The speaker, who has worked in OT security for about 25 years, describes many years of risk assessments for industrial clients. Findings were sorted into exposures, concerns and observations and delivered in reports often more than 50 pages long. Even a single item such as missing patches could be counted as one of many findings, so clients were overwhelmed. Some filed the reports away, and nothing had changed by the next annual review.

A client in 2007 asked for a plain answer: what to do first, second and third, and it had to be achievable. As a consultant obliged to report every risk, the speaker kept the full findings but added a prioritized list ranked by efficient risk reduction, asking where the next dollar or hour should go. Each report then carried a top five list for the first six months and another top five list for the following year.

Clients who used these lists cut their risk noticeably, applied limited resources to a small set of tasks, and could show management the results. The talk stresses that deciding what not to do, at least for the next 18 months, matters as much as choosing what to do. It closes by calling on OT security professionals to make those decisions for their organizations.

talks.title: Hacking A Medical Device … Way Back In 2013 At S4
talks.teaser: Covers a heap overflow on a medical device and insecure remote access practices in a hospital monitoring app.
talks.summary:
Two researchers with industrial control systems backgrounds argue that medical devices often come from the same vendors as ICS equipment and carry the same habits. They bought a device through a reseller, after finding that licensing rules make such equipment hard to obtain but not impossible. Inspecting it, they found it running Windows XP and stored credentials that the vendor said were not hardcoded.

Fuzzing an open port exposed what looked like a heap overflow. The team built a Python proof of concept that produced a privileged reverse shell, meaning anything connected to the device could also be exposed. The second case was a patient-monitoring iPad app that connected over RDP to a Windows host on the internet using shared demo credentials. After logging in, the researchers reached a command prompt with no restrictions on what they could run.

Their takeaway is that the same coding problems, design flaws and weak security habits found in industrial systems also appear in healthcare, and that culture is as much a barrier as technical fixes. Disclosure went through a government coordinator, which reached the vendor quickly, and the exploit was withheld because the issue was unfixed. Practitioners should assume users cannot be trusted and build threat models that address basic flaws first.

talks.title: S4 Classic: First Ever ICS On The Internet Session
talks.teaser: Maps industrial control devices visible on the internet via Showdown data, questioning the claim that these systems are air-gapped.
talks.summary:
The talk challenges the claim that industrial control systems are never connected to the internet. The speaker argues that proving an air gap is hard, so owners and vendors should keep demonstrating it, and that an air gap is only a baseline defense. Direct scanning can crash fragile devices, so the research relied on data already collected by Showdown.

The speaker used 33 banner queries, applied regular expressions to pull tokens from each banner, and searched exploit databases for known issues. Location came from city and country fields, with country averages filling gaps and duplicate IP addresses removed. Across about 10,000 devices over two years, 17% returned a 401 response and 53% returned a 200, meaning many could be reached without a password. A rough cost of $218 per node was estimated for discovery and processing.

Notifications went through a response team, but owners in the US could often only be reached with a subpoena, and some IP space turned out to be unknown to the buyer. The speaker closed by urging designers to assume exposure to hostile networks and asking for defensive, continuous verification of connectivity.

talks.title: Keeping Time In A Warzone
talks.teaser: Recounts how a Ukrainian grid operator lost GPS timing to electronic warfare and how a rugged switch restored it.
talks.summary:
The talk starts with a dinner conversation in which staff from Ukraine's state transmission grid operator described losing GPS timing to electronic warfare jamming, on top of physical strikes and cyber attacks. The speaker explains that substation phasor measurement units rely on a GPS-derived clock to take synchronized frequency samples across the grid, and that the satellite signal is extremely weak and easy to jam. The talk also covers how jamming is used by both sides, how a 2024 jamming incident affected parts of Poland and Sweden, and why losing a shared clock leaves operators working from incomplete data.

The team's response was a stopgap rather than a replacement. They took an industrial Ethernet switch with a high-quality crystal oscillator and placed it between the phasor measurement unit and the GPS antenna, so the clock could hold through outages of two to four hours. Firmware was then developed for enhanced clock recovery, and the switch was modified to provide the metadata tags that different vendors' equipment expected. The units were tested in Texas and then flown to Ukraine on a humanitarian aid shipment, where they were trialled in a lab using salvaged parts and deployed to critical substations within about a month.

The speaker also explains that spoofing is harder to handle than jamming, because falsified position and time can corrupt data without an obvious failure. The main takeaway is that operators should plan for loss of satellite timing, favour fast, low-cost measures that work over perfect solutions, and recognise how dependent their own infrastructure is on the electromagnetic spectrum.

talks.title: State Of NERC CIP, European Update, and OT Security Community
talks.teaser: Discusses NERC CIP's move toward cloud and virtualization, the EU's Cyber Resilience Act, and how regulators shape OT security.
talks.summary:
Dale Peterson hosts a podcast interview with Patrick Miller, who explains why his consulting firm changed its name to a global brand with a new European branch based in Estonia. They cover how the company picked its location, and his goal of keeping the firm small, around 20 to 30 people, so the team stays personally connected.

The conversation then turns to regulation. Miller compares European OT security with the US, noting that European rail and asset owners often plan further ahead, and that EU rules set a common floor which member countries can exceed, with enforcement differing from country to country. He contrasts the EU Cyber Resilience Act with the early years of NERC CIP, and describes recent NERC CIP changes that allow sensitive system data to be stored in the cloud under a bring-your-own-key model, while cloud-hosted operations remain under discussion.

The discussion also covers how the expertise of auditors affects compliance, the way prescriptive rules can be gamed, and the value of common metrics across electric, water and other infrastructure sectors. Miller closes with advice on AI in OT: slow down, understand the specific kind being proposed, and check whether it actually solves the problem.

talks.title: Dave Whitehead On SBOMs, Manufacturing in the US, and more
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Dave Whitehead On SBOMs, Manufacturing in the US, and more.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this episode of the Unsolicited Response Show hosted by Dale Peterson, guest Dave Whitehead, CEO of Schweitzer Engineering Laboratories (SEL), discusses SEL's approach to domestic manufacturing, supply chain resilience, and the industry debate surrounding Software Bills of Materials (SBOMs). Whitehead details the launch of SEL's printed circuit board (PCB) factory in Moscow, Idaho, SEL's perspective on product security lifecycles and customer vulnerability notifications, and the role of virtualization through SEL's Blueframe platform.

### Key Topics
- **In-House PCB Manufacturing and Supply Chain Control**: SEL invested roughly $100 million in a PCB manufacturing plant in Moscow, Idaho, which is operational and producing about a quarter of SEL's daily board consumption (projected to cover all internal demand within a year). Whitehead explains that manufacturing domestically reduces supply chain delays, mitigates intellectual property risk associated with sending Gerber layout files to third-party board houses, and offers a strong return on investment within roughly three years.
- **Tight Hardware and Firmware Coupling**: Whitehead notes that SEL's hardware, firmware, and RTL/FPGA designs are tightly coupled due to stringent real-time control constraints, such as traveling wave protection relays that sample at one million times per second and make trip decisions every 100 microseconds. Respinning boards to replace unavailable parts during supply crunches is feasible at their SMT assembly plants (in Pullman, Washington, and Lewiston, Idaho), but re-qualification and certification remain the primary cost.
- **The SBOM Debate**: Addressing industry buzz and government pushes regarding SBOMs, Whitehead questions the practical utility of raw SBOM files for asset owners. While SEL maintains comprehensive internal bills of materials for hardware and software to track defects down to specific lot codes and firmware versions, Whitehead argues that providing raw SBOMs creates management overhead for utilities. Instead, SEL supports sharing SBOMs or VEX documents (using formats like CycloneDX) on a case-by-case basis under NDA, while relying on direct service bulletins and customer portals for defect reporting.
- **Focus on Process Assurance Over Raw Data**: Whitehead compares SBOM mandates to quality frameworks like ISO 9001 and SEL's certification under IEC 62443-4-1 (secure product development lifecycle). He suggests that external audits demonstrating a mature development process are more effective than delivering raw inventory files to end users.
- **Organizational Culture and Edge Virtualization**: Whitehead highlights SEL's 100% employee-owned structure and weekly all-hands Friday lunches as mechanisms to maintain customer focus. Additionally, he reviews the adoption of Blueframe, SEL's application platform running on edge hardware or servers, noting it suits PLC and monitoring tasks, while ultra-fast microsecond protection functions remain on dedicated hardware.

### Technical Details
- **Manufacturing & Facilities**: $100M total investment in Moscow, ID board factory; 250,000 sq ft SMT manufacturing in Pullman, WA; microelectronics assembly in Lewiston, ID. SEL fabricates power supplies, transformers, ferrite chokes, plastics, and sheet metal internally, outsourcing mainly LCDs.
- **Software & Firmware Security**: SEL writes its own relay firmware and rejects compiled third-party binaries, ingesting only third-party source code to trim unused code and perform internal security scans. SEL conducts periodic (at least monthly) dependency reviews of third-party libraries.
- **Standards & Platforms**: Adherence to IEC 62443-4-1; CycloneDX and VEX document generation for requesting customers; Blueframe application framework running on SEL-3350, SEL-3355, and SEL-3360 platforms.

### Takeaways
Whitehead stresses that vertical integration provides superior quality control and long-term reliability for critical infrastructure equipment. Regarding cybersecurity and supply chain visibility, while manufacturers must maintain rigorous internal tracking and adhere to accredited development standards, asset owners benefit most when vendors proactively manage dependencies and provide contextualized service bulletins rather than raw SBOM data dumps.

talks.title: Presidential Candidate Will Hurd
talks.teaser: A former congressman weighs in on CISA, defend-forward operations, and how lawmakers should approach cyber policy.
talks.summary:
This interview with former congressman and presidential candidate Will Hurd covers how the federal government should handle cyber policy. Hurd says CISA, the agency he helped get passed, has performed better than many expected, though it needs more staff. He argues that critical infrastructure duties should be spread across federal agencies, with CISA coordinating the defense of government networks, and that department chief information security officers need more budget authority.

On strategy, he supports the defend-forward approach and says deterrence needs allies, since weak laws in a third country can let it become a route for attacks. He describes a Texas case in which property bought by a former Chinese military general near the grid raised concern that operators receiving shared threat information needed tighter controls. He also proposes a cyber National Guard, where scholarship recipients repay service to government and industry, and easier security clearances so practitioners can advise lawmakers. He cautions against prescriptive laws, noting that IoT rules can go stale once passed, and favors a federal privacy law.

He closes by framing cyber as one of several generational challenges alongside AI and competition with China. The takeaway is that cyber policy needs interagency coordination, practitioners inside government, and allied engagement rather than rigid rules.

talks.title: Tying Security Architecture Into Control Room Operations
talks.teaser: Shows how an IPS that stays closed by default can open for single authorized Modbus commands in about 50 milliseconds.
talks.summary:
Chad Lloyd of Schneider Electric describes work from the company's innovation lab on raising security in operational technology networks that still depend on older industrial protocols such as Modbus, while stronger protocols are years away. The starting point is the SCADA system, which holds an accurate inventory of every device on the OT network and could be used to drive firewall policy. He first covers maintenance windows for intelligent circuit breakers, where alarms are normally suppressed, so access could be opened only while a device is in that mode.

The second use case concerns device memory divided into frequent, occasional and rare access areas. The team wanted to block everything except the frequently polled area and open other regions only when an alarm counter changed. Early tests with OT firewalls failed because recommitting a configuration took about two minutes, far too slow for this purpose. Switching to an intrusion prevention system, the team inverted its usual logic: it stays closed by default and opens for one pre-announced message sent over a secure link, reconfiguring in 50 milliseconds in the proof of concept.

Chad then walks through a demo in which an attacker floods spoofed close commands during a legitimate operation. The IPS passes the matching traffic, but the resulting action still matches what the operator intended, and the SCADA system never learns that it was not the source. He notes the method works with any protocol both sides support, scales to many devices, and adds roughly 100 milliseconds from click to action. He closes by asking attendees to require standards such as 62443 from vendors so that security features get funded.

talks.title: Are We On The Right Track?
talks.teaser: Surveys the 2023 threat landscape across emerging technology and geopolitical hotspots, and urges OT teams to focus on prevention.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a 2023 outlook built on a reported statistic: 91 of surveyed cyber security experts and business analysts expected a catastrophic security event that year. The speaker asks what that means for individual practitioners and their industries, and whether their organisations are ready. Technology comes first. Generative AI lets attackers write and modify code quickly with less skill, quantum computing is expected to threaten current encryption, and IoT devices such as an AC sensor controlling a turbine could be manipulated with physical consequences. AR and VR headsets, adopted during the pandemic, and robotics and autonomous systems add further exposure.

The second focus is geopolitics. The speaker cites the North Carolina substation attack, carried out by an extremist group over a social event, and rising cartel violence in Mexico. China, Taiwan and North Korea are linked to theft and espionage, and Israel and Iran are described as trading cyber attacks constantly. The Russia-Ukraine war is presented as a testing ground for new techniques, and Chinese and Russian investment in parts of Africa is linked to more sophisticated scams and extremist groups. The India and Pakistan rivalry is illustrated by the Sidewinder group, which the speaker says carried out about a thousand attacks against military and government targets.

For operations, the speaker expects ransomware and advanced persistent threats to grow more capable, with AI-driven attacks that can evade endpoint detection and learn while inside a network. Each new vendor widens supply chain risk, and people remain the weakest link. The takeaways are to assume attackers will get in, focus on prevention and slowing them down, educate every staff member, right-size tooling to real gaps, track geopolitical intelligence, and build security into the organisation's culture.
