talks.title: Amazon Fulfillment Center Implementing OT IIoT
talks.teaser: Explains how fulfillment-center OT is segmented by work cell, with asset inventory, device identity and cloud-driven patching.
talks.summary:
The speaker, who handles security for operational technology in a large fulfillment network, explains why the environment is hard to protect. More than 3,400 sites can be spun up or down quickly, and they mix robotic arms, drive units, printers, scanners, servers and third-party equipment. Safety and availability come first, since robotic arms can injure people and a shut-down site stops package delivery.

A label printer serves as the case study. The older design put the warehouse system, a local firewall and a VPN in one logical zone, which the speaker said did not hold up. The new design isolates each work cell and separates the IPC from the PLC, even where IP ranges overlap. Assets are found through active scanning on IT networks and passive tapping or flow data in OT, then stored in a private data warehouse. Controllers authenticate with device certificates to AWS, and camera images containing personal data are encrypted at rest and in transit. Patching is simpler for cloud instances, which can be rebuilt, as during the Log4j response, while vendor-specific controllers took far longer to locate and fix. Greengrass is being evaluated to patch devices in work cells.

Logs from local systems flow to S3 and a data lake, which supports faster incident response. Remote access routes through AWS to individual work cells, and vendors cannot connect directly; someone on site must call them in, mainly for safety. The takeaway is to segment by work cell, inventory both IT and OT, use device identity, and make patching cloud-driven where possible.

talks.title: Exploiting XIoT Devices
talks.teaser: Shows how hardcoded MQTT credentials in a 4G router's firmware exposed a device fleet to remote command execution.
talks.summary:
XIoT devices sit where OT, IoT and medical device worlds meet: internet-capable products built for one purpose and managed through vendor cloud platforms. Noam Moshe explains how the research team studies such systems, starting with architecture: how a device registers, how a user claims it, and which protocols carry commands. He then maps attack vectors, including cloud takeover, information leaks and device impersonation.

The main case is a 4G router maker's cloud service. Firmware analysis exposed a configuration script with an MQTT broker address and one shared username and password, identical across units, so anyone could join as a legitimate device. The status topic streamed telemetry from devices worldwide, including IMEI and MAC addresses and Wi-Fi settings. Reverse engineering a client binary revealed an ASCII command protocol where one opcode passed its argument straight to the shell, giving remote OS command execution on routers. Since these routers link point-of-sale and remote-site networks, the speaker estimated the exposure reached tens of thousands of internal networks.

The vendor fixed the flaws and removed the hardcoded credentials. The takeaways centre on device identity: a MAC address and sequential serial number are weak, so each device should hold its own certificate and be isolated to reach only the cloud. Brokers need strict topic permissions, and wildcard subscriptions should be avoided. MQTT itself is sound when secured properly.

talks.title: Interview with HD Moore
talks.teaser: Traces the impact of Metasploit on OT security and explains how safe active scanning finds unmanaged assets.
talks.summary:
The conversation opens with the reception of Metasploit, the exploit framework that faced heavy criticism early on. The interviewee explains that vetting exploit buyers never worked in practice, so open release became the approach, and that OT modules added around 2011 and 2012 drew similar pushback, especially for medical and serial port devices. He argues the framework remains valuable as a maintained archive of security research, even though memory-corruption payload work matters less now than logic flaws and default credentials.

The discussion then turns to run zero, which focuses on asset inventory rather than vulnerability scanning. The interviewee describes a staged scan engine that fingerprints devices before sending further traffic, skips unfamiliar services, and spreads probes across ranges to limit amplification. Examples include printers that react badly to unexpected data and serial adapters that reload when connected to, plus leftover logged-in serial sessions that stay exposed on networks. Customers often find far more internal assets than they expected, and security teams typically use the inventory to cross-check other tools.

The closing portion covers OT adoption, where operators are often wary of active scanning. Some customers scan only during maintenance windows, and the company is building a passive mode that reuses its scan logic. The main takeaway is that an accurate inventory, including OT protocols on corporate networks, is needed before anything can be secured.

talks.title: Security Dashboards for Plant Managers
talks.teaser: Shows how a cyber dashboard built for plant managers turns OT security data into site-level risk metrics.
talks.summary:
Plant managers track availability, performance, quality and safety daily, but cyber risk rarely reaches them in terms they can act on. This project aimed to make cyber security support operations instead of blocking them. The team interviewed plant managers across several organisations and built a persona to shape dashboard mock-ups.

The dashboard groups metrics under preventive controls, defensive protections and security-related actions, following a stop, protect, detect and respond framing. Preventive measures cover devices with serious vulnerabilities, end-of-life systems and machines reaching risky websites. Defensive results show threats detected and blocked and USB insertions over time. Unplanned cyber downtime, such as devices pulled for emergency patching or reimaging, is also tracked. Inputs included OT passive monitoring, network access controls and EDR, plus threat intelligence and asset criticality. Sites were ranked by percentage of assets so very different sizes could be compared.

The rollout took about five months in three phases, with a focus group giving feedback before wider release. Dashboards then went out on the same cadence as existing safety and process reports, supported by working sessions. The presenters reported that cyber risk posture improved at the sites once managers could see it day to day.

talks.title: Dept of Energy OT Defender Fellowship Program
talks.teaser: Describes a Department of Energy program that connects OT defenders with federal agencies, a national lab, and each other.
talks.summary:
This podcast episode features Samantha Ravich, who chairs a center at the Foundation for the Defense of Democracies, describing the Department of Energy's OT Defender Fellowship. The program grew out of a 2016 observation that operational technology staff had few working links to the federal officials tracking threats to the grid. It is now in its third year, takes roughly 12 to 16 fellows annually, and has expanded from electricity to oil, gas and pipelines. Idaho National Laboratory supplies the technical side, while sessions in Washington bring fellows together with agency and congressional contacts.

Ravich outlined two goals: building lasting connections between fellows and federal agencies, and giving fellows a safe space to exchange practices. Success is judged partly by the strength of the alumni network and by the feedback officials receive from fellows. Candidates need to work in OT at a level where they can carry lessons back to executives, and company size is not a factor, so regional and sector diversity is deliberately sought. Timothy Pospisil of Nebraska Public Power District, a 2022 fellow, said his most useful lessons were understanding which federal groups handle which problems and the relationships built at the lab. He later chaired a large public power cyber task force that returned to the lab. He also described fellows pressing for a single reporting point during incidents instead of several agencies.

Both guests agreed that cohorts of about 15 to 16 keep discussions with government manageable, and that more than two cohorts a year would dilute the result. Water was discussed as a likely separate program, since its impacts unfold more slowly and smaller utilities face different constraints. The question of which agency would lead that work remained open. The episode's takeaway is that the model's value lies largely in trusted relationships that are hard to measure.

talks.title: OT Security: Cyber & Climate Nexus
talks.teaser: Connects OT cyber defense practice to climate-driven physical risks facing dams, grids, and data centers before design limits fail.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens by urging OT and infrastructure defenders to apply the same risk mindset they use for cyber threats to climate forces already disrupting dams, grids, water systems, and businesses. Training at Uganda's Bujigali hydro plant on segmentation, least privilege, ransomware preparedness, and backup restoration ended with operators raising a problem cyber drills do not cover: the Nile drying up and the plant running out of water.

The talk organizes threats around transmission-linked stubs for cyber, energy transition, and physical impacts. Cyber coverage spans nation-state strategic concern, ransomware as pervasive criminal pressure, and misinformation effects. Energy transition is described as reducing firm baseload while adding variable renewables, driving NERC reliability warnings tied to capacity shortfalls and gas pipeline constraints. Physical risks include kinetic grid damage discussed in a Ukraine context, crime and sabotage, and climate forces such as sea level rise, wildfire, flood, and freeze. Physical security 2.0 names threats for which traditional gates, guards, and guns offer no help, illustrated by data centers shutting down under unprecedented heat in London and speculative failure modes for major U.S. data center clusters under worsening heat domes.

A Venn diagram aligns OT cyber familiarities with emerging climate practice: prioritization by consequence, vulnerability assessments, hardening, information sharing, and risk transfer via cyber and property insurance. The close argues that backward-looking engineering standards, nominal air gaps, insecure-by-design products, and probabilistic flood terminology leave assets unready for projected extremes. The shared defender approach emphasized is disciplined engineering applied left of boom so reliability and resilience hold against both adversaries and a warming environment.

talks.title: Cyber Security And Its Impacts On Small Utilities
talks.teaser: Examines why small electric co-ops struggle with ICS cybersecurity and how programs and regulation could better fit them.
talks.summary:
Emma Stewart opens with a budget question: if a small electric utility had about 100K left at year's end, would it spend that on cybersecurity or on something else? She argues that small co-operatives, many with little or no IT staff, cannot absorb new costs without raising rates. She also says responsibility for grid security has shifted toward large vendors, while the blame for outages still lands on the local utility.

She then reviews the 100-day sprint on industrial control system security for the electric sector. It built good coordination, but it initially left out generation and transmission co-ops, did not address cost or long-term sustainability, and had no clear metrics for success. She describes how vendor product disclosures widen the gap between large and small utilities. She also explains that distributed energy resources, such as home solar, blur who owns parts of the system and who should be regulated.

Her practical lessons focus on value stacking, working with people in their operating context, and right-sizing tools so they are affordable, interoperable and easy to use. One story contrasts a sensor costing about a million dollars with a micro-synchrophasor costing about four thousand dollars, where the cheaper device gave operators more useful data. She closes by proposing a shared threat analysis center for co-ops that can take vendor data and help dispatch support, and she asks vendors and government to help deliver solutions small utilities can actually run.

talks.title: Heavy Vehicle & Me Kate Vajda and Ben Gardiner Name Fixed
talks.teaser: Compares industrial control system security with heavy truck fleets and walks through J1939, J1587 and telematics weaknesses.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with why heavy trucks matter: most products move by truck, and a prolonged trucking outage would quickly affect fuel, drinking water and medical supplies. The speakers compare industrial control systems with trucking fleets, noting shared reliance on embedded controllers, strict safety rules, skilled-labor shortages and long equipment lifecycles. They present the comparison as a shared vocabulary that lets fleet operators borrow lessons from ICS security programs.

Next they survey the vehicle networks in a heavy truck. J1939 can be pushed into denial of service or limp mode, while J1587 has no challenge-response or replay protection, so diagnostic replay can reconfigure engines and cycle ABS release valves. Depending on configuration, some equipment was described as reachable wirelessly from up to 12 feet away. Control loops increasingly use proprietary J1939 messages that trust bus traffic implicitly, and the seed-key scheme guarding diagnostics was described as weaker than it should be. Telematics units, often white-label, can bring these buses close to the internet, and gateways for segmentation are proposed as a mitigation.

The speakers note that the attacks shown are public research and have not been seen in the wild. Their crown-jewel analysis put drivers first, then real estate, then trucks, so assessments should start with each fleet's freight and business context rather than a generic IoT pen test. They point listeners to Cyber Truck Challenge materials, NMFTA working groups and the car hacking village.

talks.title: Native EDR for PLCs
talks.teaser: Shows how native PLC logic agents stream scan timing and status data that reveals network scans and online program edits.
talks.summary:
The talk adapts endpoint detection and response to programmable logic controllers, which the speaker calls controller EDR. Network sensors at every level are costly to deploy and still reveal little about what happens inside a controller. Instead, native ladder logic agents run on the controller itself. The collection, centralization, exploration and analysis steps are applied to signals such as run or program mode, uptime, faults, memory use, checksums, active forces, device identity and communication counters.

Data can be sent out by polling existing industrial protocols or by pushing a custom one-way protocol, which suits a data diode or strict outbound firewall rules. Scan cycle time receives special focus because nearly every controller reports it and it varies continuously, making it harder to spoof than static values. Mean shift clustering identifies normal operating states and a CUSUM accumulator flags sustained drift. In a captured incident, a bandwidth spike, a scan time anomaly and three memory drops after a login were correlated into a story of online edits, matching a controlled nmap scan and edits the speaker made.

Measured overhead was about one percent of scan cycle and CPU, with a few hundred bytes to about a kilobyte of memory for the custom protocol. Older controllers expose fewer metrics but make scan cycle deviations even more obvious. The takeaway is that controller-side telemetry gives security teams and controls engineers insight that network monitoring cannot.

talks.title: Financing The Future of ICS Security
talks.teaser: Explains how venture capital thinks about OT security startups, from staged bets to what makes a company worth funding.
talks.summary:
Rob Taran argues that now is a strong moment for OT security companies. He gives three reasons: large industrial buyers are finally treating cyber security as seriously as other sectors, a portfolio company valued at 1.7 billion dollars shows that money can be made, and venture funding keeps flowing, with more than a billion dollars invested in OT security in 2021.

Startup investing is compared with security risk management. Venture firms stage their bets, adding money only when milestones are hit and keeping the option to walk away. Five reasons investors skip OT startups are listed: the idea is too small, the product does not scale, there are no milestones, traction or team credibility is missing, and gross margins are low. Startups are told to start with niche services, mix software, hardware and services, and treat early customers as design partners. Customers are urged to share big problems, and job seekers should ask whether a company can scale.

In the question session, a rough rule of thumb was given: a company needs about 10 times annual recurring revenue, or around 100 million dollars in sales, to reach billion-dollar scale. Recurring revenue matters more to investors than one-off services, and on-premises options remain important for utility-backed investors even as cloud use in OT grows from a small base. AI was described as useful mainly in case-specific uses. The closing takeaway was to go big.

talks.title: Securing The Manufacturing Edge
talks.teaser: Covers the security risks of industrial edge devices that link OT networks to the cloud, and practical controls for them.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at edge devices, the small connected gateways and compute boxes now appearing on industrial networks between plant-floor controllers and the cloud. The speaker argues that these devices strain traditional OT network models, that asset owners often lack visibility into how a vendor's cloud platform is built, and that the data they collect is valuable enough to attract attackers. A manufacturing example shows why plant-level data matters when investigating quality problems after products have already reached shelves, and why moving that data outward creates new exposure.

Much of the talk covers controls. Asset inventory comes first, followed by patch management, vulnerability management, segmentation and risk assessment, which apply to edge hardware much as they do to other OT equipment. The speaker recommends hardware with a trusted platform module so that measured boot can detect tampered firmware, full disk encryption for devices that may be mounted on machines and removed, and outbound-only connections managed through orchestration. Application stores hosted on premise and approved app lists let an operator control what runs on each device. The talk also notes that cloud dependencies, such as map services, can add traffic and data locations that need review.

The closing section covers write-backs from the cloud to controllers, which the speaker says need strong authentication and a method such as consequence-driven analysis before they are allowed. The question-and-answer period touched on near-real-time patching, regulated industries being more cautious about cloud connections, and hardware root of trust in vendor products. The main takeaway is to treat edge devices as full computing assets, know where every one of them is, and settle ownership, access and update processes before deployment.

talks.title: Modern Defense Evasion in IoT Botnets
talks.teaser: Surveys how IoT botnet malware evades analysts with string encryption, ELF header tweaks, anti-debugging and corrupted UPX packing.
talks.summary:
Alexey Kleymenov examines how IoT botnets slip past defensive controls, starting from the defense evasion tactic in MITRE ATT&CK. He uses Mirai and its many clones as the baseline. Mirai hides its strings with a weak XOR scheme that reuses one short key and decodes each string only when it is needed. It also renames its thread and process, kills remote access ports, and sets up a fake listener so it is harder to restart. Other families add anti-debugging with ptrace, check for honeypots such as Cowrie, look for virtual machines through DMI and CPU data, and scan for debugging tools.

The second part covers trends seen in samples collected from honeypots. One Mirai derivative decrypts all of its strings in a single routine, which makes analysis easier for researchers and the malware alike. Some attackers alter ELF header fields that the Linux loader does not strictly check, which breaks certain reverse engineering tools and a common Python library; this affected about 1% of roughly 700 samples. A stripped-down Gafgyt clone removes most of its commands to avoid signatures. The Glupteba family stores its command-and-control details in Bitcoin transaction data, first encrypted with AES and later with a hardcoded XOR key, and the team tracked four campaigns.

For packers, UPX is the main free option on Linux. The team reports that about a third of recent samples were packed with UPX, and about 4% of those were corrupted so the standard unpacker fails. They released an open-source fixing tool that handles corruption across x86, ARM, MIPS and PowerPC. The takeaways are to keep monitoring trends, avoid relying on exact signatures because small format changes defeat them, and share samples so the wider community can build better detections.

talks.title: Lessons from the CISA COVID Task Force
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Lessons from the CISA COVID Task Force.

talks.title: The Future of OT Security, An Alternative Point Of View
talks.teaser: Traces the Purdue model's role in shaping OT security and presents the Open Process Automation approach as a path forward.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, a representative from the cybersecurity firm Sygnia explores the past 40 years of Operational Technology (OT) security and critiques the industry's longstanding reliance on the Purdue Model. The speaker argues that rigid adherence to legacy network segmentation has hampered digital transformation and modern supply-chain integration while failing to address contemporary threat realities. As an alternative path forward, the talk highlights emerging secure-by-design standards—specifically the Open Process Automation Forum (OPAF)—and discusses how architectures must evolve toward unified IT/OT visibility and hybrid detection.

### Key Topics
- **History and Threat Landscape Evolution**: Over 40 years, OT threats transitioned through three phases: insider-dominated attacks with direct physical/local access (1982–2010), nation-state military-grade cyber weapons (kickstarted by Project Aurora and Stuxnet in 2010), and today's IT-to-OT cascading risks primarily driven by ransomware.
- **The "Original Sin" of the Purdue Model**: The Purdue Model, originally created in the 1990s for a different purpose, was repurposed as OT's sole security architecture. Adding level 3.5 (IDMZ) and placing the Internet at level 5 created strict, dogmatic rules (e.g., forbidding direct L4-to-L3 communication, enforcing strictly on-premises operations, relying solely on passive IDS). These boundaries severely constrained bidirectional data flow required for digital transformation and modern demand-driven supply chains.
- **Open Process Automation Forum (OPAF/OPAS)**: An initiative launched by ExxonMobil (now on version 2.1) supported by over 600 member organizations, introducing open, interoperable, secure-by-design architectures. Other aligned initiatives include NAMUR (integrating the NOA concept) and the U.S. Department of Energy's Cyber-Informed Engineering strategy.
- **Architectural Shift & Hybrid SOC**: Moving toward distributed edge control devices while building a unified security operations center (SOC) that monitors both IT and OT estates.

### Technical Details
- **Distributed Control Nodes (DCNs)**: Edge devices running control logic, control loops, configuration management, and embedded security layers (data collection and detection). DCNs are intended to eventually replace PLCs and DCSs.
- **Distributed Control Framework (DCF)**: A transitional wrapper component enabling legacy control devices to interface with new architectures without introducing intolerable latency.
- **Open Process Automation Standard (OPAS)**: Employs the OPA Communication Framework (OCF) using OPC UA as the standard communication bus across controllers, cloud, IoT, and advanced computing platforms. Audience discussion noted that OPAS incorporates ISA/IEC 62443 security standards.
- **Sygnia's Implementation**: Sygnia joined OPAF and built an OPAS-based cyber-kinetic innovation center. They adapted their "Velocity" Extended Detection and Response (XDR) platform across levels 4, 3, and parts of 2, while using API integrations with industrial IDS for lower-level visibility as an intermediate step toward full IT/OT hybrid telemetry.

### Takeaways
- Isolating OT from IT via air gaps or rigid Purdue boundaries is no longer viable in an era where ransomware cascades from IT into OT environments.
- Process control security must shift from bolt-on network restrictions to open, secure-by-design frameworks like OPAS.
- Security teams need to actively participate in pilots, testbeds, and standards convergence (OPAF, NAMUR NOA) to redefine detection, response, and data management across the entire digital enterprise.

talks.title: The Purdue Model in a Private LTE & 5G World
talks.teaser: Explains how a company brought Purdue-model segmentation and visibility to its private cellular warehouse network.
talks.summary:
The session starts from the Purdue model, a reference framework from the 1990s that separates business networks from process control networks with a DMZ between them. The presenters explain that their private cellular deployment, built about a year and a half earlier, sat on a single flat network. That left lateral movement possible, gave no visibility into traffic, and funneled everything through one core, so the usual segmentation did not carry over.

To close that gap, the team ran a proof of concept in a warehouse with automated guided vehicles that have no native cellular support, so routers and vendor SIM cards were added. Replacing about 20 Wi-Fi access points with two private cellular radios was a noted benefit. Routing and firewall openings let the vehicles reach a fleet manager from the OT DMZ, and the team tested performance and coverage during mission runs. Later phases added vibration and temperature sensors, and the presenters cited research into risks such as signal storms, IP attacks, DNS hijacking, APN attacks and MQTT hijacking.

The team then evaluated a vendor platform that discovered and classified connected devices, tied each identity to the device profile rather than only the SIM card, and let them set policies such as blocking phone-to-vehicle traffic. A week-long on-site test was followed by a planned scale-up to a larger warehouse with about 30 radios and more than 30 vehicles, aimed at restoring visibility and stopping cross-segment movement. The takeaway is that private cellular needs its own segmentation and monitoring, and that heavy reliance on the vendor for logs makes in-house skills important.

talks.title: Problems & Solutions In Deploying SDN In OT
talks.teaser: Explains how software-defined networking can replace VLANs, spanning tree and manual switch setup in industrial control networks.
talks.summary:
The speaker, who represents a switch vendor, begins with his own time as a discrete manufacturing end user building an Ethernet plant-floor network in 2006. He recalls the design-era problems: choosing topologies, relying on rapid spanning tree to stop loops caused by miswired cables, and struggling with multicast querier placement under IGMP. Plant staff unfamiliar with IP found VLANs hard to manage, and drawings were outdated within months of equipment delivery.

He then maps each problem to software-defined networking, where standard switches are steered by a central controller. Segmentation is device-centric, so a PLC can be allowed to talk to one robot over EtherNet/IP and nothing else, replacing many VLANs. Loops cannot be created, configuration is pushed from the controller so switches need no individual backups, and one policy change can apply across dozens of switches. A controller can learn existing traffic and write policies, which eases OEM commissioning and migration. Each new flow goes to the controller once, and blocked flows are written into switches so repeated DLR beacons do not overload it.

He notes limits: SDN is not built for user-level access control, and controllers must handle dual-port devices and VLAN-trunked uplinks. Gradual adoption can start by replacing a single aggregate switch. The main takeaway is to choose an OT-aware controller and build on the visibility and per-device control it provides.

talks.title: The SBOM Challenge
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for The SBOM Challenge.
talks.summary:
### Overview
At the S4 conference, researchers from the Idaho National Laboratory (INL)—including co-speaker Hannah Pearson Kleinheiter and her co-presenter Ginger—presented the findings of the first Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) Challenge. Hosted in collaboration with Dale, the competition evaluated five commercial and open-source tooling providers across three core objectives: extracting component/file SBOMs from artifacts, enriching components with vulnerability data (CVEs/non-CVEs), and ingesting Vulnerability Exploitability eXchange (VEX) documents. Rather than revealing a single "silver bullet," the challenge demonstrated that tooling performance strongly reflects differing core metaphors, architectural priorities, and intended use cases across the participating platforms.

### Key Topics
- **Participating Tool Vendors:** Five entities took part in the evaluation: aDolus (FACT platform - Framework for Analysis and Coordinated Trust), Cybeats, Finite State, NetRise, and Security Risk Advisors (SRA, utilizing their own open-source FACT tool - Firmware Analysis and Comparison Tool).
- **Test Artifact Diversity:** INL provided three distinct artifacts representing real-world ICS and operational environments: Hitachi Energy's Transformer Protection Unit (TPU 2000, a minimal bare-metal 68k firmware binary), OSIsoft ProcessBook (a Windows-based data viewing application), and OpenWrt (an ARM-based open-source router firmware with compiled libraries requested by participants).
- **Naming Collisions and Ambiguity:** The speakers highlighted persistent industry-wide naming challenges for software components, noting that even within the challenge itself, two different participants (aDolus and SRA) shared the identical platform acronym "FACT."
- **Standardization & Formats:** Tools primarily interacted with CycloneDX and SPDX formats, alongside automated vulnerability sharing via VEX documents.

### Technical Details
- **Phase 1: Component Extraction:** Tools faced varying success based on architecture. Bare-metal firmware (TPU 2000) proved unhandled by all tools; zero components were extracted from it. For OSIsoft ProcessBook, NetRise rapidly built Windows compatibility during the competition to extract components. OpenWrt yielded significantly higher package and file counts across participants. Cybeats did not perform raw binary component extraction, focusing instead on SBOM ingestion, structure validation, and distribution.
- **Phase 2: Vulnerability Enrichment:** Participants correlated extracted components against multiple vulnerability data sources (such as NVD and international databases). High variance occurred in reported numbers; for instance, Finite State identified 85 vulnerabilities in ProcessBook tied largely to a single library, and also reported non-CVE vulnerabilities. INL stressed that a vulnerability existing in an upstream library does not guarantee exploitability within the compiled product.
- **Phase 3: VEX Ingestion:** INL supplied synthetic, fictitious VEX documents to test status updates without misrepresenting vendor security. Finite State and SRA successfully ingested the VEX files to adjust risk status. aDolus declined ingestion under their policy that only verified OEMs/vendors hold the authority to issue VEX documents. NetRise did not support VEX due to a lack of market customer requests, while Cybeats demonstrated capabilities to author and structure VEX documentation.
- **Ad Hoc Findings:** Beyond SBOM generation, NetRise detected a hard-coded password in one artifact, which was verified with the originating vendor.

### Takeaways
INL concluded that prospective buyers must define their organizational "quest" and specific use case before selecting an SBOM tool, evaluating hands-on user interfaces rather than relying solely on raw metric counts. Moving forward, INL proposed longer evaluation periods (weeks to months, modeled after CISA plugfests), examining full vendor catalogs, and establishing an energy sector SBOM exchange program under legal/liability protections (such as NDAs or DOE frameworks) to help asset owners and vendors mature SBOM consumption.

talks.title: The Decisions and Uncertainty in OT Recovery
talks.teaser: Explains why OT recovery depends on people, processes and data, and how one manufacturer is building those capabilities.
talks.summary:
The talk examines what it takes to recover operational technology when a plant system or site goes down. The speaker, who sits between IT and engineering at a consumer goods manufacturer, argues that the serious gaps are in people and process rather than tooling. A 2017 internal audit found weak processes and no full view of control components, so risk could not be quantified. IT teams, by contrast, had years of practiced disaster recovery behind them.

Through examples, the speaker shows what happens when plans are missing. In one core network power-down, switches could not be restored because the phone system ran in the cloud, cellular coverage in the data center room was poor, and the on-site PBX had been removed years earlier. In response, the company set up a critical outage process with dedicated communications staff, OT Champions in plants who supply context, and an OT Support Center to close language gaps between help desks and machine operators. Ongoing challenges include manual documentation, discovery data that does not fit a configuration database, baselining of thousands of flows by hand, and budgets that compete with capital projects.

The closing message is that recovery depends on planning, practice, the right people and trusted data, and that these must be built before a failure. In the Q&A, the speaker said the program launched without resourcing the engineering side, and results improved where plant staff engaged with automation tools. The speaker asked the community to share lessons publicly.

talks.title: Metrics: How Effective Is A Security Control?
talks.teaser: Researchers quantify how layered OT controls affect power output and kill-chain interruption in a simulated wind plant.
talks.summary:
National laboratory researchers built a cyber-physical testbed modeled on a thirty-turbine wind site with VPN access, a jump host, HMIs, and turbine controllers, then ran remote and on-site attack paths against a known Windows weakness. They paired mission-focused physical resilience scoring—expected generation against forecasts and voltage staying within utility bands—with a cyber resilience score tied to how far scripted kill chains progress before controls stop them.

Five hardened topologies compared baseline defenses with Modbus encryption and access control, NIDS plus SIEM, host IDS with encryption, and SOAR playbooks that automate isolation and credential revocation. Encryption alone preserved roughly ninety-six percent physical resilience while modestly improving cyber scores; tuned SOAR reached about seventy-seven percent cyber resilience with the same physical outcome. The team notes tradeoffs such as encrypted field traffic limiting network-based detection and playbooks tuned only to the rehearsed scenarios.

Practitioners gain a reusable framework for scoring controls against operational outcomes rather than alerts alone, plus a starting model for expected benefit from cybersecurity spend. Much of the investment calculus still relies on industry-supplied costs and attack frequency, and follow-on work targets field trials with asset owners and more control mixes.

talks.title: Security By Design Decision
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Security By Design Decision.

talks.title: The Biological Internet of Things (BIoT)
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of The Biological Internet of Things (BIoT).

talks.title: Hot New Gameshow! My Favorite Metric
talks.teaser: Five contestants pitch their favorite security metrics to two judges, who score each one out of ten.
talks.summary:
This session is a mock gameshow at S4 in which five contestants each get three minutes and one slide to pitch a favorite security metric and explain why it matters. Two judges, Maggie Morgante and Derek Harp, score each pitch from one to ten using criteria of their own choosing.

Debbie Gordon argued that breaches happen when detection staff lack the skills they need, and proposed scoring each person, team or department against NICE work roles and MITRE ATT&CK techniques to surface training gaps. Jesus Molina pitched risk from inbound information for OT systems, weighing the quantity and quality of incoming data, the filtering controls in place and how trustworthy each source is. Ron fabella offered a one-to-ten "GOAT" scale for rating community contributions, starting from generous assumptions and suggesting outreach to those rated low. Craig Duckworth presented a connected device vulnerability index that scores OT assets against published CVEs and known exploits, weighted by Purdue model level and visibility coverage, and compared it to a FICO score. Kenneth Crowther showed a revenue-at-risk method for product lines, built from digital exposure, known good and bad products and revenue, and run as a simulation in Excel to rank priorities under uncertainty.

Scores were tallied across the judges. Ron fabella and Craig Duckworth finished level at the top, a short applause round broke the tie, and both received tickets to next year's S4. The judges praised clear visuals and business framing, while questioning how much judgment sat underneath some of the metrics.

talks.title: Wireless IIoT: The Direct Path To Your Level 0
talks.teaser: Shows how exposed industrial wireless gateways give attackers a route from the internet into OT networks, via a vendor cloud.
talks.summary:
The talk covers industrial wireless IoT devices, such as cellular gateways and Wi-Fi access points, and how they can give attackers initial access to OT networks. At distributed sites, these gateways often lead straight to PLCs, HMIs and field devices, which the speaker described as insecure by design. Three attack vectors are covered: on-site wireless and cellular channels, internet-exposed local services, and vendor cloud management platforms.

For on-site channels, the research searched the Wigle database for network names containing OT terms and for MAC prefixes of industrial vendors, returning over 4,300 results for one manufacturer. One example was a food plant using weak WPA encryption. Local web interfaces were found through internet search engines, and one vendor's airlink device had a remote code execution issue that bypassed a 2018 patch, with details withheld pending disclosure. The main focus was a cloud device manager, where predictable registration identifiers let the researchers subscribe to other routers' result topics, read and change their configurations, and reach root through an unsafely built ping command. A lab demo showed a renamed router opening a reverse shell.

The speaker recommends avoiding OT terms in network names, using MAC or certificate-based allow-listing, limiting management interfaces to the LAN, removing default credentials, and disabling cloud management when it is not needed. Placing separate hardware between the cellular gateway and the local network would also stop a compromised device from reaching PLCs directly.

talks.title: Interview with Puesh Kumar, Director of CESER
talks.teaser: Covers an energy-sector security office's threat sharing, equipment testing and cyber-informed engineering for the grid.
talks.summary:
The office responsible for energy-sector cyber security and emergency response describes its mission to understand threats and hazards facing U.S. energy systems. It says the office led the government response to the Colonial Pipeline ransomware attack. Its information sharing program, now more than a decade old, is expanding from IT threats into operational technology, combining OT data with IT data to look for anomalous activity. Alerts reach the wider sector through the electricity information sharing center.

Measuring the value of such programs is described as difficult, particularly in OT, and the director argues the community needs better ways to quantify cost avoided so executives will fund protection. A testing program run with national laboratories examines industrial control components from manufacturers, and the legal groundwork on risk ownership and disclosure took a long time to settle. Early testing produced vulnerability disclosures, and the goal is to publish methods so utilities and third parties can test on their own. Agreements exist with several vendors, and a new one was signed with GE gas power.

Cyber-informed engineering, a push to design grid equipment with security built in, is presented as a strategy with concrete steps. One early target is working with IEEE standards bodies to add security requirements to substation standards. The clean energy cyber accelerator uses a cyber range at the national renewable energy laboratory, where vendor tools are tested in a grid of wind, solar and batteries; the first cohort covered multi-factor authentication and the second covered asset discovery. The takeaway is that reliability depends on security, and that engineers and security specialists must work together as new grid connections appear.

talks.title: Understanding The (Cyber) Insurance Business
talks.teaser: Explains how insurers price, reserve and reinsure cyber risk, and why cyber insurance should complement security controls.
talks.summary:
The talk starts with a simple question: why do most people know so little about insurance, and what does transferring risk to an insurer really involve? The speaker, an underwriter with about 12 years in the field, traces insurance back to early contracts in Italy in the 14th century and explains how cyber cover emerged in the 1990s and grew after 2014. An insurance family tree separates life from non-life cover and shows that cyber policies sit under specialty insurance without covering bodily injury or property damage on their own.

The middle section looks at the market and its mechanics. The cyber market is put at about 10 billion against roughly 7 trillion of gross written premium across insurance overall. Insurers earn from premiums and from investing the float held before claims are paid. Pricing blends pure premium and loss ratio methods with underwriter and actuarial judgement. Average rate changes jumped from 9% to 18% and then to 70% or more after 2019, driven mainly by stricter underwriting on security controls, which left one in four clients non-renewed or declined. Reserving and reinsurance manage accumulation, yet reinsurance capital of about 260 billion limits how much any single insurer can offer, often around 25 million per risk against demands of 100 million or more.

The closing argues that simpler coverage and better information shared with insurers would help attract capital to reinsurance and improve terms. Cyber insurance is presented as a complement to security controls, not a replacement. Listeners are urged to question insurers about premium swings and the controls behind them, and the talk ends by calling for more dialogue to build collective understanding.

talks.title: Secure Forensics Port For ICS Embedded Devices
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Secure Forensics Port For ICS Embedded Devices.
talks.summary:
### Overview
During major operational technology (OT) and industrial control system (ICS) cyber incidents—such as the Colonial Pipeline ransomware event—asset owners face significant uncertainty when attempting to answer the critical question: "Are we cyber clean?" When SCADA networks and telemetry are proactively shut down or under adversary control, operators lack visibility into the internal state of embedded devices (Level 0, 1, and 2 devices). Current recovery workflows rely on shallow front-panel LCD displays, push buttons, or sending hardware back to vendors through slow RMA processes, which rarely produce timely or widely shared threat intelligence. To solve this visibility and verification bottleneck, the speaker proposes establishing an open standard for a hardware-level "Secure Forensics Port" (SFP) directly integrated into embedded ICS devices.

### Key Topics
- **The OT Verification Gap:** Abundant network telemetry exists during normal operations, but there is an inability to inspect low-level device internals when systems are isolated or compromised.
- **Limitations of Current Incident Response:** Field responders are constrained by basic two-row LCD panels and limited physical interfaces, while vendor RMA pathways are slow, often private, and fail to scale during widespread incidents.
- **Home Court Advantage:** Physical access to field equipment is a key operational advantage for defenders, but it is currently squandered due to balkanized, vendor-specific administrative methods.
- **Secure Element Interface (SEI):** Implementing miniaturized custom hardware boards inside device chassis to take fundamental forensic measurements without requiring server racks or cloud compute.
- **Standardized Cryptographic Authorization:** Using public key authentication, X.509/certificate authority architectures, and standardized entitlement Object Identifiers (OIDs) to balance forensic access with vendor intellectual property.

### Technical Details
The speaker's team demonstrated the feasibility of this architecture by prototyping a custom board integrated into two production devices—a gas remote terminal unit (RTU) and an electric sector real-time automation controller (RTAC)—without proprietary vendor assistance. The architecture centers around a Secure Element Interface (SEI):
- **Cryptographic Framework:** Employs standard public key cryptography rather than custom algorithms. At manufacturing time, certificate authorities configure credentials within the SEI.
- **Authorization & Entitlements:** Responders connect via an engineering workstation acting as a client. Access is governed by standardized entitlements mapped to certificate OIDs. These dictate permissible actions such as reading device memory, dumping firmware, examining file systems, or uploading configurations. In this OT context, read operations are often treated as more sensitive than write operations to protect proprietary settings and firmware IP.
- **Operational Workflows:** Instead of manually evaluating one substation box at a time, the port enables concurrent, edge-based scanning to rapidly verify whether devices are uncompromised or require remediation.

### Takeaways
- **Accelerated Recovery:** A dedicated, standardized forensic interface provides a fast diagnostic path, reducing decision time for safe system restarts after an intrusion.
- **Secondary Use Cases:** Beyond incident response, the port provides a trusted backstop for supply chain auditing, asset enumeration, and predictive maintenance.
- **Call to Action:** The speaker calls for utilities, manufacturers, and standards bodies to form a technical community of interest, refine the cryptographic and entitlement specifications, and build additional prototypes across a wider range of field devices.

talks.title: Chris Blask: Cybersecurity Pioneer and Idea Man
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Chris Blask: Cybersecurity Pioneer and Idea Man.

talks.title: Semi-Quantitative Cyber-Physical Risk Assessments
talks.teaser: Explains how semi-quantitative risk assessment combines process safety layers with cyber attack scenarios for chemical plants.
talks.summary:
The talk covers semi-quantitative cyber-physical risk assessment for process plants, the middle ground between qualitative risk ratings and full quantification. Using a reactive vessel where thermal runaway could rupture the reactor, the speaker shows that a random pump failure and a cyber attack that cuts cooling produce the same overheating and consequence, so the same risk criteria apply to both. Tolerance limits are set as frequency-number curves by governments for individual, societal and environmental risk, and companies add their own criteria.

To size the safeguards, the speaker uses layers of protection analysis. Operator intervention, an automated shutdown that injects an inhibitor, and a rupture disc each reduce risk by a factor tied to their probability of failure on demand, and together they must bring the event frequency under the limit. For the cyber side, the speaker estimates the probability of defense failure given an attack rather than the likelihood of attack, since vulnerability and threat-action data are more available. Attack scenarios are modelled per element such as transmitters, controllers and engineering stations, then combined through dependency diagrams and protection rings, with the highest-probability ring setting the result.

Risk can be read from the installation side, asking which attacks could cause a given loss, or from the device side, asking what an attacker reaching one component could cause. The speaker says the method has been used for about eight years with in-house tooling. In questions, the speaker acknowledges that the outputs remain estimates that depend on expert judgement, and that European authorities increasingly want to see this evidence for new plants.

talks.title: The Value of Little Data
talks.teaser: Explains why scattered, undocumented asset details block OT security actions, and how to collect them.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that big data from OT environments rarely turns into action on its own, because the context needed to act is spread across emails, PDFs, paper files and people's heads. The speaker calls this missing context "little data": the human-readable details such as where a device is installed, whether it is plugged into power, who owns it and who to call. Location is a good example, since an IT director may mean a subnet or VLAN while an OT engineer means a specific production line. Undocumented knowledge, such as a facilities manager who always calls the same contractor for HVAC faults, is a common gap.

Two incidents show the cost of missing this data. At a space agency, a uniform patch hit a component controlling a large engineering oven, which rebooted and caught fire, and the fire went undetected for three and a half hours because the alarm also failed. At a wafer manufacturer, a ping sweep meant to build an inventory made an integrated circuit hang, causing downtime and a loss of over fifty thousand dollars in wafers. The speaker proposes a framework: pick one process, integrate data as a flow rather than forcing a single source of truth, and collect details as close as possible to where changes happen, using permissions to reduce errors.

A device onboarding case shows the framework in practice. Maintenance staff bought a point-of-sale system, sprinkler or vending machine, then needed the network team to connect it, and getting it online stretched over hours and days of email back-and-forth. The team mapped the questions that mattered, moved them into a simple form in an existing tool with approval steps, and made network access depend on a completed form. The result was a record of ownership and device details captured at purchase, which helped responders answer who to contact when something failed.

talks.title: Edgard from Nozomi (Part 2)
talks.teaser: Nozomi's CEO discusses OT security budgets, Vantage cloud adoption, and government threat-sharing efforts in a follow-up interview.
talks.summary:
In this follow-up interview, Dale Peterson talks with Nozomi Networks CEO Edgard about how the OT security market has shifted since their 2021 conversation. Edgard credits remote work and pandemic pressure with speeding up digital transformation in plants, and says geopolitical and banking turbulence now shapes buying decisions. He reports annual recurring revenue growth of 134 percent from 2020 to 2021 and close to 77 percent from 2021 to 2022, with headcount nearing 300 and expansion into building automation, hospitals and transportation.

The middle of the conversation turns to budgets and cloud delivery. Edgard argues that cybersecurity spending held up through past downturns, but OT security is a young category without established budget, so new programs often come out of other security spending. He says Vantage, the SaaS management product, was the first choice for over one-third of bookings and active proofs of concept at the end of 2022, while sensors stay on site. He defends on-premises consoles or edge layers for multi-site deployments and describes managed security partnerships with large service providers.

Late in the conversation, Edgard describes US government efforts, including an OT Coalition of vendors that CISA welcomed and a forthcoming threat-intelligence sharing standard. On return on investment, he compares it to published seat belt outcome data, which security rarely offers, and argues buyers must first close basic gaps such as unpatched systems, unchanged passwords and unreviewed remote access.

talks.title: Deceive By Design: How To Protect Critical Infrastructure With Deception Technology
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Deceive By Design: How To Protect Critical Infrastructure With Deception Technology.

talks.title: Using BOMs to Threat Model A System
talks.teaser: Shows how linked CycloneDX BOM types map attack trees, trust paths, vulnerabilities, and physical flaws for system threat models.
talks.summary:
The session opens with whether bill-of-materials artifacts can drive threat modeling beyond the vulnerability headlines common at SBOM-focused events. BOMs already span manufacturing, construction, firmware, hardware, and software; the speaker contrasts defining a system by its parts versus what it does, noting that most practitioners emphasize behavior even though BOM thinking starts with ingredients.

The core uses CycloneDX as a system descriptor: software BOMs for components and weaknesses, hardware BOMs for physical traits and identifiers usable in further research, and service BOMs for APIs, sockets, data flow direction, authentication, and encryption—not a SaaS application stack. SAS BOMs support attack-surface and trust-path analysis on generic attack trees, where adversaries prefer easy routes over zero-days. Linked BOM types also surface physical bypass options. The talk touches emerging ML and cryptographic BOM ideas, BOM linking and messy aggregation limits in current tooling, and approaches such as threat modeling in code with PyTM, open threat model formats, Graphviz DOT output, and generative assistance for diagrams.

Practitioners should treat BOM linking as connective tissue for modeling, expect manual aggregation work today, and push suppliers and contracts for authoritative BOMs while using teardowns, security testing, and other interim sources until the ecosystem matures.

talks.title: Automatic Recovery At Level 0
talks.teaser: Explains how a passive level-zero sensor spots tampered process values and drives automatic PLC recovery in industrial sites.
talks.summary:
The talk presents the view that operational technology needs zero trust, and introduces level zero monitoring: an independent sensor that watches the physical signal of a process, so operators see the real outcome whatever the controllers report. The speaker illustrates it with an offshore drilling platform in the North Sea, unmanned autonomous drones, and a floating LNG storage and regasification unit, where the tank level and vaporizer are the critical points.

The main case is an attack on a tank level meter: a compromised workstation lets an attacker reprogram the PLC so an overfill goes unnoticed. A signal integrity monitor wired passively to the meter flags readings outside a 20 to 60 percent operating window. The speaker compares three recovery options, from rewriting input tags to reloading firmware, and favours restoring a daily snapshot of known-good tags. Because an attacker can write values back too, the monitor must work with a network security appliance that logs access to the PLC, such as SSH and Modbus, and can isolate the workstation onto a standby one before recovery starts. One appliance can guard hundreds of PLCs.

In questions, the speaker said the approach also catches insider actions, since it reacts to the process outcome rather than to who caused it, and that manufacturing and food and beverage sites could use it where the process is critical enough. A frozen sensor reading is a gap, which can be covered by correlating several inputs; one box handles six. The takeaways: monitor only a few critical signals, inspect as many input vectors as possible, build a full zero trust posture, and start small.

talks.title: Cyber Persistence Theory with Michael Fischerkeller
talks.teaser: Explains how states gain strategic advantage through cyber exploitation short of armed conflict, and why defenders should plan for it.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces cyber persistence theory, which holds that most state activity in cyberspace is exploitation, the steady extraction of gains at a target's expense, rather than coercion. Exploitation can accumulate into strategic results without war. North Korea's theft of about two billion dollars from banks and crypto exchanges over four years, which funded its missile and nuclear programs, is one example; China's intellectual property theft, begun around 2010, is another.

Because offense and defense fit competition poorly, the speaker proposes initiative: a posture of anticipation that keeps adversaries reacting. Seizing it can mean corrupting servers where stolen data lands, which he frames as defense, or adopting zero trust. Agreed competition is an unspoken ceiling at the level of use of force or armed attack; states experiment freely below it, but destroying critical infrastructure would cross it and invite crisis. Risk-accepting actors may still push past it. U.S. agencies, including CYBERCOM and the FBI, have grown more proactive, and allied governments are following.

For asset owners and operators, the core recommendation is anticipatory resilience: expect exploitation, plan for it, be able to recover, and share those plans with sector peers. The speaker says state interactions in cyberspace have not yet escalated, though the theory unsettles people because it challenges deterrence.

talks.title: Lateral Movement At Level 1
talks.teaser: Shows how an attacker chains a coupler exploit into nested PLCs and a safety controller at OT level one.
talks.summary:
Many level one industrial devices sit between mixed networks, such as RF modems, field bus segments and third-party packaged units. Earlier research looked at attacks running upward toward supervisory systems, but sideways and deep downward movement from these devices received little attention. The talk argues that any device bridging security zones needs perimeter-grade hardening, and that serial, point-to-point or non-routable links should not be treated as isolated. It also explains why an attacker would want to reach safety instrumented systems, where bypasses may be enabled only through a hardware switch or limited software signals.

To illustrate the risk, the talk walks through a proof-of-concept based on a movable bridge controlled by a coupler, an object PLC and a safety controller. The attacker gets pre-authentication code execution on the coupler through a malformed FTP packet, then turns it into a proxy for the PLC's proprietary protocol. Weaknesses in that protocol's authentication allow a sniffed session value to be replayed and forged requests to be accepted. Using an undocumented command set, the attacker then changes logic in the PLC's memory without restarting it or altering the project checksum, moves into the firmware, and exploits a pre-authentication flaw in the safety controller's Ethernet module across the restricted link.

A short demo shows the full chain, and the speaker notes that protocol-level messages, watchdog behaviour and running task lists could help detect parts of it. The vendor was notified and released advisories with interim mitigations, and the talk proposes a retrofit using a secure remote password exchange with message signing. The main takeaway for practitioners is to review segmentation on level one devices, avoid assuming that serial or non-routable links are safe, and assess impact beyond the immediate connectivity of any compromised link.

talks.title: On Data, Complexity and Asking Questions That Matter
talks.teaser: Argues that exploring unrelated fields and trying new things helps people ask bigger questions in a complex world.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the claim that the world produces more data than people know how to use, that it is complex and changing, and that big questions require going beyond thinking outside the box. The speaker, a data science professor who also performs comedy and circus acts, argues that work in unrelated fields can sharpen thinking in one's own. A slot machine demonstration introduces exploration versus exploitation, linked to the multi-armed bandit problem in reinforcement learning, where people tend to over-exploit what they already know.

Three examples follow. A Beijing air pollution study used license plate driving restrictions and local beliefs about the numbers four and eight to create natural treatment and control groups. An MIT computer scientist treated for breast cancer found her hospital's records were on paper, so she partnered with her oncologist to digitize and analyze them. Physicist Jeffrey West described how a weekly conversation with a biologist helped him build a theory linking growth in organisms, cities and companies.

The talk then draws parallels between circus work and data science, where precision, rigor and discipline matter, and offers a tip for handling fear by treating it as manageable pain. It argues that turning abstract ideas like happiness and trust into data is an overlooked step, and closes with a costume demonstration and a call to get creative. The takeaway is to seek people in unrelated fields and to try new approaches before settling into habits.

talks.title: Leveraging Other Department's Tools To Secure OT
talks.teaser: Shows how OT security teams can reuse engineering, safety, sourcing and finance records to find critical assets faster.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that OT security teams can save time by reusing documents that other departments already maintain. The speakers, who moved into security from engineering, quality, sourcing and safety roles, start from the usual first step of identifying critical assets, which in operational technology grows more complex once safety is involved. They highlight failure modes and effects analysis (FMEA), an engineering tool that ranks failures by severity, occurrence and detection. They suggest adding intentional causes such as ransomware to these analyses, which can raise an item's priority, and building risk assessments and incident playbooks on top of them. Where no FMEA exists, process maps or risk matrices can give a starting view.

Safety and quality teams already keep response plans, such as 8D and PDCA, and the speakers advise adding security to their communication plans and reviewing after-action reports for possible cyber causes. Hazard analysis can support similar cyber reviews. Sourcing teams hold supplier scorecards, vendor audit records and datasheets, which can carry security requirements and checks on vendor access to systems.

Finance is presented as an ally for finding assets that are out of sight, using annual inventory audits, spare parts, calibration and high-value maintenance spending, and capital requests that explain why old equipment remains. Finance staff can also point to people with duplicate devices who make good pilot groups. The speakers close by warning that these documents would also help an attacker, so access should be controlled, and that relationships and shared risk language help win budget.

talks.title: Security Issues In Compiled PLC Logic (CoDeSys & ProConOs)
talks.teaser: Examines how compiled PLC logic in CODESYS and ProConOS runtimes can tamper with controller functions even without root.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at security weaknesses in the runtimes that execute compiled programmable logic controller (PLC) programs, focusing on CODESYS and ProConOS. Recent attack tooling aimed at CODESYS-based controllers, along with a 2022 ProConOS remote code execution bug, prompted the question of whether an attacker could keep a foothold on a PLC without root privileges, assuming the logic runs in a confined user space.

The speaker used vendor documentation and a Raspberry Pi build of the ProConOS eCLR runtime to test this. The runtime heap turned out to be readable, writable and executable, so logic code could overwrite its own instructions, stored user credentials, and the function pointers that protocol handlers and shell commands rely on. Structured text was used to read the process memory map and dump the heap. The speaker also found that initialization code in a binary runs when the file is loaded, before the controller enters run mode, so a malicious program could hook the file receive and factory reset handlers and carry itself into later projects. Testing was limited to the Raspberry Pi runtime, not PLCnext hardware.

For defenders, the speaker argued that logic should be treated as potentially malicious. Suggested measures included running logic in a separate process with inter-process communication despite the performance cost, providing out-of-band project management over a known protocol, restricting engineering ports to engineering workstations, and monitoring scan cycle timing for jitter that could reveal modified logic. Code signing and user management were described as useful but not sufficient against a malicious engineer.

talks.title: S4 Interview with Bill Fehrman CEO of Berkshire Hathaway Energy
talks.teaser: A utility CEO discusses electric sector threat intel sharing, grid recovery drills, transformer sparing and who pays for security.
talks.summary:
At this S4 interview, Bill Fehrman, chief executive of Berkshire Hathaway Energy, described how information sharing between electric utilities and the government has grown over the past couple of years. He pointed to two-way exchange with the intelligence community as a deterrent, noting his company faces 3.5 billion attack attempts a day, with 10 percent being legitimate traffic.

Asked how to measure the program's worth, he said success means keeping layered defenses and recovery capability, judged by whether those fallback strategies had to be used. For smaller utilities, he credited the E-ISAC as the channel that pushes shared lessons out to everyone. On recovery, he described drills that strip away technology until only ham radio operators and retirees who knew manual processes remain, and said the cyber mutual assistance program has been deployed once or twice. He also flagged transformer shortages, the lack of domestic manufacturing, and a cost gap that government funding could help close.

On costs, he expects customers to bear higher security costs and wants regulators to shift from lowest cost toward lowest risk. He favored aspirational incentives and regulation over backward-looking rules, and defended having one industry point of contact supported by co-chairs from public power and cooperatives.

talks.title: Ralph Langner on OT Asset Management
talks.teaser: Explains why automated, on-premise asset inventories underpin OT vulnerability management, change control and obsolescence planning.
talks.summary:
The conversation opens with the guest's move from decades of OT security consulting to building OTbase, an on-premise OT asset management product. He argues that consulting showed how large the problem is, and that the only scalable answer is automation: an inventory built through active probing and refreshed every 24 hours. He separates asset management, which records verified facts about installed devices, from ICS threat detection, which watches for malicious activity, and says the two are distinct product categories.

The discussion then covers vulnerability management, change management and obsolescence planning as parts of asset management. Vulnerability mapping depends on an accurate inventory and needs ongoing CVE curation. The guest suggested that retiring outdated Windows systems and Adobe Flash often reduces risk more than chasing individual patches. Integrations with ServiceNow, SIEM platforms and Power BI dashboards came up, along with a gap: vendors rarely publish machine-readable lists of approved patches. Engineering-focused features such as IP address reservation and planned change workflows were also described.

The closing part addresses how risk dashboards can present OT status to executives. The guest warned that showing only unpatched counts can look bleak and that a strategy beyond patching, such as allowlisting or segmentation, is needed. The main takeaway is that a reliable asset inventory is the foundation for prioritizing vulnerabilities, and that asset tools should serve engineering and maintenance teams as well as security staff.

talks.title: CISA Director Easterly On Metrics
talks.teaser: Explores how a national agency aims to measure whether baseline cyber goals actually reduce risk, not just manage it.
talks.summary:
The session is a short Q&A-style discussion with the CISA director about how the agency knows whether its efforts are working. She explains that a White House national security memorandum from the previous July asked CISA to set baseline goals, so the agency worked with NIST to produce cybersecurity performance goals spanning about 11 categories, including risk management, vulnerability management, incident response, data access and configuration management. Each category states a top-line goal, the rationale behind it, a set of objectives, and sample evidence that an organization could show to prove it met the goal.

The discussion then turns to measurement. Asked how the agency would gather information from sectors such as oil and gas or electricity, and whether reporting would be voluntary, the director acknowledged that measuring effectiveness is hard. She described changing the agency's mission statement from understanding and managing risk to also reducing risk, arguing that managing risk alone falls short of its role as the country's cyber defense agency.

She noted that corporate boards now ask how security spending reduces risk, which makes outcome-based measures more pressing. The sample evidence in the baseline is a starting point, she said, and she hopes it can feed into measures of effectiveness that track actual risk reduction. The takeaway for practitioners is that baseline controls and evidence are being framed as stepping stones toward measurable risk reduction.

talks.title: Richard Seiersen Author Of The Metrics Manifesto
talks.teaser: Explores how security teams can measure whether controls work, using survival analysis, expert forecasts and value-at-risk thinking.
talks.summary:
Richard Seiersen, a chief risk officer and co-author of an earlier book on measuring cyber risk, discusses his new book, The Metrics Manifesto, with the host. He explains that he wrote it for practitioners like himself, security leaders with software and cloud-native backgrounds who wanted evidence that their work was helping the business. Roughly half the book is R code. He says readers can follow the concepts without typing it in, since the code is posted online by chapter.

The conversation centers on the book's framework, which he describes as baseline, objectives and optimization measures. He explains survival analysis, which tracks how long risks stay open so that a slow tail of unpatched vulnerabilities is not hidden by an improving average. He also covers arrival rate and wait time as shift-left measures and escape rate as a way to track risk moving toward production, using National Vulnerability Database data as an example. The discussion then turns to operational technology, where patching may not reduce risk much, and to value at risk and insurance limits as ways to judge whether a control is worth its cost.

His takeaway is to measure the controls you consider important, and to use calibrated subject matter experts when data is sparse. He argues that serious fields all treat measurement as a basic part of their work, and he urges security professionals to look at how those fields do it.

talks.title: S4x23 Call For Presentations
talks.teaser: Offers guidance on writing a winning S4 proposal: lead with a new big idea, stay concise, and submit early.
talks.summary:
Dale Peterson, founder and program chair of S4 Events, walks through the call for presentations for the S4 conference in Miami Beach, held February 14 to 16, with submissions open until August 31. He explains that the event is built for advanced ICS security practitioners and favors forward-looking ideas over best-practice, lessons-learned and case-study sessions. Panels are rarely accepted. The main stage suits big-picture or adjacent topics such as cyber insurance or attacker psychology, stage two is reserved for deep technical dives where a speaker should pick one key point and go far into it, and stage three hosts special sessions such as half-day workshops or training.

He then gives submission advice. Proposals should be kept to a few paragraphs, opening with the big idea and why it is new, rather than spending most of the text describing the problem. Early submissions have better odds because slots fill up by late summer. Selected speakers receive a free ticket, a professionally shot video and a swag bag, and first-time speakers face a lower bar for acceptance than returning presenters. A limited number of travel stipends is available for speakers whose own company will not cover the cost.

talks.title: Ilan Gendelman of SIGA OT Solutions
talks.teaser: An OT security CTO explains electrical-signal tapping, subset sensor monitoring, and process-variable anomaly detection for plants.
talks.summary:
The episode explores how industrial environments can spot cyber-driven process manipulation when higher-layer controls may already lie to operators. SIGA OT Solutions frames its approach as process-oriented cyber detection: observing raw electrical signals between sensors and PLCs rather than relying mainly on packet data, often duplicating those signals out of band over separate paths such as cellular links so visibility stays largely isolated from production networks.

The discussion covers unsupervised learning that establishes a client-defined baseline, limits such as blind spots when a faulty sensor was always treated as normal, and the core goal of catching how attacks above level one ultimately distort physical behavior. A comparison capability highlights divergence between tapped process readings and what PLCs, historians, or other levels report, supporting spoofing or man-in-the-middle scenarios. Implementation is described as a small fraction of I/O—often cited as three to seven percent—selected through site surveys of critical processes and influential points, with examples like dozens of taps on large turbines.

The back end integrates multiple OT data sources, stresses contextual and explainable alerts, and separates operational drift from cyber suspicion, contrasted with heavyweight digital-twin modeling. Practitioners hear deployment effort, validation through daily alerting and external tests, and how selective instrumentation plus high-fidelity process data fits brownfield risk reduction.
