talks.title: Test Effect Payloads for Tuning ICS Incident Response
talks.teaser: Shows how DARPA Radix uses test effect payloads and Netflix-style chaos experiments to tune ICS incident response on power systems.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces the DARPA Radix program, which develops tools to detect, isolate and characterize attacks on critical infrastructure. Exercises run a black start power recovery on real equipment during an ongoing cyberattack, lasting about a week. The speaker stresses that defenders assume the adversary is already inside and focus on reclaiming ground they can defend.

The speaker compares this with Netflix's chaos engineering, where Chaos Monkey randomly dropped sessions and Chaos Gorilla simulated losing a data center. Radix uses test effect payloads, small tunable misconfigurations or scripted effects, to challenge responders. Examples include an unlisted host sending DNP traffic, an HMI showing altered voltage while field data stays correct, and a relay misconfigured to overcurrent at power-up.

For practitioners, the method starts with high-consequence outcomes, the systems that could cause them, and the observables an attack would leave. Teams state expected responses, run a blast radius analysis, and start small. Repeating experiments and treating results as learning, not pass or fail, matters most.

talks.title: Prairie Storm 2019: Hands On Power Grid Incident Response Exercise
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Prairie Storm 2019: Hands On Power Grid Incident Response Exercise.

talks.title: Survey of ICS Firmware Security
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Survey of ICS Firmware Security.
talks.summary: A Red Balloon Security founder revisits the company's 2018 S4 script that found VxWorks n-days across ICS firmware with twenty lines of Python. He explains why reactive patching cannot keep pace as disclosed flaws arrive in machine-time batches such as the Artemis VxWorks dump. A collaboration with Idaho National Laboratory and Cyber ITL shared public firmware, automated unpacking, and quick zero-day hunts that reproduced hard-coded keys and privilege flaws across entire product families. Cyber ITL scoring shows PLC firmware security roughly on par with consumer routers on dimensions like ASLR and stack guards, despite higher safety stakes. Legal and vendor friction around sharing firmware formats remains a bottleneck even when binaries are nominally public.

talks.title: Five Blind People and an Elephant called ICS Supply Chain Security
talks.teaser: Explains how fingerprints, software bills of materials and shared trust scores can vet control system firmware before loading.
talks.summary:
Eric Byers starts with the problem of validating third-party firmware in industrial control systems. Early conversations with people in the field each described a different supply chain concern, from counterfeit code to components hidden inside vendor packages and technicians loading obsolete versions. He recalls the Dragonfly campaign, where attackers tampered with vendor download sites, and explains why hashes and code signing alone fall short: hashes need an out-of-band reference and give only a yes-or-no answer.

The second half presents the framework his team built. Vendors fingerprint software at build time, the results become a software bill of materials, and that data is checked against public sources such as vulnerability databases and malware scanners. Results are expressed as a score, much like a credit score, and can inherit trust from a signed distribution bundle. In a demo, a Rockwell binary inherits trust from its signed bundle while a lookalike does not.

He closes by inviting vendors, asset owners, integrators and consultants to join the community and test samples on a free portal. Answering questions, he said the approach would catch tampering with download sites but not compromise of a vendor's internal development, where it could only make attacks harder. Practitioners should take away that a single hash or signature is not enough; context and shared data matter.

talks.title: Threat Hunting With What You Have
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Threat Hunting With What You Have.

talks.title: Factories Are Families: How Does Security Join The Family?
talks.teaser: See how listening to factory workers can help security fit the realities of production and safety.
talks.summary: The speakers describe how security work in factories depends on understanding operators’ priorities, workplace culture and the effect of controls on production and safety. They share examples involving equipment placement, physical access, training and production disruptions, and explain how observation and empathy can help security teams work with factory staff and reduce risk.

talks.title: Building An OT Capable SOC
talks.teaser: Outlines how operational technology security functions can fit into a security operations center, from people to tooling.
talks.summary:
The talk explores how an organisation can bring operational technology security into a security operations center. It argues a SOC is more than monitors and analysts in a dark room, and rests on three pillars: people with tiered, mixed skills; technology shaped by what data can be collected; and process that must be agreed on and tested. Functions span preparedness, proactive work such as threat hunting and tabletop exercises, and reactive incident response.

The speaker contrasts an IT SOC with an OT SOC, noting industrial protocols, diverse endpoints such as controllers and engineering workstations, and the consequences a routine network scan can have on a process. Several models are compared: extending an existing IT SOC, a dedicated OT SOC, adding security duties to a control room, outsourcing to managed providers, or a hybrid. Collection ranges from netflow and offline pcaps to span ports, syslog and historian data, and a collection management framework helps map plants, crown-jewel areas and network architecture.

A worked example follows an alert from the OT monitoring platform into the SIEM, where a tier 1 analyst verifies it. A ticket is then raised and an investigation follows a playbook, with containment and recovery steps that are reviewed over time. The closing checklist asks whether risk justifies the investment, whether infrastructure supports collection, what budget and staff are available, and how licensing scales. Success can be tracked through coverage, mean time to detect and mean time to recover, and the program should grow in phases rather than being built at once.

talks.title: Nation State ICS Attack On A Budget
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Nation State ICS Attack On A Budget.

talks.title: Ralph Langner, Zach Tudor & Dale Peterson On ICS Security in 2020 ... from the S4x20 Closing Panel
talks.teaser: Panelists debate workforce gaps, executive messaging, regulation and a quiet year for OT attacks.
talks.summary:
The closing panel of the S4x20 event brought together Ralph Langner, Zach Tudor and Dale Peterson to look at what the week had left out. They began with the near absence of artificial intelligence from the sessions. One view was that industrial data is piling up and will soon call for algorithms, while another held that basic gaps, such as large backlogs of known vulnerabilities and aging Windows 7 systems, need fixing before AI can help.

The conversation then moved to threats and messaging. Langner pointed out that no sophisticated OT attack had surfaced in about two years, and that Iran's feared retaliation had amounted to a web defacement of an obscure government site. The panelists agreed that fear-based pitches to executives are wearing thin, and that business leaders want tangible, evidence-backed risk arguments. On workforce, they saw strong demand for ICS security staff, but warned that many organizations still assign OT security to one or two people as a side duty. Regulation drew skepticism: compliance rules were described as setting minimum bars, and a proposed new standard was questioned. Endpoint protection for PLCs was described as lacking demand from asset owners.

The panel closed on a more optimistic note, expecting technology breakthroughs and open-source approaches to shape the field. The organizers then previewed the next event, with a call for papers, a larger venue and a feedback survey for attendees.

talks.title: Securing California's Distributed Energy Resources (DER)
talks.teaser: Explains how California secures networked rooftop solar systems through standards, certificates and a supply-chain PKI.
talks.summary:
The talk traces how California's rooftop solar and storage systems, known as distributed energy resources, became networked. It begins with grid trip problems seen in Germany in 2008 and explains how California adopted IEEE 2030.5 as its default control protocol, narrowing its scope to the link between utility servers and the next hop. Mutual TLS authentication with digital certificates covers servers, intermediate systems and end devices, and three communication paths are described, including aggregated systems that may represent 50,000 to 100,000 units.

The middle section focuses on threats and the certificate supply chain. Root authorities stay offline, while manufacturers act as sub CAs that receive certificates in bulk and install them on devices in factories. A compromise at that stage could enable counterfeiting, so sub CA compromise is ranked as a high-probability, high-severity threat. Utility servers and aggregators come next, and client devices are treated as a lower concern. The speaker noted that certificates under the standard never expire and cannot be revoked, an issue now under review. Responses include certification testing and a blockchain working group aimed at securing PKI supply chains.

The closing argument is that network security for these resources reaches well beyond the narrow utility interface, covering firmware updates, aggregator vetting and gateway hardening as deployments grow. Practitioners should note that the trust chain set at the factory and the certificate lifecycle need to be right before field exposure becomes a real concern. The speaker expects the approach to spread to the next 25 solar states.

talks.title: Factory Honeynet: Highly Realistic and Interactive
talks.teaser: Walks through a six-month high-interaction honeypot posing as a factory and the intrusions it attracted.
talks.summary:
The project began with news coverage of factories hit by ransomware, and the team wanted to see how such attacks actually unfold. They built a high-interaction honeypot imitating a plastics injection molding plant. The HMI was designed first, and PLC logic then produced believable process behaviour, such as a conveyor that ramps up and down and simulated pressure readings. The exposed persona was a small company with two locations, generated staff photos, and phone lines with receptionist greetings and voicemail. Only a few PLC ports and VNC were reachable from the internet, and the network was fully tapped for monitoring.

Activity stayed near zero until early summer, when the team opened VNC to the robotics workstation. Afterwards, one intruder installed a backdoor that turned out to run a Monero miner, which overheated the host laptops until the team blocked it. A ransomware operator ran TeamViewer and several tools, watched the process for about an hour and a half, and demanded a payment that was negotiated down but never made. A decryption test on a sample Omron project file showed the actor did not understand what the data was. Another intruder exfiltrated roughly seven gigabytes, while a script renamed files with no record kept, making recovery impossible. One operator left the simulated process running unchecked for four hours.

Across six months the team logged thousands of unique IPs, with only a small share classified as scanners and clear regional patterns in PLC queries. The main conclusions were that control systems should never be placed directly on the internet, and that attackers often seemed more interested in using a clean IP than in disrupting production. The speaker also stressed that a high-interaction honeypot needs daily attention, with incidents handled as they happen.

talks.title: GPS As An Attack Vector
talks.teaser: Demonstrates how unauthenticated GNSS signals could carry covert commands to receivers in industrial control networks.
talks.summary:
Mike Tucker opens by noting that GNSS receivers, mostly GPS clocks, are common in industrial control environments such as substations, generation sites and oil and gas facilities, mainly for time synchronization. The core problem he raises is that these signals are unauthenticated, so anyone with the right equipment can feed a receiver a convincing signal. Instead of focusing on spoofing, he explores using the signal as a one-way command and control channel into a network.

His first plan, built around a decommissioned clock, a transmitter, antennas and a rack of automation gear, proved too risky, with too many components to test. He shifted to a software-only proof of concept. A modified GPS-SDR-SIM generates a baseband signal carrying commands in page 17 of the navigation message, and a modified GNSS-SDR receiver parses that page and runs actions, such as scanning a local subnet for Modbus on port 502 and changing registers. He described the frame layout, where subframes four and five repeat their pages across satellites, and said his file format was still wrong, so the chain did not yet work end to end.

He closed with defenses. Commercial GPS firewalls try to flag spoofed signals by checking for unusually high signal strength, signals arriving from a terrestrial direction, or protocol gaps. In questions he said he knew of no commercial receiver that accepts commands over GPS. The practical takeaway is to question which unverified inputs are allowed into an environment and whether they are checked.

talks.title: Tuning ICS Security Alerts: An Alarm Management Approach
talks.teaser: Applies ICS alarm management standards to tuning network security alerts, cutting nuisance alerts and building playbooks.
talks.summary:
The talk addresses a gap in published guidance on handling alerts from network security monitoring sensors in industrial control system environments. The speaker proposes reusing alarm management practices from ISA 18.2 and EEMUA 191, along with the tuning guidance in NIST SP 800-94, to write a security alert philosophy that defines alert categories, priorities, metrics and change management. He ties this to forensics, arguing that after the 2003 blackout the logs lacked the detail needed for root cause analysis, and that digital evidence should be treated as part of the same effort.

The middle of the talk walks through a client case in which two network sensors were installed without tuning. They generated more than 800,000 active alerts that nobody had addressed, and the baselining feature was never used. A mesh radio system that changed IP addresses thousands of times a day triggered alerts that could have been suppressed by loading the radios' MAC addresses into the learned database. Default Zeek settings alerted on every DNP3 function code. The speaker explained false positives and false negatives with the shepherd analogy, and warned that noisy alerts cause alert fatigue, citing a retail breach in which an early warning was missed among too much data.

The closing advice is to start small at key ingress and egress points, use existing logs, and test new rules against captured traffic on a test system before deployment. Security alerts should stay off operator HMIs. Teams should also build incident response playbooks for commodity malware, credential theft and destructive attacks, with each play tied to alerts, remediation steps and named contacts across engineering, operations and the SOC.

talks.title: Cyber Nationalism: Pick A Side
talks.teaser: Panelists debate why vendors grant governments hidden access, and how that shapes trust in critical infrastructure suppliers.
talks.summary:
The panel opens with a case study of a Siemens S7-1200 programmable logic controller. Researchers found an undocumented special access feature in its bootloader chip: sending a specific bit string within the first half second after boot unlocked capabilities such as reading and writing flash memory. The speakers stress that no nation-state attribution is claimed, only that a feature like this is the kind a vendor could add for selected customers.

Olaf argues that vendors may yield to coercion from their home government, from the country where they sell, from demanding customers, or for financial reasons, and he cites the Volkswagen diesel emissions case as a hardware precedent. Deniability is central to how vendors negotiate, and the Cisco and Supermicro cases were raised as speculation rather than proof. Dan suggests multinationals may split into separate, firewalled divisions, and the panel debates whether vendors must pick a geopolitical camp, with interoperability standards likely to diverge.

For asset owners, the panel recommends threat modelling: assume attempts will be made, and recognise that a supplier's remote update path can remain a risk years after purchase. The main safeguard discussed is avoiding silent failure. Vendors that commit to disclosing anomalies, combined with many independent observers, would narrow the room for hidden behaviour, though Olaf admits there is no easy fix.

talks.title: Cisco Cyber Vision: Cybersecurity for the Industrial Internet
talks.teaser: Explains how Cisco Cyber Vision gives industrial networks asset visibility and policy-based segmentation through its ISE integration.
talks.summary:
Industrial control environments often lack a clear inventory of what is connected, and the speaker argues that visibility is the first hurdle to securing them. IT-style discovery such as port scanning can disrupt fragile devices, while copying traffic with SPAN ports becomes costly across widely spread sites like substations and field locations.

Cisco Cyber Vision is presented as a two-tier system. Hardware sensors perform deep packet inspection on industrial protocols, building asset profiles and communication baselines, and flagging configuration changes, unusual connections and known vulnerabilities. A central component aggregates that data and can run as hardware or a virtual appliance. Because inspection happens at the edge, the traffic sent back is only a small share of network load. Grouping assets by process lets IT and operations plan maintenance windows together rather than rushing patches into production.

A use case shows Identity Services Engine consuming Cyber Vision profiles to enforce segmentation policies on switches and routers without installing agents on devices. In an emergency, such as a device talking to an unexpected camera or running a cryptominer, the policy can contain the malicious traffic and let the industrial process keep running instead of isolating the node. The main takeaway is that embedded sensing and network-enforced policy suit OT better than span-based or out-of-band designs, though the speaker noted that encrypted TLS 1.3 traffic remained an open question.

talks.title: Controlled Chaos - The Inevitable Marriage of DevOps & Security
talks.teaser: Explores how chaos engineering and resilience can help security teams align with DevOps and protect industrial control systems.
talks.summary:
Kelly Shortridge argues that DevOps, which unifies responsibility and accountability for software delivery, is reshaping how organizations run their infrastructure, including industrial control systems that are moving toward cloud platforms. She says security teams should join this shift rather than stand aside. Her proposed approach is chaos and resilience engineering, built on the idea that security controls will fail and incidents cannot be fully prevented, so systems should be designed to handle them gracefully.

The talk introduces the DIE model as an alternative to the CIA triad, describing three traits of modern infrastructure: distributed, immutable, and ephemeral. Distributed design limits outage severity through redundancy, immutable servers are rebuilt from version-controlled images rather than patched by hand, and short-lived resources shrink the window attackers have to persist. For testing, she recommends game days built around business priorities and the least-costly attacker path, starting in test environments. Examples include moving IP space across availability zones, planting bait files that shut down a container when an attacker tries to modify them, flagging outdated library versions, and monitoring cloud billing spikes that may signal data exfiltration or cryptomining.

She closes by urging ICS security teams to practice these experiments now, while many field systems remain unchanged, and to become enablers rather than gatekeepers.

talks.title: Claroty: OT Security - Enter The CISO
talks.teaser: Explains how CISOs inheriting operational technology security can build visibility, risk baselines and non-disruptive controls.
talks.summary:
This session is aimed at CISOs who have just been handed responsibility for operational technology security. The speaker explains that many security leaders have little visibility into their OT environments and no baseline of asset communications to measure risk against. He points to unfamiliar industrial devices and protocols, legacy equipment that can stay in service for decades without basic authentication or encryption, and the danger that IT security tools can break production systems. He also stresses that OT staff are essential to validating any tool.

The threat picture is mostly non-targeted. Commodity malware, such as ransomware that spreads from corporate IT into plant networks, is the more common route in, which pushes governance toward a unified IT and OT framework. He argues a workable solution must be credible (mirroring IT security controls), efficient (fitting existing people, process and technology) and non-disruptive (doing no harm to production or IT operations). Capabilities he covers include risk assessment and remediation priorities, asset and communication visibility, vulnerability context for patching under operational limits, network segmentation, and detection of attackers abusing native device functions.

He closes by saying OT risk management has to be simplified: security terms need translating into language IT analysts understand, tools must integrate with existing security stacks, and deployment should be low-touch, with cloud delivery expected to cut cost and maintenance. The takeaway is to treat OT security as ongoing risk management rather than a one-time compliance exercise.

talks.title: Applying the Rust Programming Language in ICS
talks.teaser: Shows how Rust's compile-time checks prevent common memory bugs in industrial control system software.
talks.summary:
Overview
Adam Crane argues that Rust represents a critical modernization path for industrial control systems programming. Rather than blaming developers, he attributes persistent security bugs to using tools fundamentally ill-suited to contemporary requirements—specifically, C, which has remained essentially unchanged since 1972. Crane positions Rust adoption as inevitable, driven primarily by the massive productivity benefits developers gain when using a language designed for both safety and systems programming.

Key Topics
Rust sits alongside C, C++, and Go as a compiled-to-machine-code language but uniquely offers both memory and thread safety without performance overhead. Crane catalogs five categories of C vulnerabilities—dangling references, use-after-free, null pointer dereferences, buffer overflows, and data races—and explains how Rust's compiler catches most of these at compile time through the borrow checker and ownership model, or enforces them at runtime via type constraints. The Rust ecosystem provides Cargo (integrated package management and build system), comprehensive documentation, and LLVM backend support for embedded architectures including ARM, MIPS, and PowerPC. Concretely, Crane presents Rod Bus, a Modbus client library released alongside the talk and available via crates.io, which includes a zero-cost C API shim enabling seamless integration with existing C/C++ codebases.

Technical Details
Rod Bus achieves 200,000 Modbus requests per second while consuming less than 1 megabyte of RAM. Rust's ownership model prevents dangling references and use-after-free at compile time through the borrow checker; the compiler uses lifetimes (denoted with apostrophes, e.g., 'a) to statically verify that references cannot outlive their referents. For multi-threaded safety, Rust employs Arc (atomic reference counting) for thread-safe shared ownership and Mutex for coordinated access, preventing data races through type system constraints rather than runtime checks. Code examples demonstrate the compiler rejecting unsafe patterns; for instance, after moving a variable's ownership, attempting to reference it triggers a detailed error message explaining the violation. Performance comparisons show Rustls, a Rust implementation of TLS, using less than half the memory of OpenSSL in most scenarios.

Practical Deployment in ICS
Rust is most suitable for new greenfield systems with real-time and low-memory constraints. More pragmatically for existing vendors, Rust's C ABI compatibility enables gradual replacement of legacy components—an approach exemplified by Suricata IDS incrementally replacing protocol parsers with Rust and Mozilla replacing high-risk Firefox components. Crane plans to enhance Rod Bus by integrating Rustls and implementing X.509 certificate-based access control for secure Modbus, allowing vendors to enforce role-based permissions through certificate validation.

When Rust Does Not Fit
Adoption is impractical for vendors with large Windows-based deployments of Java, C#, or Go applications, or where critical library dependencies lack Rust implementations. The learning curve, while gentler than C++, exceeds that of Go or Java, presenting onboarding challenges for teams unfamiliar with ownership and borrowing concepts.

Takeaways
Rust stabilized in 2018 with a commitment to backward compatibility going forward. Adoption is accelerating in major technology projects (Microsoft, Firefox, Suricata) though ICS-specific deployments remain nascent. University computer science curricula increasingly include Rust. Rather than replacing all C codebases overnight, Rust enables pragmatic incremental hardening of legacy systems and rapid secure development of new critical components, all enabled by C interoperability and measurably improved developer confidence in correctness.

talks.title: Lessons Learned from Norsk Hydro on Loss Estimation and Cyber Insurance
talks.teaser: Walks through estimating ransomware losses from public data and how cyber insurance fits into that financial picture.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a quantitative risk analyst, uses the Norsk Hydro ransomware attack as a case study in turning publicly available information into a risk estimate, rather than dwelling on the technical details. The attack was targeted, not self-spreading, and hit office systems rather than industrial controls. Roughly 48% of endpoints and about 33% of servers were infected, and around 15% of servers were encrypted. A contagious-malware model would have treated that spread as fairly typical, which shows that lateral movement by a targeted attacker can reach similar levels of penetration.

Reported costs were 300 million Norwegian kroner per quarter, which the speaker converted to roughly 75 million dollars. Share price, credit rating commentary and competitor results showed no clear cyber effect, because other pressures such as executive turnover and a spill in Brazil dominated. The speaker argued for forward-looking discounted cash flow thinking and bow-tie models built from branching activities. Hidden costs such as staff fatigue and a rise in phishing after the breach should also be counted. A comparable campaign against other companies showed how prior complications and insurance arrangements shaped outcomes.

On cyber insurance, the speaker stressed that policies carry limits, participation shares, exclusions and gaps, so layered coverage still leaves holes. In a review of 69 policies, 58% covered business interruption, 42% covered extortion, and under 2% covered overtime costs. The takeaway is that insurance is a form of risk finance that helps an organisation survive a loss, not a full transfer of risk or a substitute for prevention.

talks.title: Moody's / Team8: Cyber Risk Ratings for Companies
talks.teaser: Explains how Moody's and Team8 are building a cyber risk rating that expresses exposure in financial terms and allows peer benchmarking.
talks.summary:
Moody's, a credit rating agency, treats cyber risk alongside environmental risk as an existential business threat. Its global cyber risk group, formed in 2018, studied how cyber events affect credit. An earlier white paper covering 35 rated sectors flagged 13 of them as high or medium-high risk based on likely financial impact.

The talk covers a joint venture with Team8 to build a standalone cyber risk assessment and rating. Boards and executives want exposure expressed in financial terms and comparable peer benchmarks. The method blends management assessments, surveys, outside-in scanning and inside testing that validates the results, with the aim of completing assessments in weeks rather than months. Three obstacles were described: thin loss data, with only about 4% of roughly 130,000 entries in one commercial set holding enough financial detail; signal decay, where long-standing guidance such as forced password changes no longer predicts resilience; and industrial control environments, which the team has not yet addressed in depth.

Rather than a 0 to 100 score that implies false precision, the team is considering ordinal cohorts that separate firms able to withstand sophisticated attacks from those that can only stop commodity ones. The rating is meant to be transparent and independent, with no remediation work for assessed firms, and the team is seeking community input. Practitioners should weigh the data limits behind any output.

talks.title: Distributed Energy Resource (DER) Attack Vectors
talks.teaser: Examines how attackers could target consumer-side devices to disrupt grid frequency as low-inertia renewables spread.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at demand-side attacks, where an attacker reaches consumer devices that draw power from the grid instead of substations or generators, and uses them to disturb grid frequency. Earlier research modeled botnets of high-wattage IoT devices such as air conditioners and concluded that grid system inertia would usually absorb the effect. The speaker argues that rising solar and other low-inertia resources make such attacks more feasible over time, and lists the factors that matter: botnet size, regional distributed energy penetration, time of day and weather.

Connected devices are hard to count because many internet-visible systems are honeypots. One example was an internet-facing device at an engineering college that was a real student-made system, not a honeypot, and the speaker framed it as a misconfiguration rather than a vendor flaw. Industrial equipment such as CNC machines draws far more power, so one compromised machine could equal dozens of air conditioners. Load shedding alone can still cause outages for customers, so full frequency collapse is not required. Virtual inertia and storage are possible mitigations but remain imperfect.

The national lab's work combines GIS modeling with data from frequency monitoring devices placed in homes, businesses and solar plants, including after a hurricane in Puerto Rico. The Q&A covered cascading inverter trips, interruptible industrial contracts and voltage versus frequency concerns. The main takeaway is that patching fails when attackers sit on footholds outside utility control, so defenders need to watch the consumer side too.

talks.title: Shiny Object Syndrome ... Is OT Anomaly Detection Worth It?
talks.teaser: Weighs the real costs and risk reduction of OT anomaly detection against dedicated staff and preventive controls.
talks.summary:
The speaker recounts an early rollout of OT anomaly detection across many plant sites a decade ago, where untuned alerts flooded networks. At one site, a colleague's plant went down during a holiday, and the outage was traced to the software, costing about $1 million. Today the speaker sees the technology as more mature, with better installation, tuning and learning, but questions whether its risk reduction justifies the cost.

The talk lays out what running such a system needs: visibility across east-west as well as north-south traffic, or strict removable media controls, since one infection stayed within a single network level. Tuning reportedly cut about 150 daily alerts at a refinery to around 25, yet each alert can take a day to investigate, so staffing must cover every hour through tiered OT SOC levels. One-time costs run about $140,000 per site, or about $680,000 with SOC setup, while annual run and maintenance for one site reaches roughly $1.6 million.

Using the engineering bowtie, the speaker argues that anomaly detection acts only after a top event has already occurred, while preventive controls act earlier. A single dedicated OT security person, running governance, training, asset inventory, media controls, patching and backups, could address more of that left side for a similar budget, the speaker contends. The closing question is whether the software reduces risk enough to justify its cost, or whether it is another shiny object.

talks.title: Nozomi - Encryption in ICS and It's Impact on Passive Monitoring
talks.teaser: Examines why industrial networks rarely encrypt, and how IEC 62351 encryption affects monitoring and attack detection.
talks.summary:
The presenters explain that encryption is uncommon in industrial control field devices such as RTUs, PLCs and sensors. They cite added operational overhead, the difficulty of retrofitting certificates and keys into existing infrastructure, timing limits for protocols like GOOSE, and the loss of visibility for monitoring tools. The talk frames IEC 62351 as a way to add security above existing power grid standards without replacing the infrastructure.

The session focuses on Part 3, which mandates TLS over TCP/IP, and Part 7, which exposes device status such as CPU, memory and certificate state through queries. For monitoring encrypted traffic, the speaker outlines private key sharing, a proxy that sits in the middle, and session key sharing, which is harder with TLS 1.3. Two lab attacks on an RTU follow. In the first, the switch acting as an NTP server is pushed four years ahead, so the RTU's certificate expires and new sessions fail. A passive timestamp comparison or an active clock-tamper query polled every 15 seconds with a 30-day alert threshold can reveal it. In the second, an insider installs a rogue CA certificate and authenticates without touching the legitimate traffic, which an active request for the device's CA certificates can expose.

The main takeaway is that encryption in OT is workable but calls for an architecture decision. Teams should weigh the risk in each segment, encrypt where it matters, and combine passive and active monitoring to keep visibility.

talks.title: Secure Coding Practices for PLC's
talks.teaser: Walks through defensive PLC programming habits that limit attack surface, validate inputs, and make faults easier to diagnose.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at secure coding habits for programmable logic controllers, a subject the speaker says engineers rarely learn in school. Control engineers are usually taught process design rather than how to program these devices. The speaker reviews the main PLC languages, including ladder diagram, function block diagram, instruction list, structured text and sequential function charts, and notes that the choice often depends on whether electricians or programmers do the work. Architecture advice follows: keep controllers close to the I/O, keep program segments small, and avoid routing many devices through one shared switch.

The middle section covers the PLC scan cycle and why the controller should not be the box that serves general network traffic. Input validation is a recurring theme. Check for system faults, validate inputs and outputs before acting, bound timer and counter values, and raise alarms when contradictory signals such as forward and reverse appear together. A read-only buffer for HMI writes lets the controller overwrite rogue values and flag the attempt. Variable frequency drives should get a simple 4 to 20 milliamp loop instead of a network connection where possible. Motor restarts should be blocked by a delay timer, and indirect addressing should be bounded to the array size. Sets and resets should be cross-checked so they are never asserted together.

The closing part recommends heartbeats between peer devices, reading vendor diagnostics such as message counts and cycle times, and recording a code version hash. The question period covered testing with simulators, the lack of commercial tools for scanning PLC logic, and the difficulty of building security review into tight integration projects. The main takeaway is that many of these safeguards are missing from specifications and must be added on purpose.

talks.title: Dispel
talks.teaser: Explains how a moving target defense layer and rapid remote access can secure vendor and operator access to industrial control systems.
talks.summary:
This sponsor-stage session looks at how operators and vendors reach equipment at remote industrial sites such as wind farms, solar installations and automated wells. The speaker says that today this usually means waiting for a specialist to arrive, driving someone out to the site, or working through a long login chain. The example walked through a typical vendor path: a VPN into the corporate network, a first jump host, a second jump host for the control cluster, and finally an RDP session. The speaker says this can take 12 to 15 minutes when done by hand, and claims the product connects users in seconds.

The middle of the talk argues that static defences fail because fixed VPN endpoints and jump hosts stay in the same place, so attackers can map them and reuse an exploit once a weakness is published. The proposed alternative is moving target defense, which keeps the path between the two ends changing. The product builds single-use, single-tenant networks across public cloud providers for each session, then tears them down or recycles them afterward. On-site hardware enforces user-specific allowlists. One customer, a water utility, reported about one million dollars in first-year savings from staff time, and the speaker said the security team was no longer seen as the blocker for operations.

The closing part covered authentication, which can either use a built-in console with username, password and multi-factor, or plug into an approval mechanism the organization already uses. For regulated environments, sessions can be screen recorded, livestreamed, or logged through syslog. The speaker asked the audience to bring the approach to their operational technology teams for a briefing and a trial, noting that a discretionary budget could fund it.

talks.title: Owl Cyber Defense - Edge Protection for the OT
talks.teaser: Explains how one-way data diodes and hardware-enforced protocol breaks can cut external connections into industrial networks.
talks.summary:
This sponsor-stage talk argues that operational technology networks are better protected by cutting external connections and limiting them to one direction than by detecting intrusions afterward. The presenters open with a Department of Homeland Security publication listing seven strategies, which they say would have prevented 98% of the reported threats and breaches. They frame the problem around an average of 583 external connections per enterprise, where each link is a possible entry point.

The middle of the talk covers the mitigation steps: convert as many links as possible to one-way outbound flows, move inbound patches through vetted one-way paths, and keep the few bidirectional links on a single device that can be switched off when idle. The speaker explains a data diode as a light transmitter on the source side that cannot receive, and a receiver on the destination side that cannot send. Their products add a protocol break that removes IP addressing, which keeps self-propagating malware from crossing. Use cases include remote monitoring without remote access, historian replication, asset-level micro-segmentation, and a pipeline pressure sensor sending Modbus or OPC data. A product called Recon handles bidirectional command-and-control using two reversed sets of diodes and a TCP/IP proxy.

The closing advice is to map connections, sort them by risk, and convert what you can to one-way flows while layering other defenses. The speakers stressed that a diode does not train staff to avoid phishing, so it is not a silver bullet.

talks.title: Cybersecurity Oversight and Governance: Managing the Risk
talks.teaser: Surveys the cyber laws, SEC disclosure expectations and board oversight duties that companies face around breaches.
talks.summary:
Cyber risk now ranks as a top concern for senior executives, and several have resigned after major data breaches. The talk surveys the threat landscape: nation-states seeking espionage, criminals stealing data for profit, hacktivists aiming to sabotage, and extortionists using ransomware. Cited figures include attackers being found internally in 59 percent of cases, outside parties alerting the company in 41 percent, repeat attacks in 64 percent of cases, and a median dwell time of 78 days.

On the law, the speaker describes a fragmented US landscape of federal, state and sector rules, with 54 breach notification laws. Industry frameworks such as NIST and ISO 27000 are effectively expected by insurers and business partners. The SEC's 2011 staff guidance and 2018 commission guidance are reviewed alongside enforcement cases: a 35 million dollar Yahoo settlement, a 100 million dollar Facebook settlement over misleading disclosures, and criminal insider trading convictions in the Equifax matter. Europe's NIS Directive, GDPR's 72-hour reporting rule and China's cyber security law round out the picture.

On governance, boards increasingly oversee cyber risk through an audit or technology committee, with the mandate written into a charter and regular reporting. The talk walks through a typical incident sequence, from containment and legal analysis to notifications, regulator inquiries, lawsuits and a post-mortem. The main takeaways are to take a risk-based approach, bring counsel in early, and document board duties.

talks.title: Critical Infrastructure as Code (CIAC) in ICS
talks.teaser: Applies infrastructure-as-code ideas to configuring control system devices, with lab findings on Ansible, git and vendor tools.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that configuration management for industrial control systems is still ad hoc and often tied to each vendor's software, leaving settings spread across laptops, servers and devices. The speaker proposes infrastructure-as-code ideas from IT and cloud work: define configurations explicitly in readable files, version them, and push them to devices, so operators can restore positive control over system state.

A lab's energy systems group tested this on its digital twin testbed, using a template database, device definitions and generated files, with Ansible over SSH and git for history and rollback. Results varied by device. Protection relays exposed text configurations over telnet and FTP, remote terminal units only yielded binary blobs, and a generator controller's vendor library was poorly documented, with a comparison call that returned only true or false. Serial-to-Ethernet converters offered the easiest JSON interface, but enabling its management mode removed password protection.

A line-ending mismatch between Windows and Unix files bricked a device after one changed file, and insecure access methods were a recurring trade-off. The speaker urged vendors to supply safe libraries and the community to agree on common functions and interfaces. In the Q&A, a standard API was suggested as a basis for automated fuzzing, though centralizing configurations also creates risk.

talks.title: Fortinet
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Fortinet - Beyond Visibility in OT.

talks.title: DHS CISA Director Chris Krebs Keynote
talks.teaser: Outlines the federal cybersecurity agency's priorities, with a focus on its industrial control systems initiative and training resources.
talks.summary:
The keynote opens with the history of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, a civilian agency created in 2018 from a legacy part of the Department of Homeland Security. The director explains that the agency cannot compel private operators to do anything; its role is to advise, share information and help owners manage their own risk. He lists five disciplines, IT security, control system security, supply chain, insider threat and physical security, and three audiences: security teams, executives and the general public.

Five strategic priorities follow from the period after a 35-day federal shutdown: federal network security, election security, soft target protection, industrial control systems, and supply chain including 5G. Much of the talk covers the industrial control systems initiative, built on four pillars: engaging the community by asking more and giving more, a technology focus that includes the MITRE ICS ATT&CK framework, data integration into a common operating picture, and mapping risk across national critical functions. An interagency working group then gathers industry input on workforce, standards, supply chain and incident response.

The closing section introduces hands-on training environments for oil and gas, pipeline and water facility scenarios, displayed on the conference's third floor and aimed at under-resourced municipal water utilities. Attendees are pointed to the agency's website, regional advisors and an upcoming ICS Joint Working Group event. The takeaway is to engage with federal partners, share what works and use available training to strengthen defenses.

talks.title: Exploitable Vulnerabilities (Weaknesses) Hidden Deep In ICS
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Exploitable Vulnerabilities (Weaknesses) Hidden Deep In ICS.

talks.title: Waterfall
talks.teaser: Safe OT Security Monitoring details Waterfall.

talks.title: Interview with Ed Schweitzer
talks.teaser: Covers designing protective relays, early grid cybersecurity choices, and why power systems demand simplicity and tight latency.
talks.summary:
This mainstage interview opens with the speaker's background as a third-generation inventor and the culture of first principles at his company. He explains that the power industry cannot treat the grid as a lab, so new technology should prove itself with customers who have a real need before standards or mandates lock it in.

He then recounts the first digital protective relay from the early 1980s, which was first sold to a Minnesota utility that used it for fault location. Built-in access levels and alarms were added after it became clear that a serial port with a modem could be abused. Later, customers added dial-back and encrypting modems, and one utility used a relay-controlled phone line so operators could grant time-limited access. He also described how added features and sampled-value designs increase complexity and the risk of misoperations, and he accepted Ethernet ports on relays while objecting to the timing non-determinism they bring.

Toward the end, he asks what inherently safe cyber would look like and challenges his staff to answer it. On legacy code, he says the company rewrites components when it can do them better. For the wider ICS community, he urges a focus on simplicity, low latency and determinism while staying secure, citing a serial encrypting transceiver that added only one byte of latency.

talks.title: 14 Hours And An Electric Grid
talks.teaser: Walks through the first 14 hours of an industrial control system intrusion, from firmware reversing to a rootkit on a serial gateway.
talks.summary:
The talk recounts the first 14 hours of a penetration test against an electric utility's energy management network, where the goal was to reach substation protective relays and disable them. The speaker documented the work hour by hour to give a realistic picture of an average engagement, partly as a counterpoint to press coverage that swung between calling such bugs trivial and calling them reachable only by nation-states.

Early on, the converter's web login and firmware unlock were examined, and its TCP sequence numbers suggested an unusual custom network stack. Reversing the extracted firmware turned up a debug routine that read arbitrary memory and exposed the device password. The firmware checksum was a simple additive sum, so a modified image could be made to pass. The speaker then built an in-memory debugger, carved out a roughly 1.7 kilobyte code cave, and wrote a DNP3 man-in-the-middle implant in C. Spoofing tables kept operators seeing normal values, and compressed truth tables modeled plant start-up states.

Firmware was deployed through an already compromised patch management system. Further exploits against an RTU and an intrusion detection device gave access to the safety half of the switchyard, and the full chain took about three weeks. The speaker argued that such techniques are within reach of many skilled professionals and that actors are often over-credited. The takeaway for vendors is to sign firmware with real cryptography rather than rely on checksums, and for asset owners that legacy ICS problems persist because replacement is never started.

talks.title: CyberX 2020 Global IOT and ICS Risk Report
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in CyberX 2020 Global IOT and ICS Risk Report.

talks.title: Interview with Robert Malmgren of CS3STHLM
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Interview with Robert Malmgren of CS3STHLM.

talks.title: Pwn2Own Miami Results At S4x20
talks.teaser: A recap of inaugural ICS-focused Pwn2Own Miami wins, prizes, partials, and Master of Pwn honors across vendor targets.
talks.summary:
Trend Micro’s Zero Day Initiative wrapped its first Pwn2Own Miami at S4, pitching industrial control targets to researchers via virtual machines when shipping physical PLCs worldwide proved impractical. Dustin Childs walks through three days of live attempts on vendors including Rockwell Automation, Iconics, Triangle MicroWorks, Inductive Automation, Schneider Electric, and the OPC Foundation, explaining the stage rules, disclosure process, and how partial wins differ from full victories when a demonstrated flaw was already reported but remained unpatched.

Successful demos ranged from project-file code execution that launched a calculator in Factory Talk SCADA to chained bugs, DLL loading, deserialization issues, denial-of-service against OPC UA .NET, and an Iconics compromise that added an unexpected administrator account. Prize totals climbed past $225,000 with only two failed attempts among twenty-five, while more than twenty issues were handed to on-site vendor representatives. A last-second Rockwell Studio 5000 compromise supplied late drama before the Insight team clinched Master of Pwn on points that included a final denial-of-service entry.

Practitioners hear which product classes drew reliable breaks versus tricky licensing and configuration pitfalls that derailed even strong research. Childs contrasts quick wins with deeper chains from seasoned contestants, notes uneven security maturity across ICS suppliers, and invites vendors and researchers to engage with ZDI and future Miami editions as the contest scales.

talks.title: Kaspersky Tools & Info For The ICS Security Community
talks.teaser: Shows how a vendor's ICS teams share training, CTF contests, threat feeds and community resources with the wider industry.
talks.summary:
A vendor's industrial security team explains how its different units support the worldwide ICS security field. The speakers cover the company's industrial protection products and a transparency initiative that lets outside researchers review its code and detection rules. They also describe an annual industrial security conference, a playlist that gathers industrial security podcasts, and a non-profit professional club for networking and knowledge sharing.

The vulnerability research and training unit shares its knowledge through free webinars, university courses and capture-the-flag events. Commercial courses cover ICS awareness, IoT vulnerability research, advanced fuzzing for Windows and Linux, and incident response using real industrial devices. A "research and destroy" exercise places students in a realistic test setup with planted flaws to see whether they can disrupt a process. The team also offers an automated ICS malware feed, Snort rules for spotting zero-day exploitation, and an ICS threat intelligence portal with actor reports.

The talk also describes a vulnerability database project, started after the team found that vendor security advisories sometimes listed the wrong affected devices. The speakers mention work with the OPC Foundation security working group, the Industrial Internet Consortium, and an open security maturity model framework. They close by saying the units differ in focus but share the goal of building a safer industrial security world.

talks.title: Interview with DHS CISA Director Chris Krebs
talks.teaser: A government cybersecurity leader explains how DHS coordinates with industry on control systems, information sharing and ransomware.
talks.summary:
The interview opens with the head of CISA describing the agency as a risk adviser and central point of contact between government and industry, rather than a regulator or law enforcement body. He says its strength is a large public voice, so it aims to name a handful of high-impact actions instead of long checklists. He also argues that executives must be persuaded, because budget and capability follow awareness at the top.

The middle of the conversation covers information sharing and recent examples. An alert in June about rising Iranian cyber activity combined intelligence, civilian agency and commercial telemetry, and after the Soleimani strike the agency held calls to reach smaller operators beyond large banks and energy firms. He describes the automated indicator sharing platform being refocused from volume toward quality, with added context. He also discusses a functional approach to risk instead of sector lists, ransomware hitting state and local governments, and the push for audit logs and paper records ahead of the 2020 elections.

Toward the end, he expands the ICS Joint Working Group with regional events, free training and a distributed model that moves capabilities between ten regions. He warns that ransomware has not yet been seen against PLCs but may reach control systems within a few years. For practitioners, the takeaways are to build logging and auditability, plan recovery for operational environments, and bring executives into the conversation early.

talks.title: Special Access Features - A Deep Dive Into Unconstrained Code Execution on Siemens S7 PLCs
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Special Access Features - A Deep Dive Into Unconstrained Code Execution on Siemens S7 PLCs.

talks.title: Jumpstart Your NIST CSF Maturity
talks.teaser: Maps OT security platform capabilities onto the five NIST CSF functions, from identifying assets through recovering safely.
talks.summary:
The session, given on a sponsor stage, looked at how operational technology security teams can mature beyond detection and response. The presenters described trends they see across large customers: asset owners combining passive monitoring with active device queries, operations teams pushing for automation as budgets and staffing shrink, and demand for tools that exchange data with existing systems rather than only sending logs one way.

They then walked through the five functions of the NIST Cybersecurity Framework. For identify, they showed how switch and port data can pinpoint a device's physical location, how crowdsourced classification draws on a device cloud of over 11 million devices, and how risk scoring can be automated and tuned per site. Under protect, they covered continuous assessment, network access control for OT with actions ranging from alerts to quarantine VLANs, and simulating segmentation from a flow matrix before enforcing it. For detect, they pointed to a threat library, ingestion of threat feed indicators, look-back through historical data, and malformed packet detection. Respond focused on ticketing and firewall integrations, while recover covered container-based sensor redeployment, traffic baselines and firmware audit logs.

The closing takeaways were to prefer platforms that lift maturity across all five functions, to choose tools shared by security, operations and network teams, and to automate risk scoring. The presenters framed these as considerations for future-proofing OT investments.

talks.title: Dale Peterson's S4x20 Mini-Keynote
talks.teaser: Urges ICS security practitioners to convince executives to fund bolder, consequence-focused change instead of routine hygiene.
talks.summary:
The keynote opens with the history of S4, which began in 2007 to build an ICS security community when fewer than 40 people attended; the event now draws several hundred. The speaker describes a second mission of encouraging creative thinking and dramatic change over incremental progress. He argues the community has largely anticipated attacks: the 2015 Ukraine grid attack used rogue firmware on serial-to-Ethernet gateways, a weakness shown years earlier through unsigned firmware, a spearphishing exercise targeted pipeline companies, and Triton exposed the danger of natively run compiled logic. The core failure, in his view, is not persuading executives to invest.

He criticizes security recommendations from 2010 and 2020 as nearly identical, mostly routine IT practices labeled cyber hygiene, which yield minimal risk reduction for large effort. He sees consequence reduction as a promising idea that saw little progress in 2018 and 2019, and urges trying different strategies. This year's main stage adds sessions on corporate risk management, including board legal duties, a Norsk Hydro loss analysis, cyber insurance, and Moody's new cyber risk rating.

He closes by urging attendees to hold strong positions loosely, meet people they do not know, and use hallway and outdoor conversations where ideas take shape. Since over half the attending companies are hiring ICS security staff, he encourages people to pursue work that makes a real difference.

talks.title: The Future of ICS Security Products ... What You Need To Know
talks.teaser: Sizes up the market for OT security products and how asset inventory, detection and vulnerability tools fit into ICS strategy.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens by arguing that ICS security has finally drawn executive attention, and that practitioners should use it to reduce real risk instead of producing busy work. Executives often hire enterprise consultants whose metrics, such as PLC patch counts, do little to lower risk, and vendors selling a single bright shiny object can shape leadership's expectations before the security team does. The central message is to set expectations that current tooling is an interim step, because the product landscape will change substantially within two years.

The middle of the talk looks at three promises made by the roughly two dozen OT monitoring vendors: detection, asset inventory and vulnerability management. Passive network monitoring can reveal new devices, but it makes an incomplete inventory. Active queries that use native industrial protocols return richer data, and some vendors now parse engineering project files as well. Passive tools can report missing patches but cannot apply or verify them, so vulnerability management still needs another product. For detection, the speaker argues that passive sensors are only one data source alongside endpoint, firewall, historian and enterprise logs, and that current integrations with SIEMs are largely one-way.

The closing section recommends treating the asset management system as the single source of truth, checking how well each product actually integrates today rather than what its API promises, and expecting consolidation as vendors are acquired or leave the market. Buyers should decide whether to run a separate OT security operations center or integrate with the enterprise one, since most attacks start in the enterprise network. The speaker's final advice is to brief management proactively on the strategy and how it will evolve, so executives do not form their views from other sources.

talks.title: Detecting Disgruntled Insiders
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Detecting Disgruntled Insiders.
talks.summary:
# Overview
This talk discusses a method developed over 15 years to identify disgruntled, at-risk insiders by analyzing organizational communications using psycholinguistic indicators. By evaluating specific linguistic patterns against established baselines, the approach systematically filters massive message volumes down to a manageable fraction requiring review or investigation.

# Key Topics
- Psycholinguistic Filtering: Reducing large corpuses of messages (such as millions of corporate emails) into small, high-risk subsets using baseline metrics.
- Behavioral Indicators: Operationalizing linguistic markers for anger, blame, and victimization.
- Statistical Baseline Modeling: Measuring the mean and standard deviation of specific language variables across relevant peer groups to identify statistical outliers.
- Case Illustration: A real-world example of a system administrator at a New York bank who pushed back against management interventions before taking down critical accounting servers.

# Technical Details
- Baseline & Filtering Funnel: In a client dataset of roughly 63 million messages from 117,000 senders, the filtering process started by querying messages containing more than five instances of the pronoun 'me' based on subgroup mean and standard deviation, immediately dropping the pool to 34,000 messages. Further psycholinguistic filtering cut this to less than 1% of messages from less than 1% of senders.
- Investigation Outcomes: From the final filtered subset, one-third of the flagged communications were referred for a full investigation under the organization's low-threshold criteria, one-third presented issues that warranted ongoing monitoring without triggering immediate investigation, and one-third were false positives.
- Psycholinguistic Variables: The system utilizes around 60 variables, covering dimensions such as anger, financial stress, sexuality, and violence. Key core variables include:
  - Negatives (Anger): Negations such as 'no', 'not', 'never', and contractions with "n't" (e.g., 'won't', 'can't'), signaling negative judgments and frustration.
  - Second-Person Pronouns (Blame): Direct references using 'you' and related personal pronouns, which surge when individuals feel cornered and direct blame externally (e.g., 'until you fire me', 'take orders from you').
  - First-Person Object Pronouns (Victimization): Use of 'me', where the sender portrays themselves as the passive object of actions taken by others (e.g., 'relieve me', 'order me'). While low usage indicates passivity, high usage serves as a strong marker of victimization.
- Domain Filtering: The method actively filters out non-relevant context, such as interpersonal relationship content (by demanding minimum references to employment) and religious phrases (such as references to 'the blood of Christ').

# Takeaways
- Psycholinguistic analysis can detect 95% of at-risk communications across 100% of examined authors in experimental baselines.
- Identifying outliers relative to the mean and standard deviation of peer communications offers an effective, systematic mechanism to drastically reduce noise and uncover severe insider threats before or during destructive actions.

talks.title: S4x19 Closing Panel: Government's Role

talks.title: Unsolicited Response S4x19
talks.teaser: Rapid-fire opinions from ICS security practitioners on IoT, vendor vulnerability handling, and how risk gets defined.
talks.summary:
This open-mic style segment gives several industry people a short slot, capped at five minutes each, to share opinions on ICS and security topics. Dale Peterson opens with a lighthearted complaint about never receiving the SCADA diva award, despite hints such as pink clothing and a camera crew. Patrick Miller argues that the community should stop criticizing IoT, since consumers will keep buying connected devices regardless, and that effort is better spent helping the community make those products more secure. Eddie Habibi stresses protecting and managing configuration changes on ICS as a practical priority.

Further along, Carter proposes working with OEMs so that proprietary industrial protocols can be exposed to security vendors, letting defenders see what should and should not talk on a control network. Vladimir reviews how industrial vendors reacted to a large set of vulnerability reports he had submitted, mapping their responses onto five stages of grief. A video segment from news presenter Kerry Tomlinson describes the challenge of explaining cybersecurity to a general audience without scaring them. Another speaker objects that detection challenge test methodologies should be open to review, and a final speaker notes more than 13 definitions of risk in circulation, offering a simple one: risk is uncertainty of damage.

The takeaway is mostly advocacy: work with vendors on protocol visibility, treat configuration management as core ICS defense, and make testing methods and shared vocabulary transparent.

talks.title: 3-Minutes on Langner's Stuxnet Deep Dive
talks.teaser: Explains how faking PLC input process images cuts control logic off from physical reality, enabled by a writable input design flaw.
talks.summary:
The clip walks through a staged attack on an industrial controller, presented as a short recap of Langner's Stuxnet deep dive. Early on, the attackers record input data for 21 seconds, and that recording is later used to fake the inputs that legitimate control logic reads. The manipulation stages then change outputs, and certain paired process values, when both on or both off, cause outputs to toggle.

The main point is that faking the input image disconnects control logic, and safety logic too, from what the field devices actually report. The speaker stresses how little code this takes and how well the attackers knew the timing, actuators and inputs of the process.

The root cause is a design flaw: the vendor left the input process image writable when it should be read-only, handling it like an ordinary block of memory. The speaker argues the fix was simple and could have been shipped a year earlier, yet the vendor stayed silent, and so did DHS.

talks.title: S4x19 Cabana Sessions
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding S4x19 Cabana Sessions.

talks.title: Throw Out The CVSS and Replace with Never, Next, Now
talks.teaser: Argues that base CVSS scores mislead, and walks through a ranked alternative based on impact and active threat.
talks.summary:
The talk takes aim at CVSS scores as the main way to rank vulnerabilities. The speaker opens with a deliberately absurd demonstration: a series of arithmetic steps turns any starting score into the same result, showing that the number alone says little about a given system. The point is that a base score ignores context, such as how exposed a system is and what a failure would cost in safety or money.

In place of CVSS, the speaker sketches a simple decision tree built on those factors and returns a ranked answer in three buckets: never, next and now. "Never" is a deliberately strong label for items that can wait until a later upgrade, "next" means the next patch cycle, and "now" means act immediately. The impact categories are kept coarse, running from no effect through insignificant to more serious losses.

To illustrate, the speaker looks at several vulnerabilities in Rockwell Automation RSLinx. Most fall into the next-patch group. One is treated as urgent because there is evidence of active exploitation linked to a Black Energy campaign, and it is scored as a high threat that calls for action now rather than waiting. The takeaway is that evidence of active threat and the consequences of compromise should drive priority, not the severity number alone.

talks.title: Investigating Triton
talks.teaser: Traces the Triton safety system incidents, from early controller outages to the August outage that took down about six controllers.
talks.summary:
The talk recounts the Triton safety system incidents at an industrial plant. The first outages in June 2017 hit one emergency shutdown controller, which engineers treated as a possible malfunction. They checked logs and removed the device for a mechanical test without involving the vendor or a cybersecurity review. The speaker calls this a missed chance to find the intruders.

The August 4 outage, on a Friday evening, took down about six controllers across several sensitive process areas, creating a risk of toxic gas release and explosions. Safety alarms began around 7:43 pm, and program-mode warnings were dismissed as routine because they only needed daily acknowledgement. Investigators found Python executables, a Triton trial log and unidentified programs running in controller memory. An engineering system imaged in time still held the tools, because the attackers had left them there; when checked later, the files had been deleted and wiped. Despite a segmented design on paper, weak DMZ firewall configuration let the attacker move from the IT network into the plant network. Antivirus caught Mimikatz activity on the IT side, but those alerts never reached a central SOC.

Each outage kept the plant down for at least a week and brought lost production, product flushing and costly third-party investigation and recovery. The takeaway: when controllers fail, widen the investigation to cybersecurity, preserve evidence, route alerts to a monitored SOC, and harden DMZ firewall rules.

talks.title: Consequence Based ICS Risk Management
talks.teaser: Compares two consequence-focused ICS risk methods, cyber PHA and consequence-driven engineering, and where they differ.
talks.summary:
The discussion centres on the consequence side of the risk equation, which security teams often neglect in favour of controls that reduce likelihood. Two industrial control system approaches were compared: cyber PHA, presented by John Cusimano, and consequence-driven, cyber-informed engineering (CCE), described by Andy Bochman.

Cusimano explained that cyber PHA borrows from process hazard analysis and safety engineering, using zones and conduits from ISA standards and a Purdue-style architecture diagram. A mixed team of automation, IT and operations staff works from worst-case consequences back to causes, threats and vulnerabilities, then scores risk against the client's matrix. He put the elapsed time at four to six weeks, with a workshop of three to five days. Bochman described CCE as starting by identifying the few processes that must not fail, mapping the surrounding ecosystem, then testing those targets from an adversary's view with intelligence partners. Some mitigations are analog or mechanical backstops, such as a tripwire that lets a generator shut down safely while digital controls stay in place.

Both speakers said the methods are more alike than different, and that neither replaces security controls, since they aim to lower the maximum impact of an attack. Cusimano said running both in one workshop did not work, so they are better done in series. Bochman noted that some organisations already apply CCE on their own, and a get-started guide is planned.

talks.title: Network Traffic Collection Methodologies
talks.teaser: Compares ways to collect industrial network traffic, from flow records to packet mirroring, and their design trade-offs.
talks.summary:
The talk addresses a question the speaker says comes up often with customers: how organizations can gain more visibility into industrial control networks, where IT and operations teams both have a stake. The focus is on permanent collection designs rather than temporary captures used during incident recovery. The speaker stays vendor-neutral and states his assumptions up front to set a common baseline.

The first method covered is flow records, such as NetFlow version 9 and the IPFIX standard. Flows show which devices talk to each other and for how long, but not the content of the conversation. Default timers of 30 seconds for short connections and 60 seconds for long-running ones shape export timing, and a typical template runs about 60 bytes per flow. Flow visibility is capped by the lowest device in the path that supports it. Raw packet capture, through local or remote port mirroring or encapsulated remote SPAN, shows full conversations and sequences, but it duplicates traffic, needs more collectors, and can strain switch capacity. Filters reduce load at the cost of visibility, and QoS cannot prioritize a single source inside a mirrored VLAN. Inline devices and taps add placement, throughput, and latency concerns.

The closing point is that flow data is often a simple first step on existing switches, while raw traffic gives fuller understanding. Staffing matters too: IT security centers already review flow data daily, but interpreting control traffic, such as a shutdown sequence, is a skill set they may lack. Designs should account for added network load, hardware support for the chosen features, and who will actually analyze the data.
