talks.title: Is The Purdue Model Dead?
talks.teaser: Panelists debate whether the Purdue model still guides ICS security as cloud, convergence and IoT reshape control networks.
talks.summary:
The panel asks whether the Purdue model, the layered reference for industrial control systems with levels from 0 to 5, is still relevant as cloud links, IoT devices and convergence reshape plants. Panelists agree the original network picture is outdated, since industrial networks now run on Ethernet and business technology is common on the plant floor, but they split on what remains useful.

One side argues the model still describes how plants are built and how information and supply chains flow, and that its time-domain layering, from sub-second sensor signals up to hours, shifts and days, still matters. The other side argues it is a weak basis for security because it has no risk overlay, and that securing a level or placing controls between PLCs and HMIs makes less sense than protecting the function a process performs and the mission chain it supports. The discussion also covers cloud placement: historians and analytics can move off site while I/O stays put, and an enterprise and industrial cloud split with dedicated interfaces could restore something close to an air gap.

Near the end, the panel notes that level one is splitting, as when a utility ran a virtualized controller apart from its I/O. The closing view is that the diagrams are outdated while the model still serves as a reference for organizational structure and risk, and that security should start earlier, during acceptance testing.

talks.title: Safety in Process Control
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Safety in Process Control.

talks.title: ICS Malware: Havex and Black Energy
talks.teaser: Surveys malware targeting SCADA and ICS environments, tracing Black Energy and Havex plugins, infection routes and criminal roots.
talks.summary:
Kyle Wilhoit of Trend Micro looks at malware aimed at SCADA and industrial control systems, starting with the broader picture: rising counts of SCADA vulnerabilities and why malware is an easy route into these environments. He then follows a group tracked as Sandworm, active since 2009 against Ukrainian government bodies, NATO-linked organizations, energy firms and telecoms. Its Black Energy malware began as crimeware and grew into a modular tool, with plugins for screenshots, network scanning, spreading across network shares and collecting certificates.

Next comes Havex, a simple PHP remote access tool used by a group the speaker called Crouching Yeti. It reached victims through spearphishing with a PDF exploit, trojanized installers and watering-hole pages running an exploit kit. Once inside, the operators pulled Outlook contacts, scanned for OPC servers on reachable networks, harvested saved browser passwords and exfiltrated results. A separate set of trojanized ICS software samples, often carrying Zeus or dropper families, used industrial naming and appeared to come mostly from China and Taiwan; the speaker judged them crimeware rather than Black Energy. A custom RAT built for the demonstration took roughly two hours and did not appear in public hash lookups.

The talk closed on defenses. Patched systems and up-to-date antivirus would have caught much of the activity shown, though the speaker warned that these tactics are changing. No advanced multi-hop firewall chaining appeared in the samples, which instead rode on traffic that already looked allowed. The speaker also described an ongoing study that runs samples for longer periods to watch for lateral movement.

talks.title: ICS Security Assessments
talks.teaser: Online assessment techniques deliver high-value ICS visibility with modest operational impact when passive reviews fail.
talks.summary:
Industrial control system assessments often start from incomplete as-built diagrams and documentation that omit whole networks and stray devices. The speaker argues that accepting some risk from active, online techniques is worthwhile because passive and offline methods rarely reach ground truth about what is actually deployed.

Credentialed scanning uses remote operating system facilities to pull software inventory, establish an asset baseline, and audit patches—including host-based applications that never expose a listening port—beyond what uncredentialed vulnerability scans typically show. When standard IT scanners or dedicated ICS product security tools cannot be brought onsite, native Windows or Linux commands can still expose network configuration, multi-homing, ports, services, and user accounts comparable to credentialed auditing. A brief EtherNet/IP query can surface device and firmware version details.

Practitioners should treat scanner scores as a starting point rather than a priority map: aligning tool output with actionable remediation still requires judgment about what matters in that control environment.

talks.title: ICS Incident Response
talks.teaser: Covers detecting and responding to attacks on industrial control systems, including alert triage and playbooks.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that knowing how a control system and its processes are engineered is the most useful defense. The speaker notes that monitoring everything is unrealistic, so organizations need to start somewhere, often on a limited budget, and that without network visibility attacks go unseen. Alerts should be given a meaning, such as who is behind them, and mapped to a response plan so staff know what to do when one fires.

Once an alert escalates, incident responders examine the anomaly to find malicious activity. Areas to check include application exploitation, unexpected third-party connections such as unusual ICCP links to vendors or other parties, and attacks on specific industrial protocols. The speaker recalls a public-facing service that was being fuzzed with malformed traffic: nothing broke, but the traffic was clearly abnormal. Other paths covered are remote access exploitation and malware delivered over USB. Alert floods can also hide a real intruder, as seen in real attacks.

The closing advice focuses on preparation. Responders should keep playbooks ready for common scenarios such as commodity malware and compromised credentials, and plan ahead for password resets on systems that cannot simply be reset. When a plant has to restore service, a manager may need to reboot or replace a PLC, especially in life-or-death situations, but the general guidance is not to reboot a PLC so its contents are preserved.

talks.title: Making Power System Cybersecurity Part of the Engineering Process
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Making Power System Cybersecurity Part of the Engineering Process.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, the speaker discusses bridging the gap between operational power system engineering and cybersecurity by making cyber controls an integral part of the standard engineering, design, testing, and commissioning workflows. Historically, cybersecurity in operational technology (OT) has often been bolted on post-deployment or handled predominantly by back-office IT and compliance bodies unfamiliar with grid operations. To resolve this, working groups within the IEEE Power System Communications and Cybersecurity Committee are establishing standardized frameworks that allow licensed professional engineers and settings engineers to document and test cyber protections directly within engineering schematics and operational processes.

### Key Topics
- **Engineering Design & Standardized Documentation:** Traditional power systems rely on standardized drawings and function codes (such as IEEE PC37.2 relay protection codes like 50, 51, and 87) that clearly define what an intelligent electronic device (IED) or remote terminal unit (RTU) does. The speaker highlights an ongoing IEEE effort to create standard function codes for cybersecurity controls (e.g., local logging, role-based access control, complex passwords, protocol/port enables) directly on operational one-line diagrams.
- **Testing and Commissioning (IEEE P2658):** Standard power system commissioning mandates rigorous point-to-point and end-to-end testing, but cyber controls frequently go unverified in the field. The working group is developing an IEEE guide (IEEE P2658) defining formal procedures for field commissioning, back-office application verification, and decommissioning/disposal of assets.
- **Shifting Responsibility to Field Engineers:** The responsibility for securing edge devices (such as relays, reclosers, and RTUs) must shift away from back-office IT, compliance-focused groups, and threat-intel whack-a-mole approaches back toward the power system, telecommunications, and settings engineers who configure device-native parameters and communication schemes.

### Technical Details
- **IEEE 1686 Compliance:** Modern IEDs built to IEEE 1686 already possess native security capabilities including local event logging, failed login attempt tracking, role-based access control, and password complexity. However, without engineering drawings mandating their configuration, these features often remain unused or unmonitored.
- **Mapping Cyber Controls to Operational Diagrams:** Proposed drawing conventions show function codes—such as C54 for local event logging, C71 for password complexity, C66 for role-based access control, and C60/C68 for specific network service configurations (e.g., HTTP and Telnet). Routing considerations, including data diodes for fault analytics and VLAN segmentation across substation switches, can be explicitly captured.
- **Alarm Integration and Cyber Lockout:** Substations can leverage RTUs as cyber concentrators by mapping cyber events directly into DNP3 points or converting them into syslog messages without overloading bandwidth. The speaker also notes simple mechanical interventions, such as a hardware-based remote lockout switch (estimated at around fifteen dollars) to block incoming control commands during suspected incidents like Ukraine 2015.
- **Field Realities & Application Verification:** A real-world audit revealed that over half of an asset owner's firewalls were misconfigured (which simple ping checks could have caught), and enabled cyber alarms in IEDs failed to route anywhere. Formal application testing in lab environments is necessary to verify performance under constraints, such as identifying dropped packets or limitations when evaluating encryption over protocols like IEC 61850.

### Takeaways
- Cyber controls must be specified on engineering drawings so that if an element is not documented, it is recognized as nonexistent in the design philosophy.
- Establishing clear testing and commissioning procedures creates accountability across design engineers, integrators, and asset owners while providing as-built documentation for troubleshooting and incident response.
- Engineers and industry practitioners are encouraged to participate in open IEEE standards working groups to shape the common technical language and guides governing power system cyber resilience.

talks.title: PLC Virtualization
talks.teaser: Explores whether fully virtualized PLCs could ease vendor lock-in, cut costs and help security, and what latency hurdles remain.
talks.summary:
Austin opens by asking what a fully virtualized PLC would look like and why anyone would move a working control system onto commodity hardware. He defines virtualization as software that looks and behaves like specific hardware, notes that earlier soft PLC products never took off partly because of doubts about Windows-based controllers, and argues that a complete virtual PLC would have to emulate the CPU, the backplane, the I/O cards and the network, not just the processor.

He makes the case for it on several fronts. Controllers are expensive, and vendor lock-in plus regional distribution channels keep buyers tied to one platform for a decade or more. Virtualization would also bring easier patching, snapshots and rollbacks, extra redundancy, and more processing power than limited industrial CPUs offer. On security, he suggests software-defined segmentation and better traffic monitoring, while warning that cheap commodity hardware often leaves security out. The main technical hurdle is latency: he cited tolerances of 250 microseconds for motion control, 280 for electrical control and 800 for process control. He pointed to a 2016 IEEE study that reached 10 to 20 microseconds of backplane latency on commodity Intel hardware by disabling hyperthreading and some virtualization features. Current real-world uses include vendor simulators, vulnerability research and virtualized DCS controllers.

He closes with the vendor side. Virtualization would make it easier to displace an incumbent, push vendors toward software rather than hardware, and open markets such as biotech and oil and gas. He compares this to the PC market, where IBM left commodity hardware while HP chose premium products. In the Q&A he said VM escape would require an attacker to get deep into the network first, that proprietary protocols would need emulation, and that interrupt latency on the software side is largely unexplored.

talks.title: ARM Hardware Security
talks.teaser: Shows how ARM TrustZone isolation can keep keys and critical IoT functions safe even after an attacker gains root access.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at why connected industrial and IoT devices are hard to secure and how a hardware root of trust can close the gap. The speaker says attackers now aim for long-term footholds on devices, such as DDoS bots, crypto miners and network sniffers, rather than destructive attacks. Field devices run unattended for years, can be physically taken apart, and often combine databases, user interfaces and control logic on one board, which makes separation of duties difficult.

The main proposal is ARM TrustZone, which splits a processor into a normal world and a secure world enforced in hardware, so software with root access in the normal OS still cannot reach stored keys. The speaker compares this with hypervisor-based virtualization extensions and cites Samsung Knox and set-top box decryption keys as products using the approach. Secure boot is presented as the foundation, but its protection ends once boot completes. Secure-world features such as a secure clock, a secure watchdog and secure JTAG add protection after that point. Open-source OP-TEE is mentioned as a low-cost starting point on evaluation boards, while the speaker notes that cheap chips lack the margin for these features and that documentation is scarce.

Practical guidance includes keeping the secure world small, limiting it to keys and critical I/O, keeping UI and most of the communications stack in the normal world, and having outside testers attack the design. The speaker describes an NXP secure boot flaw where an overloaded hash check let the device keep booting, to show the approach is not foolproof. Asset owners are urged to require secure modes from vendors, and teams are encouraged to start early.

talks.title: The Loop
talks.teaser: Explains the industrial control loop, from field sensors to valves, and why 4-20 mA current signals are used.
talks.summary:
The talk walks through the control loop, the core arrangement in process control where a system measures something and manipulates something in response. It compares this to adjusting a hotel shower: your skin senses the temperature and your hand turns the valve. In an industrial plant, a suite of sensors feeds inputs into a control system, which reads electrical properties such as voltage, current and frequency, performs calculations, and sends signals out to final control elements like control valves, variable speed motors, pumps and dampers.

The talk also covers where errors creep in: tuning, latency, and timing between a sensor's signal and an actuator's movement, with more field devices becoming intelligent. It then explains the 4 to 20 milliamp current loop. Current is used because a broken wire reads as zero, which separates a fault from a real zero-percent signal. The 4 milliamp floor lets some instruments draw power from the same loop, and 20 milliamps represents 100 percent. Passing 20 milliamps through a 250 ohm resistor produces 5 volts, which is the signal read by the industrial control system.

For security staff, the takeaway is that the loop is what is being protected. Knowing how sensors, controllers and final elements interact, and where timing and signal integrity can break down, gives a practical starting point for thinking about ICS risk.

talks.title: Public Ledger Technology: Code Signing and Device Birth Certificates
talks.teaser: Shows how GE pairs code signing with binary transparency logs to protect industrial software and verify firmware in the field.
talks.summary:
GE's talk addresses software integrity for industrial environments, arguing that trust in such systems often assumes the hardware and firmware are sound. The speaker frames three pain points: keys and hardware security modules expire before field devices retire, build servers often hold signing keys, and third parties struggle to verify software in the field. Regulators such as NIST, the FDA and the FAA are also raising integrity requirements.

To address these, the team placed a signing service between build hosts and HSMs so keys can be rotated and migrated without developers tracking slots and partitions. A Jenkins example showed a jar signer call routed through the service, with verification against the public key. For field verification, the talk explained binary transparency, borrowing certificate transparency's logs, monitors and auditors, along with Merkle tree consistency and inclusion proofs. The proof of concept hashes a binary, encodes the hash into a certificate's domain name, logs it, and lets a device check the binary against the returned leaf hash.

The takeaway is that code signing and transparency are stronger together, since signing alone is exposed to certificate authority compromise and transparency only detects problems. The speaker invited the community to help build a unified standard, host nodes of a distributed ledger, and add data such as end-of-life information, security assessments and bills of materials. In Q&A, revocation was handled by marking certificates invalid rather than removing them from the append-only log.

talks.title: Cybersecurity PHA: Consequence Based Security
talks.teaser: Shows how existing hazard analyses can reveal cyber-driven consequences in process plants, and how to choose practical safeguards.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how industrial plants, such as oil refineries, can address cyber risk by building on the process safety work they already do. The speaker recounts a European refinery engagement where plant staff doubted that a hacker could cause physical harm. The team turned to process hazard analysis, a HAZOP-style review of each process node, so the discussion could center on consequences rather than attackers.

The method checks each cause of a hazardous deviation and asks whether a cyber route could produce it, then checks whether the safeguards meant to stop it could themselves be attacked. Where a hackable consequence remains, the team assigns a security level against a risk tolerance that executives and the board should set in advance. In a batch reactor example, the cooling pump controls and a safety instrumented system valve were both treated as potentially hackable. The team added an analog circuit in parallel with the safety system so the valve acts only when both agree. The speaker argues that mechanical or analog alternatives can cut risk without the cost of a higher security level.

In audience questions, the speaker agreed that digital safety systems carry real concern and that network segmentation remains necessary. He cautioned that network-device risk analysis is less useful than consequence analysis for operators who must keep production running. The takeaway is to start from an existing hazard analysis when one exists, and use it to decide where cyber controls matter most. A free tool called Open PHA was mentioned as a way to run the work.

talks.title: A 2nd Monitoring Network at Level 0/1
talks.teaser: Explains why sensor-level electrical monitoring can verify control system process health when network data cannot.
talks.summary:
Joe Weiss and Amir open by arguing that the lowest-level control devices, such as sensors, analyzers and actuators on serial, Modbus or fieldbus networks, have no security, authentication or logging. Network monitoring only shows what those devices report, so it cannot confirm whether a sensor or process is healthy. They use the Lion Air crash and the Plum Island black-start diesel concern to show how bad sensor data can drive automation in the wrong direction.

The middle of the talk turns to physics-layer monitoring. The presenter's company taps a small share of I/O signals passively, without touching the SCADA system, and samples electrical characteristics that slower network data drops. In one power generation case, a turbine that would not start, manually or automatically, was traced to a bad temperature sensor within an evening. In another, monitoring kept showing plant conditions after the Windows HMI went down, and a pump problem was found at a separate facility. A building management case and a dam failure caused by sensors pulling out of a wall were also discussed, and a demo showed electrical signatures changing when a sensor moved even though the measured level did not.

The closing argument is that machine learning can learn how readings such as pressure, flow, temperature and motor speed relate through physics, and flag process anomalies in real time. The speakers present this as a complement to network anomaly detection, and stress that engineers, not only IT and OT staff, need to take part in control system security work.

talks.title: Attack Surface in ICS: Do you have a Badness-ometer?
talks.teaser: Surveys OT badness meters, PI security audit tooling, and the AHA analyzer for scoring ICS process risk and deployment hardening gaps.
talks.summary:
The session opens with Gary McGraw’s “badness-ometer” idea: security assessments should expose obvious gaps and “deep trouble” areas, not deliver false confidence like chasing an A+. Public IT examples such as Security Headers and Mozilla Observatory illustrate how missing controls stand out even when overall grades look fine, and industry security ratings can shift after disclosed incidents.

Harry Paul then pivots to operational technology, describing OSIsoft’s open PI security audit tools and desired-state configuration resources. The audit output ranks findings in HTML and CSV, emphasizing attack-surface reduction across secure design, sensible defaults, and hardened deployment—Windows Server Core, current product versions with compile-time defenses, and Windows-integrated authentication with signing and encryption. Severity is grounded in bowtie analysis around application-server compromise. Adam Hahn presents the Department of Energy–funded Attack Surface Host Analyzer: a lightweight host scraper feeds a GUI that scores processes by remote connectivity, exploit-mitigation features (ASLR, DEP, control-flow guard), binary signing, and privilege level, with separate emphasis on externally reachable components.

Case studies contrast legacy control-center stacks on Windows Server 2008 R2 (single-digit scores) against PI historian 2017 on Server 2016 and further-improved PI Data Archive deployments on Server Core (scores in the 60s–80s, with examples nearing 90–100 when hardening is thorough). Practitioners are urged to run assessments periodically, question unnecessary services such as print spoolers on production ICS hosts, and share feedback or case studies via the suggested social hashtag and by trying both toolchains.

talks.title: Digital Ghost: Real Time, Active Defense for ICS
talks.teaser: Presents GE's Digital Ghost platform, which detects, localizes and neutralizes cyberattacks on industrial control systems in real time.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with GE's view of IT and OT convergence, framed around growth and defense. The speakers describe industrial pressures such as safety and productivity, then explain how a digital twin, a live model of an individual asset built from design data and sensor streams, supports early warnings and maintenance planning on jet engines and wind turbines.

The second half introduces Digital Ghost, a real-time active defense platform. It pairs digital twins of plant physics and control logic with live sensor data to separate normal behavior, faults and cyberattacks. Detection flags anomalies using correlations across many sensors, localization identifies compromised sensors despite closed-loop feedback, and neutralization rebuilds their values from trusted ones so operators can keep the plant running. Simulations covering about 600 normal and 900 attack cases reported roughly 99 percent accuracy. A field test on ten gas turbines produced a false positive rate below 1 percent, and a six-sensor reconstruction tracked true values with about 1 percent average error.

The closing section covers planned work with the Department of Energy to extend the approach to renewables, oil and gas, and transmission and distribution. The takeaway for practitioners is that critical infrastructure can add a model-based layer that validates sensor readings and keeps operations running during an intrusion, not just raise alarms.

talks.title: Analyzing the ICS Asset Inventory / Detection Market
talks.teaser: Explains how ICS asset inventory and passive detection products are evolving, and what buyers should test before committing.
talks.summary:
This talk reviews the fast-growing market for industrial control system asset inventory and passive network monitoring products, and explains how buyers should evaluate them. The speaker describes how tools that began as passive detection products have added asset inventory, asset management and vulnerability management features, often because customers asked for them. The active versus passive debate is largely settled, with leading vendors now offering active discovery that sends legitimate industrial commands. Teams that cannot allow active traffic can get similar results by having engineering tools run their own diagnostic commands while a passive monitor watches the replies.

The middle section turns to detection. The speaker argues that passive monitoring is only one component of a detection strategy and that most alerts are still signature based. Rare but legitimate commands, such as a firmware upload to many controllers, can still raise useful alerts. Protocol coverage has grown quickly, but testing detection is hard. A two-hour capture at one mining site produced about 400 gigs, which was cut to 130 gigabytes and crashed some vendor systems. Building a realistic attack for testing took roughly 500 hours.

The closing advice is to slow down, pilot products at one or two sites rather than standardizing across an enterprise, and plan for the market to change. Buyers must decide where data is processed, and who will analyze alerts through a standalone console, an OT SIM, or an enterprise SOC, since each needs scarce OT security talent. The speaker also summarizes vendor momentum and notes that sales strength is not the same as technical superiority.

talks.title: Hyper-Connectivity Will Improve Cybersecurity
talks.teaser: Makes the case that hyper-connectivity, paired with visibility, can give defenders an edge over attackers in industrial environments.
talks.summary:
Dave Weinstein opens by arguing that a counterintuitive idea deserves a serious look: that hyper-connectivity could improve cybersecurity in industrial environments. He recalls historical reversals of common sense and points out that machine-to-machine communications in industrial settings have roughly tripled over five years, reaching 7.5 billion. The usual instinct is that each new connection is another opening for attackers, and the talk sets out to test whether defenders can turn connectivity to their own advantage.

The central hypothesis is that risk arises from hyper-connectivity paired with opacity, meaning an inability to see what is happening on networks, rather than from connectivity alone. He sketches offense and defense from 1980 onward: moderate growth kept the two sides balanced until about 2007, when exponential growth let attackers ride the trend while defenders kept their earlier pace. Two responses follow: inverting the connectivity curve, as the Department of Energy's consequence-driven, cyber-informed engineering work aims to do by reducing dependence on digital systems, or raising defenders' slope by using visibility. In a hyper-connected setting, visibility becomes much easier, while attackers gain diminishing returns from each added connection, which yields a hyperconnectivity risk curve.

He closes by framing these points as research questions rather than settled answers, asking whether attackers face diminishing returns and who benefits more from obscurity. His practical message is that hyper-connectivity will persist in most environments, so defenders have to manage the resulting risk through visibility.

talks.title: Triton - A Report From The Trenches
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Triton - A Report From The Trenches.

talks.title: Cyber-Physical Response - Lessons Learned from Liberty Eclipse II
talks.teaser: Practitioners learn Liberty Eclipse II lessons from a Plum Island testbed on blackout recovery, characterization, and grid restoration.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with why electric utilities struggle to rehearse cyber-driven black starts: operators know crank paths and designated plants, yet cannot de-energize the real grid, so tabletop drills dominate while malware scenarios stay untested. Speakers describe their roles supporting DARPA RADICS and Department of Energy Liberty Eclipse work focused on rapid attack detection, isolation, and characterization after utilities have already fought for days without adequate spares or trust in field gear.

They walk through five response pillars—situational awareness beyond the corporate network, secure emergency communications, characterization of infections in relays and RTUs, and coordinated cleanup—with emphasis on trust after incidents like Triton and CRASHoverride, where one compromise bricks more devices than spare inventory allows. Liberty Eclipse II staged seven daily challenges on Plum Island using physical generators, substations, multiple SCADA vendors, diverse relay models, and utility volunteers operating two islanded utilities that had to synchronize while meeting mandated critical-load deadlines.

Practitioners should note that early recovery looks like storm response—dead batteries, truck generators, communications before cyber teams matter—and that linemen, not responders, own energization decisions. The exercise exposed vocabulary gaps between power engineers and security specialists, the primacy of secured voice links, and the need for pre-agreed approval chains before firmware work on million-dollar assets. RADICS aims to automate existing industry tools rather than replace them, across stack depths from minor malware to everything-owned catastrophes.

talks.title: How to Fix the People and Skills Problem in Securing Building Automation Systems
talks.teaser: Argues that building automation security depends on the engineers who run facilities, and on how they are trained and paid.
talks.summary:
James frames the talk around the people who run building automation and HVAC systems, such as stationary or building engineers, boiler operators and service technicians. He argues that these staff are often left out of ICS and SCADA security work, and that they usually learn the trade through on-the-job apprenticeship rather than formal training.

He compares an older boiler maintenance manual with a newer model that has a digital user interface and logic controls. The maintenance language barely changed, even though the newer unit adds a software layer that a traditional technician may not be ready to handle. In one case, a younger contractor reset a boiler through an Ethernet port, and experienced staff could not make sense of what had happened. He then lays out costs: an engineer's salary around $54,000, a yearly boiler service of about $100 to $200, a per-square-foot service contract that could reach hundreds of thousands of dollars for a large convention center, and monitoring fees of $100 to $395 per month.

His proposal is to cross-train mechanical and network engineers for facility roles, so a site keeps its own staff instead of paying several third parties to watch the same systems. He suggests the savings could fund higher salaries and infrastructure upgrades. He closes by pointing to the human side of ICS security, including a worker with limited literacy who had been operating an energy system, and he notes that the session was non-technical.

talks.title: Layered Blueprints for OT Security
talks.teaser: Presents a layered model that links OT security goals, risks and requirements to implementation, using a water utility example.
talks.summary:
Sarah Fluchs opens by arguing that OT security engineering does not yet earn the label of engineering. Using a bolt-joint analogy, she proposes three questions to ask of any security solution: what the assumptions and protection goals are, whether the path from problem to solution can be followed, and whether an equivalent alternative could be chosen from the information available.

She presents the Layered Blueprints model, a four-layer framework covering function, risk, requirements and implementation. Working through a German drinking water utility, she explains how the network is first reduced to one model instance per recurring pattern, such as control room and remote sites, because OT engineers rarely think in network terms or document them. Use cases such as programming PLCs, connecting sites and controlling the plant then serve as protection goals, and a communication analysis maps which roles and protocols support each one. Risks are identified from those use cases, and requirements follow with relatively little extra work.

In the final part she addresses implementation efficiency, suggesting that a machine-readable data model could feed tasks such as firewall rule generation. She stresses that such a model must fit tools engineers already use and mentions AutomationML as one candidate. She closes by asking the audience to help build shared, open OT security solutions rather than isolated ones.

talks.title: Small Pox, Armor and ICS Security
talks.teaser: Historical stories from smallpox to WWII bombers argue that ICS defenders should ask better questions.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a series of historical stories meant to show that industrial control system security needs better questions, not just an effort to keep attackers out. It starts with eighteenth-century smallpox research, where Edward Jenner asked why milkmaids did not catch the disease. That line of questioning led to the protective effect of prior exposure to cowpox. The speaker uses this to argue that defenders get further by reframing the problem.

The middle section describes process control networks as very fragile and contrasts fragile, resilient and anti-fragile systems. The main example comes from World War II, when the statistician Abraham Wald reviewed bullet-hole data from returning aircraft and concluded that armor belonged on the cockpit and engines, where the surviving planes had not been hit. The speaker links this to cooperation between IT and OT teams, which bring different strengths. A number-guessing exercise illustrates the gap between random failure, which functional safety engineers handle well, and deliberate adversarial action. The Maginot Line example shows how a fixed defense fails once an opponent changes approach and goes around it.

The closing point is a question for listeners: what are they doing to avoid fighting the last war in their ICS security work. The practical takeaway is to examine assumptions, learn from the data on what failed, and combine IT and OT perspectives when planning defenses.

talks.title: Persisting in Level 1: The Building is Alive
talks.teaser: Traces a red-team attack on building automation networks, from an IP camera foothold to persistent control of a controller.
talks.summary:
The speaker presents a red-team project in which a small team set out to get into a building automation network and stay there undetected, with persistence at the controller level. Their requirements included cleaning traces after each step, evading security tools, keeping the attack modular and reusable, and keeping the cost low. The talk frames building automation as a mix of IT and OT, with cross-vendor subsystems such as access control, HVAC, lifts and IP cameras. Their early reconnaissance found many internet-facing devices and networks that were not segmented.

To prepare the attack, the team built a lab from vendor controllers and had students search for vulnerabilities. They reported around ten to fifteen zero-days across the devices, including a buffer overflow in a widely used controller that they considered critical. The attack chain started with a known camera exploit, moved laterally to a Windows workstation through a misconfiguration with default credentials, and then reached the access control controller by exploiting the buffer overflow. The final payload changed badge permissions and altered logging. For persistence, the team reviewed common techniques such as cron jobs, boot scripts, shell configuration files and path interception. Cron was not available on the platform, a boot script change left a device unusable, and only manipulating the global path variable worked.

The speaker put the total spend at around eleven thousand dollars and argued that such an attack is cheap for a motivated attacker. An internet device search showed almost 22,000 exposed controllers of the same model, 40% of which were still vulnerable, and 11,000 cameras, 91% of which were vulnerable. The vendors were notified through responsible disclosure, and some patches had never been publicised. The main takeaway is that building automation needs its own security measures, since an intruder who leaves traces on the network may still be detected by someone who knows what to look for.

talks.title: A New CVSS For ICS Vulnerabilities

talks.title: PASTA - Portable Automotive Security Testbed with Adaptability
talks.teaser: Presents PASTA, a portable tabletop automotive testbed with working vehicle controls for studying attacks on in-vehicle networks.
talks.summary:
Toyota researcher Oshi Toyama introduces PASTA, a portable automotive security testbed built so people can study attacks on in-vehicle networks without a real car. He starts with the problem: vehicles were not designed with security in mind, and on older models the OBD-II diagnostic port had no central gateway, so an attacker plugged into it could send messages to ECUs. He cites the Jeep Chrysler remote hack on a running car, which led to a recall of about a million vehicles, as an example of the risk.

The platform is a small tabletop vehicle with steering, wheels, headlights, doors, brakes and hazard lamps, plus a simple simulator in a carrying case whose behavior is shown on three LED panels. Control commands travel as CAN messages through the platform rather than driving the simulator directly. Attack surfaces include the OBD-II port, junction boxes and JTAG ports, and each ECU can be reprogrammed in C. Safety functions are not yet fully implemented, so the speaker demonstrated how messages sent through the OBD-II port can take over the platform's behavior.

The design rests on four ideas: open, safe, adaptable and portable. Users should be able to rewrite CAN message definitions, ECU behavior and message frequencies. The speaker argues that the same principles suit ICS testbeds: match the testbed to the skills it should teach, keep educational versions affordable, use genuine protocols, and publish specifications openly. The project was still ongoing, with the specification and GitHub page not yet public, and questions about price were left unanswered.

talks.title: Will Your Protection System Work In A Cyber Incident?
talks.teaser: Explains how a test lab checked grid protection networks by breaking links and switches while adding security layers.
talks.summary:
The talk asks whether grid protection systems keep working during a cyber incident. The speaker explains that protective relays exchange decisions within strict timing limits, such as a 100 millisecond transfer-time class, and that performance and quality requirements from IEEE, IEC and national bodies apply. Any added security layer, such as domain controllers, logging, backups and VPNs, must not degrade protection.

The team tested this with hardware-in-the-loop setups, where a real-time simulator modelled a transmission system and substation racks responded to injected faults. Using 300 switches and routers from several vendors, they broke single links, multiple links and switches, including root bridges, while measuring protection response times. Root bridge failure caused a much longer speed and latency impact than a link failure, while the added security functions had relatively little effect. The speaker also described using Ostinato to load the network and noted that an unknown MAC address could disrupt spanning tree across the switches.

In the Q&A, the speaker explained that customer patience limited the number of cases, so the team settled on about 15 network scenarios and shared predicted traffic paths before showing results. Third parties also ran Metasploit-based tests and scans against the network. The takeaway is to design predictable traffic paths, account for root bridge failure, and measure outcomes instead of assuming them. Next steps include software-defined networking and intrusion detection and prevention with industrial security vendors.

talks.title: S4x19 ICS Detection Challenge Results
talks.teaser: Reports results of an ICS detection challenge where vendors and open-source teams analyzed mining network captures for planted attacks.
talks.summary:
This session reports on a community ICS detection challenge that tests whether products can build asset inventories and spot attacks hidden in real industrial packet captures. The scenario was a mining operation modeled on northern Quebec, built from hundreds of gigabytes of captured traffic with a 130 GB subset used for the detection phase. A third vendor withdrew late, so the organizers gave the captures and a score sheet to two commercial vendors, Dragos and Kaspersky, and an open-source team, with a few days to analyze them. The attack entered through the DMZ, moved through jump hosts and a terminal server to a historian, and reached PLCs, with decoy malware placed in the business network.

Kaspersky presented five incidents from its product, including an exploitation attempt, a downloader's command-and-control traffic, GrayEnergy connections, a suspicious PLC response, and a PLC that stopped after a firmware update. Dragos walked through its platform's zones, timelines and asset context to follow Havoc and GrayEnergy behavior, including a brute-force against NTLM accounts that pivoted across zones. The open-source pair found some activity but missed parts of the chain and produced false positives, such as redundancy traffic mistaken for ARP spoofing. None of the teams fully traced the final step.

The speakers drew several lessons. Many alerts came from unusual but legitimate OT behavior, so analysts need baselines, maintenance schedules and knowledge of device quirks. Scaling to many sites will require correlation and local triage. Neutral, data-driven tests give buyers a better basis for choosing a product than demos alone.

talks.title: The Industrial Radio Project - Hacking Cranes Using SDR
talks.teaser: Shows how researchers found replay and command injection flaws in wireless remote controls for industrial cranes.
talks.summary:
The talk presents Trend Micro research into the wireless remote controls used on cranes and other heavy lifting equipment in construction, ports, mining, utilities and nuclear work. The researchers asked where these systems are used, how they work and what risks they carry. They tested devices from 14 vendors across several regions, most operating in the 400 to 900 MHz range, and found that captured radio commands could be replayed to move real cranes.

To understand the protocols, the team logged SPI traffic between a microcontroller and a sub-GHz radio chip with a logic analyzer, then mapped those operations to register accesses using the chip datasheet. They built an emulator that tracked radio state and linked it to a flow graph so captured traffic could be replayed over the air and compared against physical devices. Findings included command injection, abuse of the emergency stop to cause denial of service, and malicious re-pairing. One vendor obscured its messages with an XOR keyed to a pairing ID, which the team recovered by building a dictionary of possible IDs. They saw no proper authentication or encryption in the devices they examined.

The speaker also described a remote scenario in which a training video revealed a manufacturer, whose documentation explained how dip switches set the operating frequency, and recorded traffic from a public spot without replaying it. Demonstrations on owned equipment, with permission, included a handheld SDR, a wristwatch-sized transmitter and a remote device connected over LTE. The takeaway for operators is to ask vendors whether their equipment is susceptible and to apply patches. Many vendors released fixes, while one declined to patch a discontinued product.

talks.title: S4x19 Dale Peterson Mini Keynote - Create The Future
talks.teaser: Argues that ICS defenders are falling behind and should ask different what-if questions to reshape their approach.
talks.summary:
Dale Peterson opens the S4 event by arguing that the industrial control systems community is not keeping pace with the threats. He says the field has moved from the old belief in an air gap and security through obscurity toward accepting that ICS can be secured, but progress is being measured mostly through cyber hygiene checks such as asset inventories, password management, hardware configuration and patching. He argues that this approach will not stop a moderately skilled attacker, and that working harder on it will not close the gap while attacks grow in number and sophistication, including attempts to manipulate safety systems.

In the middle of the talk he points to business trends that speed the problem up: more interconnection between asset owners, vendors, integrators and service providers, new cloud services, and a rapid rise in low-cost controllers and sensors. He says the answer is to ask different questions. Instead of asking how often servers need patching, he suggests asking how to significantly reduce the security burden on the OT team, and he notes that the program deliberately places opposing ideas side by side.

He closes by encouraging attendees to take unfamiliar ideas seriously, to test them with what-if thinking rather than dismissing them, and to spend conference conversations building on new questions instead of complaining about current problems. He notes that many projects and companies have grown out of informal discussions at earlier editions of the event.

talks.title: S4x18 Debate: Enterprise SOC or OT SOC?
talks.teaser: Two debaters argue whether an asset owner with industrial control systems should run one enterprise SOC or a dedicated OT SOC.
talks.summary:
This session is a structured debate on how an asset owner with industrial control systems should organize security monitoring: one enterprise security operations center covering both IT and OT, or a dedicated OT-focused center. The audience voted before and after the arguments, and both debaters were asked to make the strongest case for their side, with the shared premise that either model needs real OT expertise.

The enterprise side argued that most intrusions begin on the IT network before they reach industrial systems, so an OT-only center risks seeing attacks too late. It cited a SANS white paper describing multi-stage ICS attacks, warned that coordination breaks down at handoffs between separate teams, and argued that one team is cheaper to run. It also held that IT staff can learn OT awareness faster than OT staff can pick up IT protocols and malware analysis.

The dedicated OT side countered that a center's value comes from its mission, not its label, and that industrial operations prioritize recovery time and root cause analysis. It said threat collection should focus on the adversaries that target industrial environments, noted that remote vendor access rather than phishing was the main entry path it had seen, and proposed a small, well-trained OT group that stays culturally connected to IT. Dan also noted that hybrid models with OT specialists inside an enterprise center could fit either view. Hands raised before and after the rebuttals shifted very little.

talks.title: China As The Most Active Shaper Of The Cybersecurity Space
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for China As The Most Active Shaper Of The Cybersecurity Space.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Adam Segal explores how China has emerged as the most active shaper of cybersecurity and cyberspace globally. Segal emphasizes that policies originating in Beijing—spanning domestic regulation, technical standards, diplomacy, and foreign infrastructure investment—will fundamentally impact international technology and security ecosystems. Under President Xi Jinping, cybersecurity has been placed at the very top of the national agenda, framed around the core doctrine that modernization and national security cannot exist without digitalization and cybersecurity.

### Key Topics
- **Chinese Strategic Motivations**: China's cyber strategy is driven by three core interests: domestic stability and regime legitimacy (enforced through rigorous censorship, real-name registration, VPN bans, and the Great Firewall); cybersecurity and national security (rooted in a perception of vulnerability to foreign backdoors and reliance on Western vendors like the "eight guardian warriors"); and techno-nationalism (the ambition to transition from "Made in China" to "Invented in China," avoiding the middle-income trap via initiatives like Made in China 2025, massive semiconductor investment, AI leadership plans, and quantum communications).
- **Domestic Regulatory Measures**: Beijing has rolled out sweeping legislative frameworks, including the National Security Law ("secure and controllable" mandates), the Anti-Terrorism Law, and the 2017 Cybersecurity Law. These introduce the designation of Critical Information Infrastructure (CII), requiring mandatory security reviews (potentially involving source code inspection administered via the Ministry of State Security), data localization, and strict mandatory threat information sharing, supplemented by specific action plans for industrial control systems (ICS).
- **International Strategy & Diplomacy**: Internationally, China projects its technical and regulatory standards through the multi-trillion-dollar Belt and Road Initiative across roughly 65 countries. In international diplomacy, China promotes "cyber sovereignty" under the UN Charter rather than Western interpretations of the laws of armed conflict, leading to the breakdown of consensus in forums like the UN Group of Governmental Experts (UN GGE).
- **Key Uncertainties**: Segal highlights three major variables shaping the future: implementation friction and bureaucratic competition among Chinese agencies (e.g., CAC, MIIT, MPS, MSS, PLA); conflicting pressures on globalizing Chinese tech firms (such as Huawei and ZTE) caught between international market expectations and tighter domestic state control; and evolving US policy amid looming trade disputes and Section 301 investigations.

### Technical Details
- **CII Review & Localization**: Critical Information Infrastructure operators face ambiguous designations overseen by the Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC), MIIT, and MPS. Network equipment entering CII is subject to state security reviews, potentially demanding source code access, alongside mandatory in-country data storage.
- **ICS Security Initiatives**: A 2018–2020 action plan specifically addresses industrial control systems, establishing emergency management protocols, domestic standard R&D platforms, and legally mandated threat intelligence sharing to reduce dependence on foreign-serviced systems.
- **Offensive & Deterrent Operations**: Chinese defense analysts conceptualize critical infrastructure cyber operations as deterrent measures against advanced Western Pacific adversaries. Technical incidents highlighted include pre-conflict operational mapping of critical infrastructure and state-level traffic redirection, exemplified by the "Great Cannon" attack that hijacked Baidu ad streams to launch denial-of-service strikes against GitHub.

### Takeaways
- Foreign leverage against Beijing's cyber strategy is limited because policies tie directly to existential regime interests. However, historical precedents (such as the WAPI standard push and Green Dam censorship software) demonstrate that unified resistance from foreign governments and multinational corporations without commercial defections can force policy compromises.
- Escalation risks remain elevated due to the lack of bilateral military-to-military communication—stalled since the 2014 PLA indictments—and absent definitions regarding thresholds for cyber acts of war.
- Potential counter-strategies include building multilateral consensus on cyber norms among allies (e.g., EU and Japan) and demanding strict commercial and regulatory reciprocity against Chinese technology companies operating abroad.

talks.title: NOW!: Dale Peterson's S4x13 SCADA Apologist Keynote
talks.teaser: Frames the event's theme around moving ICS security from explaining flaws to committing to fix them now.
talks.summary:
Dale Peterson opens the S4x13 conference with a short keynote built around the event's "NOW" theme. He recalls the previous year's project that showed how popular PLCs from large vendors could be broken, and notes that critics dismissed the findings as long-known problems. He argues that the control systems community already understands both the flaws and the fixes, so the real question is why change has not happened.

He names a pattern he calls the "SCADA apologist": an expert who correctly describes how insecure control systems are, then softens the message by saying the fixes will take a decade or more. He recounts how such explanations have reached decision makers, who then concluded the problem cannot be fixed. He also warns against messages that claim any system can be hacked no matter what is done, since that can discourage spending on protection.

He closes by urging attendees to pair a description of the problems with a commitment to fix them now. He points out that replacing a control system is a one-to-three-year project that can be budgeted and started today. He asks attendees to leave the event spreading that message, and then hands over to the first presentation.

talks.title: Comparing Government Approaches To Critical Infrastructure Security
talks.teaser: Compares national cyber strategies, infrastructure regulations and corporate governance codes across European countries and beyond.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens by asking whether industry will survive to be protected, pointing to a McKinsey report on US manufacturing. Factory equipment's average age rose from 7 years in 1980 to nine, and factory buildings from 16 years to 25. Plants fell by 25% and jobs by 33% over 20 years, so the speaker suggests security is not industry's main problem. The talk then recalls the Castillo de San Marcos in St. Augustine as an early example of protecting assets.

The core of the talk reviews cybersecurity approaches in several European countries, South Africa, China, Singapore and the United States, across national strategies, infrastructure protection rules and corporate governance codes. The US currently has no single formal strategy, and few strategies address boards or operational technology. Most countries have specific infrastructure rules, but a 2008 EU directive covered only energy and transport, while other countries identified up to 16 sectors.

On the corporate side, the speaker cites the TalkTalk incidents, a UK parliamentary view that the CEO owns cyber responsibility, and a growing list of executives who resigned after cyber issues. Governance code recommendations are generally not mandatory, and none of the codes mention industrial security. A US Senate bill, S.536, would have required companies to declare board cyber capabilities and explicitly covered industrial control systems, but it has not passed. The speaker suggests boards and national strategies must address industrial security directly.

talks.title: Modbus Secure Update from S4x18
talks.teaser: Explains how Modbus TCP is wrapped in TLS, with certificate-based device identity and the key-management questions it raises.
talks.summary:
The talk examines how Modbus, a protocol dating to 1979 that moved onto Ethernet in 1996 without authentication, can be hardened. The proposed approach wraps Modbus TCP in TLS, which lets endpoints authenticate each other, detects altered messages, and offers integrity-only or encrypted modes depending on device resources. Each device holds its own X.509 certificate, with a role identifier embedded in it, a mechanism that loosely follows IEC 62351.

An interoperability event brought together several vendors with Arm devices running from 133 MHz to 1.2 GHz and different TLS libraries, including OpenSSL, Mocana and embed TLS. Connections came up quickly, but certificate chain validation caused the biggest difficulties. A full handshake took about two and a half seconds on the slowest hardware, while session resumption cut setup time by roughly an order of magnitude. The group settled on TLS 1.2 with strong cipher suites, and Schneider Electric described work with Entrust DataCard on an on-premise certificate authority appliance, targeted for the end of Q2.

Audience questions centred on operations. The presenter said the certificate authority should stay offline in a locked environment, with the private key owned by the customer, and that revocation could use CRLs distributed out of band or OCSP with stapling, which avoids downloading full lists. Other concerns included re-keying plants, training technicians who know the process but not IP addresses, and using multi-tier CAs. The main takeaway was that encryption is workable, while key management remains the hard part.

talks.title: An Examination of Hardware Convergence in ICS
talks.teaser: Shows how shared chips and reference designs spread across unrelated ICS products, and why hidden vulnerabilities matter.
talks.summary:
The talk presents laboratory research into hardware convergence in industrial control and IT systems, which the team framed as convergent evolution. Borrowing from biology, the speaker suggests unrelated products can end up sharing components under similar cost and market pressures, and asks how that shared hardware changes long-term risk, given that IT moves quickly while OT moves slowly. A common chip carries its weaknesses into every product built on it.

The team dismantled two smart meters from different manufacturers and catalogued their chips, finding overlap that appeared to come from shared reference designs. For one chip family they found no published vulnerability, while another had active security research, which the team took as a sign that a relevant flaw would likely surface. They then bought a malware-prevention kiosk and obtained its vendor documentation. Component by component, most parts showed no published flaws, but a Genesis Logic GL3220 chip in the multimedia card reader was linked by others to BadUSB. The team reported this to the vendor without confirming it, and the vendor informed its customers.

Key takeaways were that reference designs are reused across manufacturers with little change, documentation is often incomplete, and vendors may not know their own sub-suppliers or detect silent chipset swaps. Teams should identify key chipsets, libraries and software in their products and treat inherited vulnerabilities as a normal part of risk, since building from scratch is increasingly rare. The Q&A also raised the trade-off between shared components and defense in depth.

talks.title: Lessons Learned From A Major ICS Detection Deployment
talks.teaser: Walks through lessons from piloting and scaling passive ICS network monitoring across an oil and gas company's plants.
talks.summary:
This talk shares lessons from a large ICS detection deployment at an oil and gas company with a long-running industrial security program. The customer wanted a cloud-hosted platform that could handle heavy traffic, retain full packet captures, and give operations, SOC and ICS teams a shared view. The rollout started with a passive pilot: sensors on existing network taps captured traffic under a capture profile set for each site, keeping full fidelity for ICS protocols and selected IP protocols, while other traffic was compressed before upload.

Pilot findings included unexpected protocols, misconfigurations, new devices appearing on process control networks that should have been static, and remote access sessions reaching safety systems. Within Modbus traffic, the team flagged port scans against slave devices, unusual write function codes, pipelined requests and TCP resets as possible signs of abuse. Threat intelligence was applied to live and stored traffic, so newly learned indicators could be checked against historical data.

The main takeaways concerned process as much as technology. Defining how sites and teams respond to an event, and wiring alerts into existing workflows, mattered as much as the product. Vendor engagement was essential, since automation vendors had to accept the sensors and taps. Accurate asset inventories and visual maps of zones and conduits helped SOC, security and site staff share one view. The deployment used a single-tenant cloud with encrypted data and plug-and-play sensors, and next steps included firewall integrations and tracking reductions in unclassified traffic.

talks.title: Case Study Fuzzing Before and After You Are Ready
talks.teaser: Walks through an ICS vendor's fuzzing journey on its PI Server, including what failed and how to build a program.
talks.summary:
Fuzzing feeds large volumes of mostly machine-generated, malformed input to a program to find failure modes worth analysing, trading cheap machine time for costly human bug hunting. The speakers introduce Peach, an open-source, extensible fuzzing platform. In their case study, roughly 1.5 million mutated files were fed into each Office and OpenOffice version from 2003 to 2010 while a debugger watched for crashes. Office results dropped from 2003 to 2007, which the speakers tie to Microsoft's security development lifecycle.

Anthony Tang describes the vendor's PI Server journey, from vulnerability reports by Idaho National Laboratory in 2005 to a Modbus-specific fuzzer around 2009. Early wins came without dedicated staff, so fuzzing became a checklist item. In 2011 a developer volunteered, and the team modelled network traffic captured in Wireshark, starting with dumb fuzzing and moving to smarter, format-aware fuzzing. By PI Server 2012, fuzzing accounted for roughly half of the security issues found.

Akshay Agarwal then draws out lessons: tooling should handle proprietary formats and protocols, scale across machines, support monitoring and state awareness, and fit existing development tools. Reporting must serve both engineers and executives. In the Q&A, the speakers suggested vendors prove their programs with coverage reports or acceptance rules, such as one ICS customer requiring a file format to pass a million iterations without a crash. The takeaway is that fuzzing is a long-running investment that needs dedicated, trained staff and executive buy-in.

talks.title: Security of Medical Devices
talks.teaser: Shows how ICS-style flaws in a secondhand medical device and a patient-monitoring iPad app enable takeover.
talks.summary:
Billy Rios and Terry McCorkle, who come from industrial control systems research, explain why they turned their attention to medical devices. Many large vendors sell into both fields, and they found that the development habits, security attitudes and lifecycle practices seen in ICS carry over to medical equipment. They describe obscurity as a practical obstacle: some devices were hard to buy, with resellers refusing sales that might need a license, though secondhand units and support software still turned up for sale.

The first case was a Philips device bought secondhand for a couple hundred dollars. Inventory tags showed it had belonged to a hospital, and forensic imaging of its drive revealed it ran Windows XP and held credentials that appeared to belong to that hospital. Probing an open port suggested a heap overflow, and a proof-of-concept Python script delivered a reverse Meterpreter shell running with privileges. The second case was a patient-monitoring iPad app that connected over RDP to a server exposed on the internet, using shared demo credentials and stored logins. Once inside, a swipe gesture opened the keyboard, and the session ran as an unrestricted user.

The speakers reported the issues through ICS-CERT and DHS rather than directly to vendors, and the vendor responded quickly. They are withholding the exploit because the issue is unfixed. Their takeaways: obscurity does not protect these systems, vendors need a security mindset, and clinical users should not be expected to defend against basic flaws.

talks.title: Why Johnny Can’t Patch Can Vulnerability Patching Work in the ICS World
talks.teaser: Operators learn why patch availability rarely means field deployment in ICS and how compensating controls can close the gap.
talks.summary:
Industrial control environments inherited decades of designs that prioritized safety and reliability over security, leaving insecure protocols and sprawling software stacks on the plant floor. The speaker recounts a 2008 refinery engagement where 78 Windows hosts carried thousands of published vulnerabilities and conservative estimates suggested dozens of undiscovered flaws per machine in unlisted control applications. Research on operating-system fixes notes that a substantial fraction of patches are faulty, which is especially dangerous when reboots, expert onsite labor, and process downtime make each change risky.

The talk argues that researcher–vendor disclosure stories end too early at patch release. Case studies include a vendor blocked by a third-party OS supplier, another that closed backdoors while remote support and customers resisted, and the speaker’s own firm offering a free upgrade that most customers never downloaded. An end user once asked to withhold PLC findings for months because a shutdown was a year away.

Practitioners should treat patching as necessary but not sufficient. Compensating controls—firewall rules, IDS signatures, product reconfiguration, and network blocking when PLCs cannot be updated—can deploy faster with less change-management fear and easier rollback. Examples include a read-only Modbus firewall for safety integrated systems and firewalls whose rules are generated from exported control logic. Effective mitigations must preserve safety perceptions, stay simple for control engineers, minimize field configuration, and account for total cost of ownership rather than purchase price alone.

talks.title: Finding N-Day Vulnerabilities in an ICS Embedded Devices
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Finding N-Day Vulnerabilities in an ICS Embedded Devices.

talks.title: Cyber Insurance: Linking the CISO to the CFO
talks.teaser: Shows how to translate ICS cyber risk into insurance terms a CFO and risk manager can act on.
talks.summary:
The session addresses how security leaders can describe cyber risk in terms a CFO can weigh. The speakers present a cyber impact framework that sorts losses into first-party and third-party categories, split between financial and physical damage. They explain that insurance is the transfer option security teams often overlook, and that cyber behaves like a super peril, since one event can trigger several different policies at once.

Two client cases anchor the discussion. In the first, an industrial manufacturer's control systems were compromised and its production line stopped. Its property policy extended to data corruption, but the limit was far below what a cyber policy would have offered for that exposure. In the second, a regulated utility was hit by ransomware that locked its IT side, cutting off service requests and regulatory reporting. Its cyber policy responded, and the speakers noted that coverage for fines and penalties has been expanding, though insurability of fines is still untested. They also walked through common myths about cyber insurance, such as the idea that it does not cover ransomware or insider threats.

The takeaway is to run tabletop exercises, attach dollar values to each scenario, and check every policy's triggers and limits against those numbers. Insurance should be tailored like any other control. Practitioners should also find out who the risk manager is and what coverage already exists before the next incident.

talks.title: Avoiding OT Vulnerabilities
talks.teaser: Explains why ICS vulnerability tracking stalls across plants and presents a continuous inventory-and-remediation approach.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with why vulnerability management is hard in industrial control environments. Security teams must research a steady flow of ICS advisories, then determine which facilities run an affected model, firmware or version. Lower-level devices such as PLCs, controllers and safety systems are harder to reach than network-attached servers, span many vendors, and are often decades old. Traditional scanners need credentials or vendor-approved agents, while passive monitoring rarely yields detailed device data.

A gas detector scenario illustrates the stakes. An attacker phishes an engineer, captures VPN credentials, reaches an engineering workstation, and exploits a flaw in a detector's web administration interface. Altering calibration, alarm or transmission settings can trip several detectors and shut down the process, and restoring the original settings afterward hides what happened. The speaker estimates such an event could cost millions in lost production and hundreds of hours of wasted response time.

The proposed remedy is continuous ICS vulnerability management. Configuration data is collected from devices without installing agents, normalized into an inventory at each facility, and synced to a corporate database. Advisories are matched against that inventory, ranked by CVSS score, and remediation is tracked against agreed timeframes. The product detects and tracks rather than patching devices itself. Questions covered how configuration files are gathered from engineering projects, backups and vendor interfaces, and how the product builds on an existing deployment.

talks.title: Denial of Surface: Shodan and ICS
talks.teaser: Uses Shodan banner data to show how many industrial control devices sit on the internet despite air-gap claims.
talks.summary:
The talk questions whether industrial control systems are truly isolated from the internet, as vendors and asset owners often claim. The speaker argues that an air gap should be continually proven rather than assumed. Active scanning can crash fragile devices, so the speaker used Shodan's public banner data instead, running about 33 queries that surfaced roughly 10,000 devices over two years of collection.

Banners were parsed with regular expressions into tokens, then checked against exploit databases for known issues, not zero-days. About 17% of results returned a 401 authentication response and 33% returned a 200 with no login needed. Geolocation filled in city and country for about 75% of results, and failed lookups were plotted visibly so they could be fixed. Processing cost was estimated at two dollars and 18 cents per node, with roughly 79.5 nodes per week passed to ICS-CERT, which coordinated with 63 CERTs worldwide.

The speaker closes by urging debate over whether connectivity should be a default design assumption, and encourages defenders to scan their own networks. Audience questions covered legal hurdles: in the US, reaching owners often requires a subpoena, and some European certs treat IP addresses as personal data.

talks.title: Effective Engagement with Boards (of Directors)

talks.title: Ralph Langner on Lean OT Security
talks.teaser: Argues that OT security efforts should borrow lean startup and lean manufacturing ideas to cut waste and win end-user buy-in.
talks.summary:
Ralph Langner opens by arguing that asset owners still are not doing enough for OT security, even after incidents such as Stuxnet and the cyber-physical attacks in Ukraine. He describes his own attempts to change this, including lobbying policymakers in Washington, and notes that a vendor name-and-shame project was dropped after a while. He also says that scare tactics about future attacks have persuaded buyers poorly.

He frames the gap as a cognitive problem: why do security products rarely spread the way consumer apps do, and why is the community's default answer that users simply do not get it? Drawing on the Lean Startup movement, he compares the OT security community to a failing startup that focuses on its own big ideas rather than on end users. From lean manufacturing he takes the idea of reducing waste, meaning the implementation cost and inconvenience that a control places on users. He argues that users need to see some short-term, tangible gain before they accept a control.

His proposed concept, Lean OT Security, targets asset owners who already try to implement security and aims to make that execution more efficient rather than debating standards or risk levels. It solicits cooperation from end users, whom he describes as the real experts on their own use cases, which he calls authority reversal. He closes by urging projects to show tangible efficiency gains within six months so that they do not stall.
