talks.title: ICS Detection Challenge: Phase 1 Asset Identification and Inventory
talks.teaser: Compares ICS asset discovery tools on anonymized midstream oil and gas packet captures, scoring devices identified and accuracy.
talks.summary:
This session reviews phase one of an industrial control systems detection challenge, an asset identification exercise in which vendors received offline packet captures from a midstream oil and gas operator. The captures came from 15 locations and were merged into a single stream of about 15 million packets and 800 unique IP addresses. Because the data was heavily anonymized, the organizers found that identifying strings had to be scrubbed across many protocols, not only in IP headers, and that sensitive names hid in places they had not expected.

The competitors had roughly an hour to process the files and were scored on completeness, correctness and timeliness, with extra credit for unique findings. The presenters said the tools were generally strong at identifying major automation suppliers and Rockwell and Cisco products, including serial numbers and models, but they fell off for field devices such as drive controllers and smaller components. One vendor identified fewer devices but with more detail and accuracy, while others produced more entries that appeared to be intelligent guesses. Several tools also exposed clear-text passwords, though no single tool found all of the planted ones, and one caught a program download to a PLC.

The session closed with takeaways for asset owners. Discovery tools can surface devices that owners or integrators have forgotten, and adding configuration files, logs and other data sources could improve results. The scoring model also needed clearer definitions of what counts as an asset. Phase two, which asked tools to detect injected malicious traffic, was scheduled for the following day.

talks.title: Language Theoretic Security (langsec) Applied to ICS
talks.teaser: Explains how grammar-based parsers can make ICS protocols like DNP3 safer, using the Hammer parser kit and langsec principles.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a practical problem: how a receiving system can know that input is safe to process. The speakers argue that most defenses rely on blacklists built up through trial and error, or on trusting whoever sent the data, and that parsing and processing are often tangled together. They introduce the Chomsky hierarchy and explain why some formats need context to interpret, which makes correct checking hard.

Sergey Bratus then shows why parsers are a frequent source of bugs. He describes an integer-handling flaw in chunked encoding that hit Apache in 2002 and reappeared in Nginx around 2013. His proposed remedy is to build parsers from small elements upward into a grammar that reads like the protocol specification, and he argues that this can also improve performance. Meredith Patterson follows with a Hammer-based parser for the DNP3 link layer, covering range checks, bit-level fields, CRC validation and an end-of-input rule. She describes a transport-frame case where a missing check led to an unhandled exception, and notes that DNP3 length fields reach across layers, making it strongly context-sensitive.

The main takeaways are to separate recognition from processing, validate syntax before allocating memory, and whitelist what a grammar accepts rather than trying to enumerate attacks. The question period covered embedded allocators, the effort of hand-written drivers, state across multiple packets (which the current library does not address), and licensing, with Hammer under GPLv2 and a planned BSD-licensed standard library.

talks.title: Nozomi's SCADAguardian and Case Studies
talks.teaser: Shows how passive OT network monitoring builds asset inventories and detects process anomalies, with customer case studies.
talks.summary:
This vendor-led session walks through Nozomi Networks' SCADAguardian, a passive appliance that attaches to an industrial control network through a span port, network tap or virtual machine. It inspects traffic from the physical layer up to the process layer, learns a machine-learning baseline of how each PLC should behave, and adds modules for network visualization, asset inventory, vulnerability management and reporting.

The speakers then use the Industroyer attack, also called Crash Override, to frame the threat. They describe three phases: infection, discovery through passive reading of unencrypted industrial protocols, and an attack built from what was observed, using legitimate protocol commands rather than a specific vulnerability. The recommended defenses are real-time visibility, an accurate asset inventory, and combining signature detection with behavioral analysis, supported by geographically distributed deployments that feed a central operations center.

Three customer cases follow. A one-person operations team at a small Vermont electric utility reclaimed time by mapping its network passively instead of using active scans. A large global utility used passive fingerprinting to build an asset inventory matched against vulnerability data, so it could prioritize firmware risk. A security vendor chose the product for threat detection, where grouping anomalies and signatures into incidents, such as a contractor's laptop appearing on the network, gave quick context. The session closes with examples of subtle anomalies, including timing changes, abnormal setpoints and unfamiliar function codes, and with audience questions about the machine-learning methods.

talks.title: VC Panel on Investing in ICS Security
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in VC Panel on Investing in ICS Security.
talks.summary:
### Overview
At the S4 conference main stage, host Dale moderates a panel discussion featuring venture capital investors Patrick (representing ClearSky, a $300 million cybersecurity-focused fund) and Tyler (from Shell Technology Ventures / STV). The discussion examines the surge in venture and angel investment within industrial control systems (ICS) and operational technology (OT) cybersecurity. While deal flow has rapidly expanded from a few deals a year to dozens, both investors offer a realistic, critical assessment of the crowded market, explaining investment criteria, business hurdles, technology patterns, and long-term exit expectations.

### Key Topics
- **Fund Structures and Investment Theses:** ClearSky operates as a security-focused fund with ties to NextEra Energy (Florida Power and Light), seeking financial ROI while leveraging deep engineering resources to safeguard critical infrastructure. STV operates two capital buckets: one targeting Shell's 'new energies ambition' (future fuels, renewables, mobility over horizon 2 and 3 timelines) and another funding technologies deployed into core operations (such as unconventionals/shale, drilling, and production). STV views industrial cybersecurity as horizontal 'connective tissue' enabling digital transformation, remote operations, and automation.
- **Market Saturation and Lack of Differentiation:** Patrick notes he tracks nearly 30 companies competing with nearly identical architectures: network sniffing via taps, reverse-engineering proprietary ICS protocols, rule/threshold-based analytics, and baseline machine learning alerts. Investors find it difficult to discern true technical leaders when products function more as features rather than comprehensive, defensible platforms.
- **Shift from Fear to Business Value:** Tyler and Patrick advise entrepreneurs to move away from security buzzwords ('threat', 'cyber', 'risk') and address the buyer's operational bottom line. Enterprise buyers and P&L owners invest in cost reduction, operational uptime, and enabling remote field operations rather than buying standalone security boxes.
- **Sales Cycles and Industry Ecosystem:** The ICS domain faces sluggish, highly regulated enterprise sales cycles. Success requires navigating established industrial automation vendors (Honeywell, Schneider Electric, Emerson) and building go-to-market leadership (such as experienced CROs, VP of Sales, and CFOs) rather than relying solely on technical rockstars or threat intelligence backgrounds.
- **Realistic Exit Valuations:** Panelists emphasize that unicorns are unlikely in ICS security. Most startups will experience acquisitions in the $40M–$70M range by dominant IT security platforms or industrial automation suppliers looking to incorporate niche functionality as features.

### Technical Details
- **Network Appliance Limitations:** Both investors caution against relying on standalone proprietary hardware sniffers that decode legacy protocols (e.g., PLCs from 1995), warning that end-user engineers are fatigued by managing numerous disjointed monitoring boxes and consoles.
- **Forward-Looking Architectural Trends:** Investors look for architectures aligned with IT/OT convergence, including containerized applications, Software-Defined Networking (SDN) for flexible control implementation, virtualization, and built-in security for next-generation wireless industrial networks, microgrids, low Earth orbit (LEO) satellite links, and cloud/edge industrial IoT (IIoT) analytics platforms.

### Takeaways
- **Build for Future Infrastructures:** Security must be natively built into emerging technologies (renewables, distributed microgrids, remote automated operations) rather than retrofitting outdated legacy architectures.
- **Address Buyer Economics:** Founders must move beyond 'founderitis,' build strong business teams, partner with key supply-chain automation vendors, and engage decision-makers who hold direct P&L accountability.
- **Expect Strategic Consolidation:** Moderate return expectations (2x–3x) and feature consolidation are standard; successful serial founders use acquisitions as stepping stones for subsequent ventures.

talks.title: Understanding and Using the Cyberwar Meta
talks.teaser: Argues that cyber war policy leans on flawed analogies and proposes a game-style meta lens for judging offensive strategy.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that cyber war discussions are going wrong. The speaker compares the shifting strategies players call the meta in games such as Overwatch and League of Legends with how policy experts explain cyber conflict, often using simple game theory or nuclear-era analogies. The speaker suggests a meta-style model would better predict which offensive and defensive strategies will work.

Much of the talk criticises policy work. It cites a paper on vulnerability rediscovery whose data, the speaker says, proved unreliable after review, and a failed UN group effort on norms. Policy is built on ideas such as code carrying intent or data having a fixed physical location, which the speaker says do not match how software works. On the offensive side, the speaker describes modern implants as chains of persistence choices, tools and complementary skills, and says bug classes that seem rare can be used across the whole internet.

The closing advice is to red-team a society's weak points, such as election or social media manipulation, and to ask offensive teams what an operation would cost and how likely it is to fail. The speaker concludes that policy needs technically trained decision-makers and better data, and that cyber conflict mainly targets ideologies.

talks.title: A Network Sandbox for ICS Malware
talks.teaser: Explains an industrial sandbox that virtualizes OT components so analysts can triage ICS malware faster.
talks.summary:
Analysts receive huge volumes of malware from public sample pools, honeypots, customers and incident response, and examining each sample by hand is slow. Typical IT sandboxes run a sample for five to ten minutes and watch for IT-oriented behavior, so they can miss industrial malware that only acts when it finds control-system components. This talk presents a sandbox built to flag ICS-related behavior and cut analysis time.

The sandbox virtualizes the OT artifacts that malware checks for. Simulated OPC libraries and servers let scanning code, such as the OPC discovery seen in Havex, keep running so its follow-up actions can be observed. Process names tied to industrial software are presented as running, which matters for a Kill Disk attack that looks for two such processes and tries to terminate them. Industrial files and extensions, and traffic on IEC 104 ports, are also simulated and monitored, so the sandbox can record protocol-specific commands. A Ukrainian case involving a manually operated dropper showed that the environment must run for days and match a victim profile, since later modules arrived only after a day or two.

A live demo showed ICS-related alert counts, a Havex sample attempting to access the OPC server list, and captured traffic exchanged with simulated servers. The speaker stressed that this is an aid for analyst triage and for directing manual reverse engineering, not a network defense control. Q&A covered how an IT analyst can find the OT-relevant parts of a sample and hand them to OT experts, and planned work on GUI-driven installers using symbolic execution.

talks.title: TRITON: Ralph Langner & Zach Tudor Thoughts at the S4x18 Closing Panel
talks.teaser: Panelists weigh what the Triton safety-system attack reveals and which defensive lessons matter for industrial sites.
talks.summary:
This closing-panel discussion looks at Triton, the attack on a safety system in an industrial plant, and what the community should take from it. It opens with the vendor response. Schneider Electric's decision to speak openly on stage is presented as real progress, compared with the defensive reaction Siemens gave after Stuxnet in 2010. The speaker, Ralph Langner, argues that the attackers' operational security was poor, and that experimenting on a live target while trying to disable a safety system, which exists to prevent harm to people, makes little sense.

The middle of the talk covers what public accounts still leave out: how the attackers reached the engineering workstation, whether a dropper or command-and-control channel was involved, and what the payload was designed to do. The speaker suggests the payload could be inferred from the physical process a safety controller protects and the actuators wired to it, since a safety controller has a very narrow purpose. He cautions against early nation-state attribution and against overstating the attack before the facts are known. He also notes that basic controls, such as application whitelisting or file integrity monitoring on engineering stations, could have blocked the intrusion.

The closing point concerns legacy infrastructure. The controller involved was about 16 years old, which shows how hard it is to secure installed industrial systems. The panelists encourage practitioners to put replacing aging controllers in front of executives as a serious option, and to expect more detail once the asset owner and investigators share findings.

talks.title: Vulnerability Inheritance in PLC's
talks.teaser: Traces how a third-party PLC runtime's unauthenticated protocol flaws carried into vendor controllers and stayed unpatched.
talks.summary:
This talk comes from Digital Bond's research division, which looks for unknown flaws in industrial control products so vendors can fix them early. The speaker defines a vulnerability as any mechanism that allows unauthorized changes to configuration or control, a broader view than the one used by ICS-CERT. Embedded products often bundle third-party software such as operating systems and web servers, and the vendor stays responsible for fixing it through firmware updates.

The main case is a PLC runtime library from the software company 3S, used by hundreds of control vendors. Its second protocol version had password checks that the controller did not enforce, so an attacker could skip them and upload ladder logic, start or stop control, and retrieve any file. Version 3 changed the protocol but kept the same design flaws. Against a Hitachi controller, the two-byte session ID left only about 16,000 usable values to guess. A Sanyo Denki robot controller, and rebranded hardware from several other companies, carried the same runtime plus an old VxWorks debug service and a backdoor FTP account, and Festo, the vendor involved, refused to fix the issue.

The lesson is that patching insecure-by-design protocols is extremely hard, because external OPC software now depends on the missing security. Vendors should inventory third-party components, red team their products during development, plan secure firmware update paths, and verify components rather than trust them. Advisories that repeat vendor claims can mislead owners, and customers can require component lists in contracts.

talks.title: Remote Control Automobiles: Hacking The Snapshot Dongle
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Remote Control Automobiles: Hacking The Snapshot Dongle.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, Corey Thune (senior researcher with Digital Bond Labs and former consultant with Southfork Security) explores the intersection of industrial control systems (ICS) and modern automobile security. Emphasizing that modern vehicles are essentially 4,000-pound critical control systems operating on public infrastructure, Thune investigates the security risks introduced when third-party dongles are plugged into vehicles' internal networks to stream telematics and driving data back to corporate networks.

### Key Topics
- **Automotive and ICS Parallels**: Vehicle networks like the Controller Area Network (CAN bus) share significant architectural similarities with traditional ICS and SCADA networks. Both were historically treated as isolated systems and designed without built-in security controls.
- **CAN Bus Vulnerabilities**: CAN bus is an unauthenticated, unencrypted broadcast network. Any device connected to it can send messages to critical safety components such as the engine control unit (ECU), brakes, or steering mechanisms.
- **Third-Party OBD-II Dongles**: Devices like Progressive's Snapshot dongle plug directly into the federally mandated On-Board Diagnostics (OBD-II) port to collect driver data, bridging the vehicle's internal CAN network with external cellular networks (e.g., GPRS).

### Technical Details
Thune conducted a hardware and firmware security assessment of the Progressive Snapshot dongle manufactured by Xirgo Technologies (Zirgo Tech):
- **Hardware Teardown**: The device features a power regulation daughterboard, a CAN transceiver, a CAN bootloader to monitor wake states, an Atmel ARM CPU, an external flash chip, JTAG pads, and an off-the-shelf u-blox cellular daughterboard.
- **Firmware Extraction & Analysis**: Thune extracted the firmware directly by pulling the flash memory chip with assistance from Robert Leale and reading it. Analysis was conducted using `strings` and IDA Pro (leveraging the `eyeball2` plugin by Reid Wightman). Strings revealed internal file paths referencing Minnesota-based development, project codename "ocarina", and underlying FreeRTOS firmware.
- **Cellular & Logic Analysis**: Using a Saleae logic analyzer hooked up to the cellular board's UART interface, Thune monitored the AT commands exchanged between the CPU and cellular modem. The AT commands revealed that cellular network profile configuration lacked proper authentication, and communications utilized unencrypted channels like FTP rather than modern secure protocols.
- **Lack of Defensive Controls**: The device lacked fundamental modern embedded security practices, including firmware signing, secure boot mechanisms, mutual authentication, and encrypted transit.

### Takeaways
Thune concludes that third-party vendors are connecting insecure-by-design internal control networks to the wider internet without adopting foundational security mechanisms developed over the past decade. If an OBD-II dongle or backend carrier infrastructure is compromised, attackers could potentially pivot into the vehicle's CAN bus and issue unauthorized commands affecting vehicle operation. To mitigate these risks, Thune recommends hardware and software isolation—strictly limiting dongle firmware to read-only or constrained diagnostic CAN commands over segregated serial interfaces rather than allowing arbitrary bus communication.

talks.title: Avoiding Insecurity in ICS Protocols
talks.teaser: Contrasts serial ICS link encryptors with embedded DNP3 authentication and urges simple, layered trust boundaries.
talks.summary:
Legacy electric-sector communications still rely on bandwidth-limited, multi-drop serial links, so adding cryptography is rarely a matter of picking NIST-approved primitives alone. The speaker revisits prior fuzzing work to argue that insecure outcomes often come from unimplementable or overly entangled specifications, not from unknown algorithms.

The core comparison pairs Schweitzer Engineering’s Streaming Encryption Protocol with DNP3 Secure Authentication on the same wide-area use case. SEP keeps frames small and streams ciphertext with minimal latency for bump-in-the-wire deployments, trading away message integrity and accepting weak multi-drop filtering semantics. DNP3-SA folds authentication into the existing DNP3 object model, optional function-code policies, challenge versus aggressive modes, and parsing paths that may process ambiguous, unauthenticated application data before an HMAC can be checked—complexity that aligns with vulnerability clustering in Project Robus findings on the DNP3 stack.

Practitioners should treat pre-authentication parsing as the critical bottleneck, separate authentication from authorization, and favor a thin envelope layer above transport rather than peppering security through sprawling application standards. Asset owners need to understand encryption-only links, HMAC holdback latency, and when committee features expand attack surface faster than they reduce risk.

talks.title: Detecting Counterfeit Smart Grid Devices
talks.teaser: Shows how system-call monitoring and correlation can flag counterfeit smart grid devices without inspecting their hardware.
talks.summary:
Smart grid environments mix many networked devices, from resource-limited controllers such as PLCs to multi-core systems with substantial cache and RAM. The talk argues that counterfeit components in this setting are a serious threat, citing at least 7.5 billion dollars in lost revenue for US semiconductor companies, and notes that counterfeiting has been little studied in the smart grid domain. No real counterfeit devices were available, so the team modeled attacker behavior as a Poisson process. Six counterfeit cases were defined across the two device classes and three adversary goals: leaking information, poisoning measurements, and storing data for later transmission.

The framework works at the operating system level rather than inspecting hardware. It collects system calls from running applications using ptrace and library interposition, then compares them against a genuine ground-truth device. Resource-rich devices are checked with a simple statistical correlation, while resource-limited devices get a more advanced correlation over the order of system calls. The checks run in a cascade, so the heavier method is used only when the simpler one does not decide, which saves energy. A configurable threshold of 0.6 separates genuine devices from suspect ones.

Experiments used a small testbed with an open-source IEC 61850 GOOSE publisher and subscriber, a Raspberry Pi as the resource-limited device and a laptop as the resource-rich one. Results were averaged over 30 runs per case. Simple correlation missed some resource-limited counterfeits that the advanced method caught, and overhead on time, memory and CPU stayed small. The speaker closed by pointing to future work on machine learning and distributed detection, and by noting that real adversaries may not follow a Poisson pattern.

talks.title: An Economic Analysis of ICS Attacks
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of An Economic Analysis of ICS Attacks.
talks.summary: Alvaro Cardenas summarizes NSF-backed research with Colombian grid operator ISA on guerrilla attacks against transmission towers. FARC and ELN strikes once averaged near one tower per day, forcing military clearance of landmines before helicopter crews could rebuild structures in roughly four days. An undercover investigation caught a maintenance contractor paying guerrillas to topple additional towers inside its exclusive service region, inflating repair profits until ISA randomized multi-vendor dispatch and barred local hiring. The team formalized attacker incentives, showed how splitting contracts slashed expected payoff, and discussed why valuing blackout harm remains inconsistent across published estimates. The talk contrasts opportunistic physical sabotage with scalable cyber entry points and notes ongoing work simulating Ukraine-style relay manipulation on the isolated Texas interconnection.

talks.title: Secure ModBus (TCP/802)
talks.teaser: Explains a proposal to add TLS mutual authentication and certificate-based roles to Modbus TCP while keeping legacy compatibility.
talks.summary:
Daniel Clarke of Schneider Electric presents a proposal to add security to Modbus, a protocol from about twenty years ago that is still widely deployed in manufacturing. The goals were to keep the protocol simple, preserve compatibility with installed devices, and let operators secure the most at-risk data flows first. The design wraps Modbus TCP in TLS, which brings replay and man-in-the-middle protection, integrity, and the ability to change algorithms over time. Mutual authentication is required, while encryption is optional.

During commissioning, each device receives an x.509 certificate from a network PKI function, binding its name to a public key. Modbus has no field for roles and changing it would break existing systems, so the role sits in a certificate extension under a registered identifier. The role is checked during the handshake and again in the protocol handler, limiting what a compromised device can reach. Secure Modbus uses port 802 so legacy devices are not sent handshakes they may mishandle. Certificate status comes from revocation lists or from clients presenting status with each connection.

In the Q&A, the speaker confirmed the work covers Modbus TCP only, and a utility attendee said IP would add NERC CIP obligations. Self-signed certificates were raised as a false-security risk, and the speaker said a certificate authority should be required. The cost falls mainly on connection setup, and the proposal is still being finalized with major vendors.

talks.title: The Great Debate: Anti Virus and Monthly Security Patching Should Be Abandoned In ICS
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of The Great Debate: Anti Virus and Monthly Security Patching Should Be Abandoned In ICS.
talks.summary:
### Overview
This session, titled "The Great Debate," features a structured panel discussion on whether antivirus (AV) and monthly security patching should be abandoned in Industrial Control Systems (ICS). Facilitated by Dale Peterson, the session opens with two opposing advocates: Billy Rios, arguing for maintaining rigorous patching regimens, and Michael, an engineer arguing from an operational availability standpoint against disruptive monthly updates and AV overhead. The floor is then opened to conference attendees, sparking an extensive discussion on operational uptime, risk modeling, testing, and system architecture.

### Key Topics
- **Adversary Relentlessness vs. Operational Stability:** Billy Rios outlines the attacker mindset, emphasizing that offensive researchers and adversaries do not stop seeking opportunities. Drawing on his experience as a former Internet Explorer security program manager, Rios argues that patching is difficult and demanding, but necessary to raise the bar against relentless attackers.
- **Engineering and Availability Constraints:** Michael presents the perspective of critical infrastructure operators (power, water, natural gas), emphasizing that the primary imperative is process reliability and deterministic real-time control. A single untimely reboot or a delay of seconds can disrupt turbines or critical processes, while patches and AV signature updates inherently introduce unquantified operational risks.
- **Vendor Roles and Testing Realities:** Participants discuss the limits of testing. Rios highlights that enterprise software vendors include major applications in test matrices only when demand or risk is severe, urging ICS asset owners to exert pressure on vendors. Others note that industrial systems are often semi-custom implementations, complicating vendor guarantees.
- **Partial Patching and Risk Management:** The room debates realistic patching practices, such as patching only operating systems or applying updates quarterly or semi-annually. Commentators note that decisions are rarely binary; asset owners must weigh business risk, process interruption costs, and compensating controls.
- **Antivirus Inefficiencies and Contractor Auditing:** Multiple speakers note AV's weaknesses, including its vulnerability to polymorphic code and inability to stop targeted penetration testing. Ralph Langner shares observations that roughly half of his clients experienced malware outbreaks despite having AV installed, emphasizing that lack of policy enforcement and auditing—particularly regarding third-party contractor laptops—undermines basic defenses.

### Technical Details
- **Reboot Risks and Latency:** The debate notes Ralph Langner’s observation that 21 seconds of disruption could impair sensitive industrial processes like uranium enrichment, illustrating why unexpected reboots and AV scan latency during alarm storms present direct physical hazards.
- **System Hardening vs. Bloat:** Speakers point out that deterministic ICS environments should minimize attack surfaces by removing unnecessary software and hardening systems rather than relying purely on stacked defensive agents like AV and whitelisting.
- **Alternative Patching Paradigms:** Attendees explore academic and engineering solutions, such as employing formal mathematical methods to verify patch safety without requiring reboots, as well as leveraging virtualization to enable rapid rollback of faulty updates.

### Takeaways
Informal votes taken at the conclusion show that while many participants recognize AV is technically dated and limited against advanced threats, the vast majority still rely on it to catch low-hanging automated malware and USB-borne threats. Similarly, attendees overwhelmingly reject completely abandoning security patching, agreeing that while monthly cycles may be unfeasible for 24/7 continuous operations, patching remain an essential risk-reduction practice when combined with testing, architecture redesign, and compensating controls.

talks.title: How Deep Is Your Deep Packet Inspection (DPI)
talks.teaser: Proposes a way to grade industrial deep packet inspection products on protocol depth, control-plane filtering and response validation.
talks.summary:
Many industrial products claim deep packet inspection, yet buyers have little common basis for comparing them. The speaker, from the Tofino engineering team at Belden, first separates the data plane, which carries routine process traffic, from the control plane, where actions such as changing logic or updating firmware take place. The talk then looks at how Modbus, DNP3, and Ethernet IP frames are structured and why deeper protocols demand more complex parsing.

The core of the talk is a grading scheme with six comparison items. Sanity checking, where an engine validates every frame against the full specification, is treated as the most important. Other items include action filters that block specific function codes or address ranges, state checking that matches requests to responses, validation of response messages flowing back toward operators, handling of vendor-specific codes, and resistance to multiple embedded messages in one frame. Signature-based approaches are criticized as reactive blacklists that need constant updates. Because scores are subjective, the speaker also suggests weighing usability, latency, throughput, and how a device responds to blocked traffic.

In the question round, a test mode was described as a way to log what would be blocked before rules are enforced. Asked whether rules could be written in process terms, such as a temperature limit, the answer was that they still map to protocol commands on the wire. The closing message is that the industry should work toward a shared method for evaluating these products.

talks.title: The Antikernel
talks.teaser: Presents a hardware-based operating system design that removes all privileged code from the processor.
talks.summary:
Andrew Zonenberg argues that conventional kernels give broad privilege to code that rarely needs it. He walks through monolithic kernels, microkernels and separation kernels, then describes the 1990s MIT exokernel, which was built for performance by separating resource protection from abstraction. Moving non-security functions out of the privileged mode shrinks the trusted base and the attack surface, which he presents as the starting point for his design.

The proposed anti-kernel is a set of independent hardware state machines with no software running in privileged mode. Thread scheduling is a simple hardware round-robin queue, and communication between components runs over two on-chip packet networks: one for remote procedure calls and interrupts, and one for DMA and bulk data. Source addresses are stamped by a formally verified transceiver, and routing is hardwired, so access can be controlled by message origin. A hardware allocator hands out physical memory pages, and protection is enforced when a page is actually accessed rather than when it is mapped. A hardware ELF loader can also check signatures on program headers before a process starts.

The prototype runs on an FPGA, with a critical core of under ten thousand lines and the network and parts of the name server covered by formal correctness proofs. Speed has not been optimized, and future work includes moving to RISC-V, adding peripherals, and writing an SDK. The main takeaway is that the design targets critical systems such as medical and avionics devices, where isolation and fault tolerance matter more than raw performance, and that each component's trusted base depends on which resources it chooses to rely on.

talks.title: Security Guards vs. Motion Detectors: Depth or Breadth in ICS Security Monitoring
talks.teaser: Compares thick and thin network sensors for ICS monitoring, weighing deep site visibility against coverage across many facilities.
talks.summary:
The talk frames network security monitoring for industrial control systems as a choice between depth and breadth, using a retail analogy: guards watching every aisle versus motion detectors that flag movement but reveal little. A budget thought exercise makes the tradeoff concrete. A full-visibility sensor at 2 euro per site would cover only half of 100 facilities within 100 euro, while a metadata-only sensor at 1 euro per site gives every site some monitoring. The speaker stresses that alerts still need people with the right skills and time to act on them, so the answer is usually a blend.

Two architectures are compared. A thick sensor keeps collected data and analysis on site, which suits local management and long historical capture but makes cross-site correlation and scaling hard. A thin sensor sends metadata or alerts to a central location, which standardizes deployment at ingress and egress points but sees only part of the traffic. Three field examples follow. At one facility, a machine that should have been offline was contacting a command server tied to an old botnet, traced back to a USB device plugged in years earlier. At a power generation site, public IP addresses were found inside a control network because of how a vendor had set up the hosts. At a chemical plant, a guest wireless network had a route into the control network, so the real risk was an IT misconfiguration rather than an industrial protocol flaw.

The speaker proposes a maturity sequence: segment networks, inventory existing logs, confirm staff skills, monitor ingress and egress, and only then add process-specific monitoring. Visibility can be gained without inbound access using data diodes, unidirectional gateways, or network taps. Practitioners should measure progress with metrics such as time from detection to response and the share of alerts closed without action.

talks.title: The Lost Decade: ICS Vulnerabilities Since 2001
talks.teaser: Presents a multi-year count of public ICS vulnerabilities and uses vendor case stories to show where the industry is lagging.
talks.summary:
The talk examines publicly disclosed industrial control system vulnerabilities from 2001 onward and argues the field has fallen behind. The speaker sorts them into platform software, control system software, and bundled third-party components such as ActiveX controls and embedded operating systems, counting mainly the last two. Disclosures climb sharply around 2010, which the speaker links to attention after Stuxnet.

Case studies show how vendors handled reports. One embedded controller maker fixed only some of the eleven issues reported in 2001 and left customers to handle the rest. A third-party component inside a German vendor's software carried five known flaws for years without being discussed. A web server in a Rockwell module had many prior vulnerabilities, and a real-time operating system's debug service stayed open on a known port long before an advisory was issued. Several patches were also described as incomplete, with public exploits still working afterward.

The closing section offers resolutions for asset owners and vendors. Asset owners should track third-party components, test patches themselves, and keep their own defenses strong. Vendors should inventory bundled software, fix root causes instead of single instances, and publish security contacts. Questions from the audience raised prioritising by real-world impact and the reluctance of some researchers to contact vendors directly.

talks.title: Functional Safety & Cybersecurity ... Diving into the Details
talks.teaser: Shows how functional safety practices like FMEA and coverage testing can be combined with OT cybersecurity design.
talks.summary:
The session argues that functional safety and operational technology cybersecurity overlap enough to be designed together, and that safety budgets can help fund security work. The presenters map the IEC 61508 safety lifecycle against the IEC 62443 security standard, with both starting from requirements and moving through design, implementation, module testing and system validation.

A worked example follows a customer who wants to load PLC programs from a USB memory stick on a robot cell with no network. Threat modelling with STRIDE on the USB entry point and data flow shows that corruption calls for stronger integrity checks than a CRC, such as a hash, while information disclosure needs encryption. Separate memory areas keep security patches from changing safety functions. The development part covers coding standards, static analysis, cyclomatic complexity to size test cases, and code coverage, which can expose untested code or hidden backdoors.

In the question session, speakers discuss certification. They agree that security cannot be proven the way safety can, so claims should describe what a system was tested against rather than call it certified. Patch management is flagged as a new challenge for safety systems. The takeaway is to engage safety colleagues early and design for both safety and security together.

talks.title: Detecting ICS Attacks Through Process Variable Analysis
talks.teaser: Shows how predicting process variables from learned correlations can flag injected false data in car and ICS networks.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at monitoring process variables, the measured values such as speed, temperature or pressure, to spot when false data is being fed into a system. The speaker contrasts hand-tuned threshold rules, which need heavy expert effort and scale poorly, with passive, self-learning monitoring. He gives a primer on CAN bus messages in cars, which carry up to eight data bytes with no built-in authentication, and a park assist example where spoofed speed and gear messages could defeat the conditions that normally block the feature.

The research team captured CAN traffic from a 2016 car and decoded candidate signals such as vehicle speed, engine RPM and turn signal states. Strong correlations between variables held steady over time, so they trained an LSTM network to predict speed from the other variables. When high-speed values were injected, the gap between predicted and reported speed grew large enough to flag the attack. A second prototype needed no protocol knowledge: it used five CAN IDs, built 40 single-byte predictors, kept the best performers and combined their errors into one weighted anomaly score. Training came from two ten-minute drives, and the score rose during the attack.

The speaker argues the same method could extend to Modbus and PLC-based industrial networks, using a four-variable process as an example. Forging several correlated variables at once is hard, which makes stealthy spoofing difficult. In the Q&A, replay attacks were raised as a limit because replayed data stays consistent with itself, and alerts need extra context before operators can act on them. The main takeaway is that learned relationships between process variables can expose tampering without deep knowledge of the protocol.

talks.title: Rogue Firmware Upload in PLC's and Other Field Devices
talks.teaser: Shows how PLC Ethernet cards accept unauthenticated firmware, and how web and FTP flaws expose field devices.
talks.summary:
The talk examines whether the Ethernet cards in PLCs and other field devices will accept attacker-supplied firmware. Daniel Peck covers black-box research on two devices, starting with a Rockwell Automation 1756 Ethernet module. Using a hex editor and a disassembler on vendor firmware images, the researchers found uncompressed HTML, recovered a VxWorks symbol table, identified a PowerPC processor, and worked out the two checksums, one for the header and one for the whole file, that guarded uploads.

The second device used a binary UDP protocol whose specification was found on an old consulting site, which let the team upload modified firmware as well. Web interface flaws allowed cross-site scripting that exposed config files with usernames and passwords, and one module shipped an undocumented FTP server that could be switched on by editing a config file. The speakers then described misuse ideas: delayed attacks, bricking cards across a site, a proof-of-concept field device worm, and using field devices as hidden footholds, much like printers on a corporate network.

The main advice is for asset owners to find out whether their field devices accept unauthenticated firmware uploads, disable that capability where possible, and monitor for it. Vendors should authenticate the source and content of firmware, ideally with digital signatures, and let users check what is running. Audience discussion noted that a short outage during an upload is hard to tell apart from ordinary network faults.

talks.title: "It Never Happened Before" 5 Minutes from Richard Clarke Keynote
talks.teaser: Explains why executives delay security spending and urges industry-by-industry regulation, citing the Ukraine grid outage.
talks.summary:
The clip opens with a common executive response to security funding requests: leaders ask for a return on investment and dismiss threats that have not yet affected their organization. The speaker counters that a grid attack was demonstrated years earlier in the Idaho Falls Aurora experiment, and that it later happened for real when operators in Ukraine watched a cursor move across their screens, closing circuits they could not control, and the power went out on a December night.

The second obstacle he describes is scale. Decision-makers see industrial control systems as too large to secure and too costly to change, so they stall. He argues the question should shift from whether something is likely to whether it could happen. His proposal is for governments to set industry-by-industry dates after which any newly deployed system must include a security package, beginning with healthcare, then electric power, industrial control systems and automobiles. Research would take place in the years before each deadline, and legacy equipment would be replaced over time.

The takeaway is that a single company or sector is unlikely to act alone, so regulation is needed for security investment to happen at scale. For practitioners, the clip suggests that security requests land better when they are framed around possible impact and enforceable deadlines, rather than only around past incidents.

talks.title: Applied Fiction: Training That Engages The Team
talks.teaser: A utility training program turns employees into story heroes as they explore attacks, choose defenses and build security skills.
talks.summary: The presenters describe a training program for utility employees that uses a fictional story, learner choices and a facility simulator to teach security concepts. They explain how the approach introduces physical and electronic attacks, lets learners explore defenses, and checks understanding throughout the training. They also report engagement results from 1,800 employees and discuss how storytelling can help people connect security practices to their work.

talks.title: ExxonMobil OPA Interview
talks.teaser: Explains ExxonMobil's push for open, interoperable process control systems and the business and support hurdles it faces.
talks.summary:
The interview covers ExxonMobil's Open Process Automation program, which started because many of the company's refinery and chemical plant control systems were facing obsolescence. Leaders found that proprietary protocols made third-party integration costly and that security had been bolted onto systems built before the internet. They set a vision for an open, secure, interoperable and portable platform, and when existing control suppliers resisted changing their business models, they recruited Lockheed Martin and built a coalition through the OPA forum.

Early results cited include the forum growing to 37 member companies within months, eight of them end users. A lab prototype, led by Lockheed Martin, is planned to test interoperability, portability, reliability and flexibility, with an RFP issued to suppliers. Much of the discussion focused on commercial questions: whether suppliers would lose lock-in, who would be accountable for integrated systems and support, and whether standard hardware and software could keep plants consistent over time. The proposed answers centre on a single systems integrator, independent conformance testing and public interfaces rather than fixed network designs.

A recurring point is that most of the required technology already exists in adjacent industries such as telecom, avionics and IT, so the hard problems are commercial rather than technical. The discussion closes with the program framed as a breakthrough effort, meant as a leap rather than an incremental change.

talks.title: IoT Botnets in 3 Minutes
talks.teaser: Shows how quickly exposed IoT devices get infected, and how Mirai, Hajime and BrickerBot fight over them.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with how fast an unsecured IoT device gets compromised once it is connected to the internet, with infection possible within minutes. The speaker describes an early Mirai-style botnet that exploits a weak default login, uses a clear-text command channel to its controller, and scans for new victims, so the network grows rapidly.

Next, Hajime is presented as using the same infection route but then closing the device's ports and claiming to secure it, while keeping the device under its control within a more sophisticated command network. The speaker estimates that around 300,000 devices are currently held this way and says Hajime's ultimate goal is unknown.

Finally, the talk covers BrickerBot, whose author calls himself the Janitor. He claims to have bricked about 2 million devices since October 2016, framing this as a form of internet chemotherapy against IoT-driven DDoS attacks. The speaker's closing point is that device owners and manufacturers should be held accountable when their devices are taken over.

talks.title: Innovative CIP Security Training
talks.teaser: Shows how a power-grid simulation and a packet-firewall game made security training engaging for 2,000 staff.
talks.summary:
The speaker explains that about 2,000 employees needed their first introduction to security, and that the early engagement numbers were poor. Only 4% of the workforce was engaged after the opening material, with 60% and 36% figures given for the rest, and 36% of staff had dropped out. The presenters concluded that traditional training was not working and combined an instructor, an immersive experience and a simulation to change that.

The main part of the session is a simulator set in a power grid, where robots take over the operator console and overload transmission lines. The simulator is also used to teach abstract topics such as how a firewall works, which cannot be shown physically. In the firewall demo, an authorized packet is checked by the intrusion prevention system and allowed through. A packet sent by a robot attacker then gets past the same check by claiming to come from a trusted corporate archival server, which shows that some attacks can trick a firewall.

After the simulation-based approach, the presenters reported that 83% of employees were engaged, and attendees said it was the best training they had taken. The takeaway is that organisations should upgrade their people as well as their systems. Engaging emotion and using story and fiction to fill gaps in technical understanding helps people remember what they learned.

talks.title: Applied Fiction: Training That Engages The Team
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Applied Fiction: Training That Engages The Team.
talks.summary:
Chris from Meta Mythic and Lisa from Arizona Public Service present their initiative to transform cybersecurity training through applied fiction—a methodology that makes learners the heroes of interactive narratives rather than passive recipients of compliance content.

**The Problem:** Arizona Public Service faced regulatory pressure from NERC CIP grid regulations to train 2,000 employees in cybersecurity for the first time. Traditional training methods—binders of procedures, 40-50 slide PowerPoint presentations, and 10-question quizzes—produced severe disengagement: 36% actively disengaged (intentionally avoiding training), 60% not engaged (clicking through minimized windows), and only 4% genuinely engaged.

**The Core Insight:** Humans are integral parts of security systems and require meaningful development, not dismissal as "stupid users." The speakers advocate upgrading the "wetware" (human knowledge) alongside technological improvements, drawing on the timeless power of storytelling—fables and parables have taught truth for centuries through fictional narratives.

**Applied Fiction Methodology:** The approach preserves three critical training elements: an instructor presence, immersive learning environment, and real-world simulation. Security professionals become the "sage" (Obi-Wan Kenobi figure) enabling employees as "heroes" (Luke Skywalker). Fictional enemy characters represent attack vectors blended with actual security threats.

**Technical Implementation:** Training opens with an immersive security checkpoint scenario (quarantine/access denial) immediately capturing attention. Employees personalize experiences by selecting call signs and choosing facilities to defend (substations, plants, control centers). They encounter approximately 12 attack scenarios—both physical (badge readers, eye scanners, body sensors) and cyber (USB drives, firewall packet inspection)—explained through narrative and humor. Learning occurs across 40+ decision points with point accumulation. Crucially, no pass/fail threshold was imposed, removing fear barriers and enabling continuous reinforcement based on detailed performance data by employee group and location.

**Results:** After training 1,800 employees, engagement metrics dramatically shifted: disengaged dropped to 4%, not engaged to 13%, and engaged reached 83%—far exceeding the speaker's initial 40% target. Employees voluntarily adopted the "defender" identity, reporting it as the best training they'd experienced. Even senior executives sent unsolicited positive messages.

**Takeaways:** The speakers emphasize three lessons: (1) systems include people—upgrade human knowledge as rigorously as technology; (2) storytelling is inherently human and proven effective for learning; and (3) security professionals must enable employees as heroes, not lecture them as failures. They invite listeners to join "the learning rebellion" and offer free access to training samples online.

talks.title: Why I'm Hacking My Own Heart?
talks.teaser: Follows a security researcher with a pacemaker as she examines her device's bugs, wireless links and failures.
talks.summary:
Marie Moe, a security researcher with an incident response background, explains that she received a pacemaker after a pause in her heartbeat left her unconscious. Her doctors could not answer her questions about the code running inside her body, so she started investigating the device herself. A technical manual led her to a second wireless interface, a home monitoring unit that sends logs to a vendor server, which she had not been told about.

Two incidents shaped her concerns. Shortly after implantation, a faulty upper rate limit, combined with a programmer display bug, capped her heart rate at 80 beats per minute during exercise, and it took about three months of manual testing to find the true setting. Later, her device failed during a flight. Cosmic-radiation bit flips in its memory triggered a hard-coded backup program that paced at 70 beats per minute, and the fix was a software change rather than surgery. Her lab has also examined home monitoring units from three brands. Separately, a battery failure affected 400,000 implanted devices from another vendor, which later received an FDA warning letter.

Her main message is that medical devices need more security research, open communication standards and clear requirements, along with more transparency for patients. She notes that updates are currently applied through a programmer during hospital visits, and asks who is liable when something goes wrong. She ends by saying the benefits of her implant outweigh its risks, and that she wants the technology made more secure.

talks.title: ICS Anomaly Detection Panel
talks.teaser: Panelists from ICS security vendors discuss how asset owners should choose among many anomaly detection products.
talks.summary:
A moderated panel, led by Dale Peterson, brought together representatives from Security Matters, Nozomi Networks and Claroty. It began by defining an ICS anomaly detection product as one that learns normal network, device, process and user behavior, then flags deviations that may signal an incident. The panelists questioned whether the word anomaly is too narrow, since many operational problems stem from human error, and they said deep packet inspection devices, signature-only IDS tools and standalone threat intelligence do not belong in this category.

Discussion then turned to when a buyer should adopt such a tool. The panelists agreed the answer depends on the use case and program maturity, since some organizations need asset and communication visibility before anything else. For selection, they suggested shortlisting by capability, then testing with the buyer's own protocols and packet captures rather than relying on vendor demos. Useful tests include early and late kill-chain activity, and alerts should be clear and carry context. Passive deployment was favored, though the panel debated whether active probing has a role.

On cost, the panel said maintenance is similar across vendors, while analyst staffing and training drive ongoing spending, depending on whether a SOC already exists. Outsourcing to managed providers was considered viable. Looking two to five years ahead, the panelists disagreed on how much machine learning will help, with some favoring rules built from recurring anomalies and others expecting better detection. They agreed that OT and IT monitoring should be combined.

talks.title: Cyber Process Hazards Analysis (PHA) to Assess ICS Cybersecurity Risk
talks.teaser: Explains how a process hazard analysis method can be adapted to rate cyber risk to industrial control systems.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces cyber PHA, a methodology for assessing cybersecurity risk to industrial control systems that adapts process hazard analysis, a long-established practice in chemical, oil and gas and other hazardous industries. The speakers explain how classic HAZOP and LOPA studies focus on equipment and human error and assume control systems behave as designed, so they miss deliberate cyber actions. Because control and safety systems often share HMIs, engineering workstations and networks, one vulnerability can disable several layers of protection at once.

The method, which draws on ISA and NIST guidance, treats control system zones and components as the nodes of a worksheet and turns deviations into threats, such as a control system failing to perform its expected function. Each scenario is scored on the same risk matrix used for safety, existing safeguards are assessed, and the remaining residual risk is identified. Chris, who has applied the process across a large plant footprint, describes how the output lets teams rank the many recommendations a study produces by cost against complexity, and gives a documented basis for defending spending to project managers.

Practical takeaways include assembling a core team that covers everyone who owns systems connected to the plants, bringing in an experienced partner who can facilitate and train staff, and starting with an as-built understanding and a high-level vulnerability assessment. A phased approach helps focus on the most important sites first, and the speakers suggest using the work to train IT staff who have never visited a plant. Results should be revisited periodically, since the threat environment keeps changing.

talks.title: Securing ICS in an IIoT World ... The Simple Solution
talks.teaser: Proposes a four-step framework for letting cloud vendors access ICS remotely without exposing the process to unacceptable risk.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that broad terms such as industrial IoT, and the NIST definition of a cyber incident, have grown so inclusive that they stop being useful for deciding how to protect control systems. The speaker argues that ICS should be secured by context, since a nuclear plant, a chewing gum factory and a small water utility with two IT staff need very different approaches. The focus is traditional SCADA and PLC control linked to cloud services.

Predictive maintenance can usually be delivered through a one-way device, but vendors increasingly want remote operations and engineering access. In one anonymized case, negotiations stretched over more than ten calls across a year before data sharing was agreed. The proposed approach has four steps. First, the vendor defines granular remote services and the owner judges the impact if that provider were compromised. Second, a perimeter device with deep packet inspection enforces only those approved actions. Third, that device is tested, ideally through vendor test reports. Fourth, allowed traffic is fuzz-style tested against PLCs and engineering workstations to confirm nothing crashes or misbehaves. Process safeguards, such as a physical switch that must be flipped before a remote command takes effect, can further limit the impact.

The closing warning is that ICS has repeatedly been connected first and secured later, as happened with corporate networks, Windows and virtualization, and unrestricted vendor access is hard to pull back. Owners should define services and their consequences before opening a connection.

talks.title: Cyber Physical Attack Engineering
talks.teaser: Presents a methodology for finding digital inputs that cause direct harmful effects in industrial plants.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from Stuxnet and argues that its real novelty was not its zero-days but its aim at the physical process rather than the control system itself. The speaker contrasts this with typical ICS intrusions, where an attacker gains control of a controller or HMI without a clear route to physical damage. He defines cyber physical attack engineering as applying technical analysis and experiments to identify digital attacks that produce harmful physical effects.

He then walks through the attack surface from the outside in. Taking over an HMI, abusing proprietary engineering interfaces that lack authentication, and sending Modbus commands usually offer limited physical risk because protection logic still blocks harmful actions. Manipulating control, protection or safety logic is far more serious, and so is tampering with sensors, since spoofed or miscalibrated readings can keep overpressure valves from opening while the legitimate logic keeps running. Stuxnet's overpressure and rotor speed vectors serve as the main examples. He also groups physical outcomes into catastrophic destruction, mass casualties through hazardous material release, equipment degradation, and product compromise, and suggests process transients and support systems such as lubrication as useful waypoints.

He closes by framing the problem as a maze from cyber entry points to physical exits, where defenders can find and cut viable paths. Existing safety analyses are a starting point, but they must be extended to cover malicious compromise. He argues that contractor laptops deserve more attention than they usually get, and he calls for a shared taxonomy and methodology. The main takeaway is that concrete, process-level risk findings are more likely to win the attention of asset owners and boards.

talks.title: Richard Clarke Keynote at S4x17
talks.teaser: Argues that unprecedented cyber disasters still warrant action, and proposes industry deadlines for securing connected devices.
talks.summary:
Clarke opens with a familiar boardroom problem: security teams ask for budget, and executives reply that the feared scenarios have never happened. He argues this view is wrong and lists events from the past year that were once considered unthinkable. These include a malware-driven power outage in Ukraine, the public posting of NSA attack tools online, and a half-billion-account breach at Yahoo that forced a renegotiation of Verizon's pending acquisition. He also covers a botnet of 450,000 surveillance cameras used against DNS infrastructure, ransomware that disrupted hospitals, and a San Francisco transit payment system hit by ransomware that let riders travel free while it was down.

He then draws on a book covering fourteen case studies in which experts predicted disasters that decision makers ignored, from Fukushima and Hurricane Katrina to the 2008 financial crash. He names "initial occurrence syndrome," the belief that something which has never happened before will not happen, as the most influential reason for inaction. A magnitude problem and the refusal to assign probabilities make it worse. Meanwhile cyberspace is becoming more hostile, tools once limited to nation states are reaching criminals and non-state actors, and connected devices keep multiplying without built-in protection.

His proposed remedy is regulation with deadlines. Industries such as healthcare would require security on devices deployed after a set date, with older equipment replaced over the following years, and he points to Y2K as precedent for a fixed-date effort. He is not optimistic that Washington will act, but closes by suggesting that a preventive rule could still be the first of its kind.

talks.title: The Drone Threat To ICS
talks.teaser: Maps the threat landscape of drones against industrial and utility sites and proposes a modified DREAD model for ranking them.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with Kevin Finair's work on Mesmer, a counter-drone platform meant to give operators airspace awareness and mitigation options against RC aircraft. He then surveys the drone threat with examples: commercial quadcopters carrying grenades and explosives in conflict zones, a fixed-wing aircraft with an improvised warhead, a model truck fitted with a rifle, and a drone with a chainsaw attached. Reconnaissance cases follow, including a paparazzi flight over a private island and a Zigbee survey that logged about 700 unique devices from the air.

To structure the discussion, he adapts Microsoft's DREAD model into a version he calls DREAM, which replaces the last value with a subjective mitigation score. He also borrows the police use-of-force continuum, arguing that responses to drones should escalate from detection to video monitoring to active mitigation, with each higher step demanding more cost and effort. He scored 25 drones using his own weightings, grouping them from ones he does not care about to ones he does.

He closes with forensics. Pulling logs from a DJI drone by powering it on in read-write mode is poor practice, and evidence that may reach a court needs forensically safe tooling. Because each vendor's log format must be reverse engineered, he calls for community tools. He shares his threat models for others to edit and urges organizations to build their own threat lists and response options through repeated internal discussion.

talks.title: Ransomware in ICS ... It Begins
talks.teaser: Shows how ransomware reaches industrial plants, using Brazilian factory and power company cases to explain recovery and response.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that attackers now chase money, and that industrial control systems have become easy targets. The speaker, who summarises yearly incident research from Brazilian infrastructure customers, says recorded incidents rose sharply in the latest year. Ransomware has existed since 1989, but its appearance inside plants is new. An Israeli electricity board case, with a demand of 1,000 bitcoins, shows the shift.

Ransomware is more damaging in OT, the speaker says, because it can lock supervision stations, engineering stations and historians, and it can spread through remote access or VPNs. The first case was a furniture factory in Goiás, where supervision and programming machines were encrypted. Production stopped for 15 days, with losses near 100 thousand dollars, and the machines were rebuilt without paying because the OT team had no healthy backups. The second was a Brazilian power company whose Windows SCADA machines were infected through a USB flash drive, briefly costing supervision and control. Operations moved to a secondary control center, and the attackers asked 300 dollars per machine.

The speaker urges organisations to prepare an incident response team with a written procedure that includes notifying authorities. A secondary control center lets operators switch over while infected systems are cleaned, and backups must be tested because they are the main technical route to recovery. Paying is a last resort, since attackers may ignore payment or deliver a faulty decryptor, and paying signals that more can be extracted. The talk ends with a warning that ransomware will keep getting more sophisticated, so defence in depth matters now.

talks.title: The Key Role of EPC's in Industrial Cybersecurity
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning The Key Role of EPC's in Industrial Cybersecurity.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In mega-projects across oil, gas, water desalination, and critical infrastructure, Engineering, Procurement, and Construction (EPC) companies play an indispensable role. These firms execute massive, multi-billion-dollar turnkey projects over 6 to 9 years. While asset owners increasingly require cybersecurity at the conceptual phase, EPCs often lack the core competencies needed to properly interpret, design, and implement these requirements. Using an analogy to "The Good, the Bad and the Ugly," the speaker highlights that cybersecurity across critical infrastructure fails not from bad intent, but from misaligned incentives, complex multi-tier supply chains, and a severe capability gap.

### Key Topics
- **The Structure of Industrial Mega-Projects**: Projects typically span 6–9 years across conceptual design, front-end engineering, detailed engineering, procurement, construction, and extensive testing (FAT, IFAT, SAT). While 64% face cost overruns and 73% experience schedule delays, cybersecurity represents a miniscule fraction of the total project budget despite carrying critical operational and safety risks.
- **Challenges Faced by EPCs**: EPCs typically operate under lump-sum (fixed-price) contracts with compressed schedules. While they have deep expertise in automation, piping, and physical safety, they struggle with IT/OT convergence, lack internal cybersecurity skills, and face difficulty differentiating between cybersecurity service providers.
- **Supply Chain and Subcontractor Realities**: A single oil and gas mega-project may encompass ~70 main systems (e.g., ICSS, power management, telecom, ancillary systems) from roughly 20 industrial vendors. While four or five large vendors have developed mature industrial cybersecurity capabilities, many smaller tier-2/3 component vendors lack any dedicated security personnel and cannot comprehend or address risk assessment findings.
- **The Scope Gap and Financial Friction**: EPCs frequently sign fixed-price contracts agreeing to broad owner security requirements without fully understanding the technical or cost implications. Years into the project—sometimes as late as year six—an independent security review reveals massive deviations between what was requested and what was built, triggering costly scope expansions, contract renegotiations, and project delays.

### Technical Details
- **Project Scale Example**: Based on a real-world $3.5B project spanning 8 years: over 4 million engineering man-hours, 50,000+ design drawings, 20 million construction man-hours, 66,000 tons of infrastructure, 250 km of piping, and 225 km of cabling.
- **Cybersecurity Review Scope**: Across ~70 industrial systems, cybersecurity reviews involved vetting over 1,000 IP addresses and more than 600 technical documents totaling over 220,000 pages.
- **Testing & Verification**: Security validation must span architecture reviews, risk assessments, Factory Acceptance Testing (FAT), Integrated FAT (IFAT), and Site Acceptance Testing (SAT).

### Takeaways
- **Build Internal EPC Capabilities**: EPCs must develop in-house industrial cybersecurity skill sets and integrate them directly into existing discipline teams (process safety, instrumentation, and automation).
- **Dedicated Project Security Roles**: Projects must designate a permanent industrial cybersecurity lead/role from day one to maintain end-to-end accountability across procurement and vendor management.
- **Form Cybersecurity Working Groups**: Asset owners, EPCs, and industrial vendors must establish joint cybersecurity committees early in the project lifecycle rather than meeting years into construction.
- **Engage Independent Trusted Advisors**: Similar to Project Management Consultants (PMCs), engaging an independent industrial cybersecurity trusted contractor helps bridge gaps across complex supply chains and oversee lifecycle compliance.
