talks.title: Identifying the Disgruntled Insider
talks.teaser: Shows how email psycholinguistics and a critical pathway model narrow a large workforce to employees showing insider risk.
talks.summary:
The talk presents a method for finding employees who may become insider threats by analysing their workplace email with psycholinguistic measures. The speaker, a consulting psychologist, explains that the approach grew out of therapy referrals and investigations, and that a recurring lesson was how little of an insider's behaviour an organisation usually sees.

The screening scores messages for negation, blame language, victimisation, and first-person references used when the writer feels acted upon. Each sender is compared with the mean and standard deviation of a peer group, and outliers are surfaced. Filters for employment content and keyword exclusions cut the noise. On one client dataset of about 63 million messages, the filters narrowed the set to fewer than 1 percent of messages and senders. Of 116 flagged people, a third were referred for fuller investigation, a third were placed in monitoring, and a third were false positives. A second framework, the critical pathway, was built from adjudicated insider cases and corporate cases to describe what people bring to a job, which stressors trigger their vulnerabilities, and which concerning behaviours appear along the way.

A developer case showed how risk can be tracked over time: two periods of elevated risk lined up with a poor review and family relocation stress. For anonymous threats, the speaker builds a writing footprint from errors, layout, style, themes and syntax, then compares it with suspects, using a rare shared misspelling as one example. The main takeaway is to pair the tool with technical indicators such as unusual download activity, keep scores transparent and reviewable, and work within a multidisciplinary insider risk team.

talks.title: Interview with Justine Bone of MedSec on St. Jude Disclosures / Short Selling
talks.teaser: Interview with MedSec's CEO about disclosing St. Jude cardiac device flaws and the unusual short-selling partnership behind it.
talks.summary:
In this S4 main-stage interview, MedSec chief executive Justine Bone discusses research into implantable cardiac devices. Over roughly 18 months the team examined major manufacturers, and St. Jude Medical's products stood out as the least secure. The weaknesses included missing or weak encryption and authentication, poor input validation in the radio protocols between devices, and hardware with easy access to ports and firmware, allowing root privileges to be obtained quickly.

The talk then turns to the unusual disclosure path. MedSec licensed its findings to Muddy Waters, which published a report and announced a short position. Bone explained that earlier reports from other researchers had been ignored, so the team chose a route intended to force accountability. The vendor responded with a lawsuit, while the FDA and DHS later confirmed the issues. St. Jude released an update for the home monitoring unit, but the implants remained unpatched, and a battery recall left patients weighing whether to disconnect their monitors. On the ethics of profit, Bone said cost recovery is acceptable, but funding research this way is not something to encourage.

The closing part looks ahead. Future implant firmware updates will need clear answers about who may deploy code and how it is verified, since the research showed that commands could be sent by an attacker. Bone's stated goals were holding the manufacturer accountable and giving patients the information needed to discuss risks with their doctors.

talks.title: Dale Peterson S4x17 Keynote Come Together
talks.teaser: Argues that ICS security is improving as vendors ship secure-by-design PLCs and IT, OT and management finally work together.
talks.summary:
Dale Peterson opens the S4 conference with a keynote built around this year's theme, coming together. He contrasts his frustration in earlier years, when the ICS community had seen little progress for a decade and PLCs were insecure by design, with a more hopeful outlook now. Vendors are starting to add signed firmware, secure boot and authenticated control protocols, so asset owners finally have a real choice when they buy equipment. Training has also grown, and broader frameworks such as the NIST cybersecurity framework push organizations toward whole programs instead of single purchases.

The core of the talk is three groups that need to work together. First, OT and IT: running a control system resembles running mission-critical IT, so OT needs IT skills for virtualization, storage and network management, while IT must adapt its support hours and respect control engineers. Second, operations and senior management: boards are willing to fund ICS security, but plant managers must bring risk to executives before an incident forces the conversation. He cites a food and beverage company that learned from peers and an electric utility whose board acted after reading an outside report. Third, the ICS field and related disciplines such as machine learning, cloud services, psychology for spotting disgruntled insiders, and threat and economics research.

The takeaway for practitioners is to bring IT skills into OT, make the funding case to leadership early, and welcome knowledge from outside the ICS community. He also outlines the conference's three stages, the main stage, a technical stage and a sponsor stage, along with the social events planned for the week.

talks.title: Project Basecamp
talks.teaser: Introduces Project Basecamp, a multi-researcher study of popular PLCs and the Metasploit and scanner tools released from it.
talks.summary:
This session opens a longer presentation on Project Basecamp, a research effort that grew out of a Black Hat talk on Siemens S7 PLCs and a press panel where experts agreed that PLC weaknesses were widely known but rarely addressed. The speaker compares the situation to the early web, when session cookie hijacking was documented for years until the Firesheep tool made it trivial and vendors moved to HTTPS by default. The project aimed to create a similar wake-up moment for PLC security.

Six researchers each received at least one PLC, drawn from the lab or donated, from widely used vendors including GE, Schneider's Modicon and Quantum, Rockwell Automation and SEL. They were asked to test attack categories informed by past vulnerabilities, such as custom firmware upload, and results were marked red for easily exploitable issues, yellow for harder ones, and green where attempts failed. GE devices fared worst, Schneider Quantum came a close second, and SEL devices showed no red findings.

To put the work in practitioners' hands, the team partnered with Rapid7 on Metasploit modules, with the first one for GE D20 password retrieval being released the same day, and with Tenable on Nessus plugins for SCADA devices plus a passive scanner that flags default credentials. The speaker presents the project as an early step, with the technical details to be covered by the lead researcher.

talks.title: Serial Killers: Ethernet/Serial Gateways Exposed
talks.teaser: Surveys security flaws in serial-to-Ethernet converters from Moxa, Lantronix, Grid Connect and Digi used across industrial networks.
talks.summary:
Serial-to-Ethernet converters link older serial equipment to IP networks in power plants, oil and gas facilities, point-of-sale systems and other settings. The talk explains why these gateways matter after a 2015 attack on a Ukrainian electric utility, in which converters were bricked and power restoration was slowed. The research tested devices from Moxa, Lantronix, Grid Connect and Digi in mid-2015, starting with a teardown of the Moxa hardware.

For Moxa, the custom processor and proprietary management protocols on UDP 4800 and TCP 4900 were the main concern. Some models let an unauthenticated user retrieve the administrator password and SNMP credentials, and a single oversized web request could crash the device. Lantronix and Grid Connect shared an OEM chip, and their default four-digit configuration password could be guessed without brute-force protection. Their firmware was unsigned, so modified images could be loaded. Digi's 1SP device allowed easy debug access and crashed on a malformed TCP header, and its Windows configuration tool had a buffer overflow triggered by an inflated length field.

Vendor responses were thin. Moxa promised fixes that did not arrive in the stated timeframe, and Digi said it would not fix issues in that older product. The speaker's main takeaway is that proprietary management protocols are the biggest risk. Reverse-engineered protocol structure can support intrusion detection signatures, and blocking management ports at the perimeter plus monitoring traffic to them are practical defenses. The talk also noted that converters without firmware verification could serve as persistence points for an attacker.

talks.title: Problems with ICS Proprietary Encryption (or Encraption)
talks.teaser: Examines weak home-made ciphers in industrial control gear and why they give operators a false sense of confidentiality.
talks.summary:
Dashchenko, a penetration tester and ICS security researcher, argues that custom encryption in industrial control systems often gives owners a false sense of confidentiality. He opens with why encryption is hard to adopt in plants, where real-time operation and reliability worries lead operators to distrust new cryptography and assume isolated networks are safe.

He then walks through cases from his research. One SCADA product kept encrypted logins and passwords in a file, forced passwords to uppercase, and could be decoded by calling a single routine. Another stored credentials in the registry, and vendor documentation required the same administrator account on every network component, so one break-in could open a whole facility. A PLC used in critical infrastructure limited passwords to eight digits and scrambled them with a Caesar-style shift keyed to a built-in value, padding short entries with zeros. The weakest case was an XOR scheme: connecting to a remote port crashed the controller, so only a physical power cycle restored it, and the flaw exposed credentials, allowed password changes and let unauthenticated users send commands.

Disclosure was also difficult. One vendor's technical manager would only open Office or PDF attachments, and another vendor took more than a year to patch, so the researchers turned to a national CERT for help. His advice is to avoid proprietary cryptography, rely on vetted algorithms and protocols, and treat home-made encryption as a red flag during due diligence.

talks.title: Brave New Industrie 4 0
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Brave New Industrie 4 0.

talks.title: Hardware Hacking - Extracting Information From Chips
talks.teaser: Surveys chip attacks from power analysis to transistor-level modification, with a case study of an embedded device.
talks.summary:
The talk treats chip security from the view of an attacker who wants to clone or reproduce a product. Examples run from pay-TV smart cards and printer cartridges to phone cables that check for authentic parts. The speaker argues that the protection a chip needs depends on its threat model, comparing standard microcontrollers, bank cards, passports and pay-TV cards.

The attack classes are grouped by effort. Non-invasive methods include power analysis, clock and voltage manipulation that causes faults, and probing bootloaders, update paths and programming interfaces. Semi-invasive work opens the package and uses infrared imaging of the die to identify a chip and locate its memory, along with laser fault injection. Fully invasive work means microprobing, reading opcodes off the bus, chemical staining to read ROM contents, and focused ion beam edits to fuses. Rough cost estimates run from tens of thousands of dollars for non-invasive attacks to 100,000 dollars and up for fully invasive ones.

A case study of an open-source USB and Bluetooth trust-anchor device, assessed against a stated threat model, showed that its programming interface could reset the chip, that read and write protection was never enabled so the bootloader could be patched, and that a built-in platform feature let an attacker load custom code, which the vendor could not patch. The closing advice is to keep secrets out of firmware, avoid identical keys across devices so one extracted key does not break every unit, add tamper resistance and evidence, and do risk analysis before design.

talks.title: The Next Generation Secure PLC
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of The Next Generation Secure PLC.

talks.title: PLC and Level 1 Device Integrity in ICS
talks.teaser: Explores how PLCs can prove genuine firmware and protect ladder logic through secure boot, HSM signing, and hardware trust boundaries.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames device integrity in industrial control systems as making it visible whether a field device still runs vendor firmware, untampered configuration, and uncompromised ladder logic and credentials. Past incidents illustrate the stakes: protocol fuzzing that corrupted flash and bricked gear, destructive firmware attacks on serial-to-Ethernet converters during the Ukraine power event, and remote vehicle research where a firmware update removed isolation between wireless interfaces and the control bus.

Defense must span manufacturing and operations. On the supply side, risks include substituted components, swapped firmware at the factory, or skipped security-enabling steps; on the user side, trade-secret logic and ICS participation secrets must stay confidential. The technical foundation rests on signed firmware verified at boot, a chain where immutable boot ROM checks the bootloader and the bootloader checks application firmware, with signing keys held in an HSM rather than loose software. Manufacturing should include negative tests so bad images fail to boot. User assets sit behind hardware-enforced trust boundaries such as Arm TrustZone or Intel trusted execution, using per-device keys so a lab attacker who defeats one unit cannot scale the break across the fleet.

Practitioners should treat IEC 62443 integrity expectations and explicit national PLC protection targets—including assumed physical theft for offline analysis—as design inputs. The closing message is that layer-on-layer software policy is insufficient; hardware roots of trust and lifecycle controls must be planned from early component selection so compromised devices fail visibly instead of becoming silent pivots deeper into the control network.

talks.title: Europe, ENISA and ICS Security
talks.teaser: Shows how ENISA supports ICS and SCADA security in Europe and walks through the NIS Directive.
talks.summary:
ENISA, the European Union's agency for network and information security, presents its mission to secure Europe's information society. It works through published studies, stakeholder engagement, training, the Cyber Europe exercise and policy implementation, producing about 50 studies a year. Its infrastructure work covers the internet, critical information infrastructure, SCADA systems, transport and health.

On industrial control systems, the agency's work began in 2011 with recommendations for member states. Last year it analysed the security posture of ICS and SCADA in critical sectors through stakeholder interviews, describing four different profiles and collecting good practices. A separate study examined telecommunications dependencies in smart grids to give operators a practical tool for risk assessment. This year's work extends the telecom dependency question to ICS, with an asset and threat map, a review of protocol vulnerabilities, three attack scenarios with a proof of concept, and mitigation guidance for owners, vendors and member states.

The talk then turns to the NIS Directive, which was proposed alongside the 2013 European cybersecurity strategy and was expected to enter into force in August 2016. Member states get 21 months to transpose it and six months to identify operators of essential services. The directive calls for national cybersecurity strategies, a cooperation group, a network of computer security incident response teams, and security and incident reporting duties for essential service operators and digital service providers. Operators in Europe should check whether these obligations apply to them.

talks.title: Attacking The Plant Through WirelessHART
talks.teaser: Shows how weak key handling and exposed debug ports let attackers join, spoof and sniff WirelessHART plant networks.
talks.summary:
The talk presents three months of research into how WirelessHART is implemented in process control plants, covering transmitters, gateways and network managers from several suppliers. The attack surface runs from field devices through gateways to the plant network and the control systems. Scenarios included impersonating a gateway and manipulating process values; supply chain attacks were out of scope.

The protocol walkthrough explained the join phase, where a device needs a network ID and join key before the gateway hands out the session and network keys. Join keys could come from default values published in vendor manuals, from firmware dumps, or from decrypting a captured join exchange. All transmitters tested used the same vendor system-on-chip with JTAG and on-chip debugging enabled, so firmware could be dumped. The team had pinpointed where the join key sits in firmware but had not yet extracted it. The data link layer only authenticates, while the network layer uses AES-128 CCM* encryption. A dissector was built by extending an existing Zigbee framework. In the lab, cloning a transmitter's identifiers let a device rejoin as an existing one, while a race to displace a live device was only partly tested.

The conclusions were that the protocol is well designed but its implementation has weaknesses, and that a compromised gateway would be severe, including loss of process visibility. Recommendations included physical security, regular key changes, access lists where supported, and key management checks during commissioning and maintenance. The presenters said vendors were receptive to cooperating on fixes.

talks.title: Shell's Approach To ICS Security
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Shell's Approach To ICS Security.

talks.title: Cybersecurity for the Factory of the Future and NextGen ICS
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Cybersecurity for the Factory of the Future and NextGen ICS.

talks.title: Defense Will Win (In ICS / SCADA Security)
talks.teaser: Argues that defenders can win against attackers in industrial control system conflicts by changing how success is measured.
talks.summary:
A common claim in cyber conflict holds that offense always wins, because an attacker needs only one success while defenders must succeed every time. The speaker argues this runs against history, where defense has repeatedly taken over in new arenas, from trench warfare in World War I to early air power. Industrial control defenders also hold natural advantages: they know their process better than attackers and can change systems without breaking in.

The central problem, in his view, is how success is defined. Today any impact on a control system, even a brief outage or a minor incident at a small water facility, is treated as an attacker win. He proposes asking whether an attack caused an unacceptable impact instead. Cases used to illustrate this include a one to six hour Ukrainian grid outage affecting about 230,000 people, which was costly but not catastrophic, and Stuxnet, which damaged centrifuges at Natanz in a way comparable to bombing. He also cites fraud thresholds and data breach prosecution rates as examples of accepted harm.

His recommendations cover three areas: cyber maintenance, meaning patching, inventory and manageable change rather than deploying technology that cannot be maintained; protection layers that attackers cannot reach, such as separate safety systems or a vibration trip on a turbine; and recovery time objectives that management accepts. In the Q&A, he noted that asset owners are adding requirements to vendors, and an anecdote about a national red team showed that basic hardening blocked it from reaching its objective.

talks.title: ICS Security Assessment Methodology, Tools & Tips
talks.teaser: Walks through scanning and testing tools and a methodology for assessing live industrial control systems without disrupting operations.
talks.summary:
This owner-operator assessment talk explains how to evaluate an industrial control system for good security practice and known vulnerabilities, rather than searching for zero-days. The speaker argues that online scanning is only one part of the work, alongside architecture and configuration review, policy checks and interviews with operations staff. Findings should be ranked by impact and efficient risk reduction, so a fragile single point of failure or an exposed DMZ system may matter more than an unpatched panel far from the network edge.

The middle section focuses on scanning without causing unacceptable impact. Where possible, test a lab or staging system first; otherwise use redundant units, pick quiet periods, and agree with operations which components can go down and how they would be recovered. Two examples show the risk: a port scan hit a firmware-upload port on a safety PLC and left it without working firmware, and a scan crashed a real-time server while its standby survived. For enumeration, nmap with protocol-specific NSE scripts sends legitimate commands to identify devices, versions and locations. Nessus is the main broad scanner, and the speaker recommends credentialed scans, learning the product's hidden settings, and custom compliance audit files. Metasploit and similar tools are used to verify findings or demonstrate exploits.

The closing advice is about follow-through. Look at the root cause of missing patches rather than just the list, prioritize patching for exposed systems, and patch everything at least yearly. Set recovery time objectives and test them, and remove single points of failure.

talks.title: Hacking ICS Via DNS
talks.teaser: Shows how lookalike domains, zone transfers and DNS tunneling expose or move data out of industrial control networks.
talks.summary:
The talk covers DNS in two parts: lookalike domains registered against industrial manufacturers, and DNS weaknesses inside industrial control networks. It explains common squatting styles such as typos, homoglyphs and bit flips, and why squatters use them for phishing, advertising or resale. A survey of 11 manufacturers found 433 squatting domains, though some were pruned because legitimate businesses also use similar short names.

Of those domains, 195 had mail servers, so test messages were sent to two addresses at each. 173 rejected both, 22 gave no bounce, and one lookalike domain accepted mail; months later the test sender received a fake invoice carrying a remote access trojan. Checks of 254 squat domains with live pages found redirects, 10 hosts serving Windows and Mac OS X malware chosen by user agent, 10 fake tech support pages, and a lookalike Schneider Electric domain that later redirected to the real company. Legal action is slow, so registering lookalike names is suggested as a proactive step.

The second part covers DNS servers that answer zone transfer requests, which in a Dow Chemical case leaked 50,000 IP addresses, mostly internal. It then shows DNS tunneling tools such as iodine and dnscat2 that let attackers move data out of control networks, a pattern the speaker says is common in assessments. Recommended fixes are to block DNS from control networks or forward only the corporate domain, and to watch for tunneling traffic with IDS rules.

talks.title: ICS Spear Phishing
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for ICS Spear Phishing.

talks.title: Mikko Hypponen Cyber Geopolitics
talks.teaser: Traces how borders, war and the internet shaped cyber espionage, deterrence and trust in vendors' technology.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a long view of how city walls became borders and how technology, from mapmaking to gunpowder and the longbow, has driven warfare. It then moves to the Cold War, which the speaker links to the origins of the internet as a military network. The speaker argues that most state-linked intrusions are espionage rather than war, and that calling them cyber war is misleading.

The middle section compares nuclear deterrence, which worked because tests made it clear who held weapons, with a cyber arms race where capabilities are hidden and attacks are hard to attribute. A hypothetical attack on a beverage bottling plant shows how publicly available plant details and staff profiles could be used against an operator. The speaker then turns to vendor trust, citing reported interception of Cisco routers, the Flame malware's forged Microsoft update signature, Siemens PLCs in attacks on Iranian nuclear systems, and questions about Huawei router flaws.

The closing argument is that customers need to know how their vendors relate to their governments and intelligence agencies, and that vendors who publish those policies help build trust. The speaker urges security professionals to shape technology based on trust rather than paranoia.

talks.title: Hardware Hacking Live at S4x16
talks.teaser: Shows how ultraviolet erasure of a microcontroller's lock fuses can expose locked firmware, and how to spot vulnerable chips.
talks.summary:
The talk treats firmware extraction as an attacker's goal and focuses on cheap, known methods rather than expensive lab work. The target is a microcontroller whose code-protection bits live in floating-gate memory. Such a chip is vulnerable when those bits sit physically apart from the code memory and the unlocked state is all ones, because ultraviolet light can erase the protection without touching the program.

The speaker demonstrates on a Microchip PIC12F683. The locked chip reads back blank data and only its configuration word. After the package is removed with acid, the die is examined and the memory arrays are identified by cell size, grouping and nearby charge pumps, which points to the configuration fuses. Black nail polish masks the program memory, and the exposed fuses are erased under a UV eraser for an hour or more. Once the chip is back in its development kit, the configuration reads as erased and the firmware can be read out and disassembled.

The total cost is low, needing a microscope, a hot plate, acids, nail polish and acetone, so a student with basic lab access could attempt it. Defenders can avoid the risk by choosing parts where zero means unlocked, placing lock bits in the same address range as the code, or using differential fuses. Metal shields and co-located lock bits offer weaker protection, since UV can reach the edges of shielded cells or partially expose flash.

talks.title: The Witch Doctor vs The Engineer
talks.teaser: Explains how failure analysis and state transition modeling can tie smart grid security controls to specific system functions.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that many security requirements for industrial systems are handed down without a traceable reason, which leaves engineers unable to show why a control was chosen or whether it addresses a real need. The speaker contrasts this with a scientific approach and points out that a widely referenced control catalog does not document how its controls were derived.

The middle of the talk follows work from ASAP SG, a Department of Energy research effort with utility sponsors, to write security profiles for the smart grid. The first profile for advanced metering relied largely on expert judgment and borrowed control sets. Later profiles added use cases, then a failure analysis that asked how each step of a function could fail, so controls were justified by the failures they prevent. A later profile found that about three quarters of its failures matched an earlier one, which led to a shared library of failures. For substation automation, where use cases would be too numerous, the team combines state transition diagrams with zonal analysis. A receive-input example shows which system states count as failures.

The closing section admits that the approach does not yet offer an empirical link proving that a given control mitigates a given failure, and that testing whether a control was implemented correctly remains an open question. In the Q&A, the speaker argues that tying controls to functionality moves cost tradeoffs to business managers, who can decide whether a feature is worth its required controls. The practical takeaway is to document scope, assumptions and failure modes so requirements can be justified and revisited when systems change.

talks.title: Langner's Stuxnet Deep Dive
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Langner's Stuxnet Deep Dive.

talks.title: Critical Penetration: Finding The Disaster Built Into The Plant
talks.teaser: Shows how to map physical consequences to controllers to find cyber-physical attack paths in nuclear and industrial plants.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with heavily guarded facilities, from a fictional space station to the Natanz enrichment plant, that fell after attackers studied their design plans and found flaws that look obvious only in hindsight. The speaker argues that nuclear safety systems were built around random component failure, so redundancy and diversity add little against a cyber attacker who can reuse the same code across redundant units.

A critical vulnerability is defined as a design feature that lets an attacker erode the operator's ability to prevent an unacceptable consequence, with the threshold set below actual disaster. The method works backward from consequences. Analysts map outcomes such as radiological release to physical objects, set critical constraints on them, then trace the physical dependencies and digital controllers that drive those objects. In a nuclear example, rapid coolant cooling could follow from disabling all feedwater heaters at once or opening all feedwater valves, a combined case that the design control documents, which assume random failure of one component, do not cover.

The Stuxnet case gets the same treatment, with constraints on centrifuge rotor pressure, rotor speed and resonance frequencies, plus the valves and Siemens S7-315 drive controllers that could break them. The final step is to identify control options, meaning which actuators an attacker can reach and how. The speaker urges defenders to run this modeling before attackers do, since an event outside the design basis could escalate faster than incident response can react.

talks.title: IronGate: Technical Deep Dive
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning IronGate: Technical Deep Dive.

talks.title: General Michael Hayden's S4x16 Keynote
talks.teaser: A former NSA and CIA director argues that cyber policy trails technology and that the private sector must lead the defense.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In his keynote address at S4x16, General Michael Hayden (former Director of the CIA, Director of the NSA, and Principal Deputy Director of National Intelligence) sets out a broad strategic, historical, and policy perspective on cyber defense. Emphasizing that he speaks as a former government official and liberal arts history major rather than a technical specialist, Hayden explores why cybersecurity remains fundamentally difficult to solve from a governance and policy standpoint.

### Key Topics
- **Cyber as a Warfighting Domain**: Hayden traces the doctrinal shift in the U.S. military recognizing cyberspace alongside land, sea, air, and space. Unlike natural domains, cyberspace is entirely man-made, originally architected by pioneers like Vint Cerf for ARPA to move large volumes of data quickly among a small group of trusted, known nodes—making modern defense structurally challenging.
- **Threat Landscape Taxonomy**: Hayden outlines the evolution of threat actors (nation states, criminal gangs, and hacktivists) and attacks. While early activities focused on information theft, threats have escalated down the taxonomy to network corruption, data destruction, and physical-world disruption (e.g., Stuxnet destroying centrifuges at Natanz, attacks on Sony Pictures and Sands Casino, and electrical grid incidents in Ukraine).
- **Nation-State vs. Rogue Actors**: Disagreeing with dramatic warnings of sudden "cyber Pearl Harbors" from peer powers like China, Hayden expresses greater concern over isolated, sanctioned states with nothing to lose (such as North Korea, Iran, or an isolated Russia) employing destructive attacks or utilizing criminal proxies.
- **Government's Inherent Delays**: Hayden argues government will be "permanently late to need" due to bureaucratic sclerosis, the rapid pace of technological change, and political-cultural ambivalence about surveillance and state power in the digital sphere.
- **Policy Responses and International Tensions**: Hayden reviews recent steps such as cybersecurity information-sharing legislation, executive orders imposing economic sanctions for commercial cyber espionage, DOD cyber strategy (including counter-battery responses to catastrophic attacks), and Xi Jinping's bilateral commitment regarding commercial theft. He also critiques the European Court of Justice's Safe Harbor ruling and differences in European governance structures, while expressing support for strong end-to-end encryption contrary to the FBI's stance.

### Technical Details
- **Evolution of Cyber Effects**: Threats have progressed from stealing data as a product or harvesting bulk records (e.g., OPM, Anthem, United Airlines) to data wiping and physical impact.
- **Physical Degradation Examples**: Stuxnet's destruction of roughly 1,000 centrifuges at Natanz and the disruptive attacks on Ukrainian power infrastructure.
- **Architectural Paradox**: The Internet retains its core protocols built for high-speed transmission among trusted nodes, while operating at global scale with millions of untrusted, anonymous endpoints.

### Takeaways
- **The Private Sector as the "Main Body"**: In military operational terms, Hayden concludes the private sector is the "supported command" (the main body) in cyber defense, while government acts merely in a supporting capacity.
- **Law Follows Technology**: Just as the expansion of railroads drove continental commerce, standard time zones, and the Interstate Commerce Commission, technological advancements and private-sector norms—rather than legislative mandates—will dictate the future of privacy and security.
- **Preserving Foundational Values**: Defenders and policymakers must avoid creating defensive controls, regulations, or precedents that undermine the open, unitary, and accessible nature of the web.

talks.title: Marty Edwards, Director of DHS ICS-CERT, Interview
talks.teaser: The ICS-CERT director explains how the program balances assessments, incident response and vulnerability coordination.
talks.summary:
The interview opens with the director's path from control systems engineer to federal leader, and why he took the role to gain more influence over security culture in the control systems community. The conversation then clarifies the branding: the legacy proactive program was folded under the ICS-CERT name, which now covers both proactive work such as training and assessments and reactive work such as incident response, vulnerability coordination and intelligence analysis.

A large part of the discussion covers measurement and scale. Current metrics mostly count activities like alerts, advisories and tickets, and he admits these do not show real outcomes. Assessments began as hands-on coaching with the CET tool and aim to help smaller companies start a security program. Because a small team cannot reach thousands of sites, remote assessments, partnerships with other agencies and aggregated publications are being explored. Incident triage weighs sector impact and whether a core service is affected, and the team sometimes takes lower-priority cases to fill gaps.

The closing points cover the mix of incidents on corporate networks versus control system networks, with attackers increasingly reaching the control layer through direct internet exposure. He also describes how vulnerabilities are coordinated, noting that the work depends on what researchers report, and he argues for advisories that state deployment scope and threat actor capability. The practical takeaway is that operators need dedicated control system staff, and vendors need better knowledge of where their products are deployed.
